papers.abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.
authors: Giannis Daras, Marios Papachristou, Adam Klivans, Antonio Torralba, Constantinos Daskalakis
bullets: Addresses SFT overfitting and catastrophic forgetting when post-training data is limited.
Uses a frozen pretrained model as a noisy teacher and matches softened conditional distributions.
The temperature controls trust in the pretrained model, connecting regular SFT and knowledge distillation as limiting cases.
Outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, with up to 21% average relative improvement.
Scope: relies on temperature selection to balance adaptation against preservation of pretrained knowledge.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a data-efficient SFT method for autoregressive LLMs via temperature matching, directly relevant to language-model post-training.
papers.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
papers.tldr: Ambient SFT improves data-efficient fine-tuning by softly preserving the pretrained model’s broad predictions through temperature matching.

papers.abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
authors: Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan
bullets: Targets prompt responses for video-based agents operating over bounded histories.
Caches each frame’s recurrent-state transformation and composes transformations associatively as the window advances.
Uses a specialized data structure and GPU kernels to limit caching and composition overhead.
Across five hybrid VLMs and four benchmarks, it achieved the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 tests.
Reduced p95 time-to-first-token by 6.6× on average versus the faster of two vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of the hybrid VLM. Multiple input frames are converted into visual tokens by a vision encoder and passed alongside text tokens into a unified backbone. This backbone interleaves recurrent layers, which update a fixed-size state for each token, with attention layers, which retain per-token key–value entries.

Figure 8. Mean GDN state error. Relative Frobenius error averaged over each model’s GDN layers, comparing Spool with Spool without reconstruction against the vLLM reference. The evaluation uses all 9,000 Beyond3D questions.

Figure 1. Spool maintains a sliding video window without replaying retained frames. (a) Shifting the window retains four of five frames. (b) Prefix-cache invalidation forces the retained context to be rebuilt. (c) Spool composes cached recurrent transformations and reclaims key–value slots by moving surviving tail entries into holes left by eviction.

Figure 4. Efficient recurrent-state reconstruction with cached transformations. Spool caches each block’s affine state transformation and then replays them without the effect of a given block. A segment tree composes consecutive transformations, enabling reconstruction of the active window in O(logW ) operations. In this example, frames 5–8 occupy cyclic slots 1–3 and 0, with frame 8 wrapping around to slot 0. Spool first applies F5, then the combined transformation F6,7, and finally F8 to the prefix state Sp. This recovers the window state using only three cached transformations, without reprocessing video tokens or updating the tree during reconstruction.

Figure 5. KV tail filling and RoPE rebasing. Top: surviving tokens 11 and 12 fill holes in slots 1 and 2, releasing the final page; P denotes the fixed prefix. Bottom: filling changes storage slots while preserving position coordinates. A separate rebase shifts all cached positions by a common offset (−100 here) and rotates cached keys consistently.
Figure 3. Cost of window rebuilding. Here we plot time for a frame to be processed by Qwen3.5-9B on 1 A100. Every time the window must be rebuilt from scratch, a 29.2x latency cost must be paid.
Figure 6. Component ablation: latency per ingested frame (ms, ↓) as caching components are added, from a naive cache to the segment tree cache and KV filling.

Figure 7. Effect of state reconstruction on output fidelity. (a) Output KL divergence from vLLM-Omni remains near 0.04 through 1024 expired frames with reconstruction, but accumulates without it. (b) Accuracy gain (points) from reconstruction on PhoStream’s backward questions, which target earlier video content, grouped by expired frames relative to window size. Both variants perform identically before expiration; reconstruction gains 2.4 points after half a window expires and 3.8–4.7 points beyond two windows.

Figure 9. Per-layer GDN state error for Qwen3.5-9B. Relative Frobenius error against the vLLM reference for all 24 GDN layers, averaged over questions within each expired-frame bin. The evaluation uses all 9,000 Beyond3D questions and a 64-frame retained window.

Figure 10. Empirical CDFs of online TTFT. Rows correspond to Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Nemotron-VL Nano-12B, and Qwen3.5-27B. Columns correspond to PhoStream, StreamingBench, FastBench, and BEYOND3D.

Table 1. Online p95 TTFT (s, ↓). Spool can maintain real-time performance as live video streams in, achieving the lowest tail latency in all 20 model–benchmark tests: a geometric-mean speedup of 6.6× over the faster baseline and 33.8× over vLLM-Omni. Gains are largest on smaller models (0.34 s vs. 12.22 s on PhoStream with Qwen3.5-9B, 35.7×) and remain clear at the largest scale (0.33 s vs. 1.99 s on StreamingBench with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B). (Parentheses are speedup over the faster baseline.)

Table 3. Offline accuracy (%, ↑). Spool’s windowed state maintenance preserves the backbone’s answer quality: without timing pressure, it stays within −1.6 to +1.8 points of the more accurate baseline in each of the 24 tests and has the highest mean accuracy, 54.4% vs. 54.1% for vLLM-Incremental and 53.7% for vLLM-Omni. Combined with the large online gains (Table 2), this shows that Spool’s online advantage comes from answering on time, not from changing what the model sees. (Parentheses are percentage points change over the more accurate baseline.)

Table 4. Peak GPU memory (GiB, ↓). Each of Spool’s components has a modest memory cost: the segment tree trades 2.3– 4.4 GiB for 4.7–14.8% lower per-frame latency (Figure 6), and KV filling recovers 0.38–1.77 GiB of it while lowering latency further. Overall, the full system uses 9.2% more memory on average than the naive cache.

Table 2. Online accuracy (%, ↑). By answering on time, Spool drops fewer questions under live load and answers more correctly than both baselines where they fall behind. On BEYOND3D, it improves over the more accurate baseline by 3.6–18.4 points (mean 9.5), such as 30.32% vs. 11.94% with Nemotron-VL Nano-12B. On the other benchmarks, it stays within −2.5 to +3.6 points. Averaged over all tests, Spool reaches 52.8%, compared with 50.3% for vLLM-Incremental and 45.4% for vLLM-Omni. Questions dropped while the server is busy count as incorrect. (Parentheses are percentage points change over the more accurate baseline.)

Table 5. Online p50 TTFT (s, ↓). Spool’s latency advantage is concentrated in the tail: vLLM-Incremental answers typical questions quickly but stalls on a minority, which dominates its p95 (Table 1). Spool still has the lowest or tied-lowest p50 in 18 of 20 tests (1.9× geometric mean over the faster baseline, 32.2× over vLLM-Omni), with the largest gap on FastBench with Nemotron-VL Nano-12B (0.14 s vs. 2.66 s). vLLM-Incremental is marginally faster on StreamingBench with Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, by 0.01– 0.02 s. Parentheses: speedup over the faster baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Low-latency streaming inference for hybrid VLMs via state transformation caching.
papers.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Spool enables exact, low-latency sliding-window inference for hybrid vision-language models by efficiently removing expired video frames without replaying the full window.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.
authors: Gene Chou, Guandao Yang, Fujun Luan, Lars Mescheder, Wei Dong, Stephan Richter, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Existing autoregressive video diffusion models are too slow for fluid interactive experiences.
Profiling shows VAE decoding and KV-cache updates contribute over half of end-to-end inference latency.
FastFrames replaces these components with lightweight alternatives in a family of fast models.
The 1.3B model achieves 36 ms per frame on a single B200 GPU while matching a much slower state-of-the-art model’s quality.
The 14B model achieves 45 ms per frame on an 8×B200 node with significantly better visual quality and realism, enabling real-time camera- and physics-conditioned generation.

Given a single keypress, FastFrames is 16× faster to respond. Right: generation latency of officially released implementations and our optimized implementations. Figure 4 Qualitative comparisons. We compare FastFrames-S with Causal Forcing++ at 1.3B parameters and FastFrames-L with Krea-Realtime at 14B. Each example shows frames at 0 and 5 seconds. FastFrames-S achieves comparable visual sharpness to Causal Forcing++, such as the details in the sculpture (first example) and leaves (second example), while being nearly 8× faster. FastFrames-L achieves comparable visual realism to Krea-Realtime, including composition of “paper origami dragon” (third), and legible text of “stay curious” (fourth) while being 10× faster. See our website for video playback.

Only FastFrames meets an acceptable threshold (Deber et al., 2015) for seamless interactivity (≤ 50ms latency, equivalently ≥ 20 responses per second (RPS)) while matching or exceeding comparable baselines in visual quality.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
bullets: Studies whether agents need explicit instructions for how to self-improve.
Agents receive basic tools, resources, a goal, and a compute budget, but no prescribed learning loop or real-world data.
In gameplay, agents construct their own context-based self-learning algorithms and update text artifacts from collected experience.
Their strategies resemble self-regulated learning and self-generated curricula from prior cognitive and machine-learning research.
Learned artifacts improve performance across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay}, and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start (t = 0) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later (t = 60), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update.

Figure 7: Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection. (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k plays for each game (k ∈ [2, 6]). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED.

Figure 6: Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2.

Figure 8: Excerpts from a Claude Opus-5 teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses. In the first example (task-strategies) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second (learning goal orientation) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions.

Figure 11: Generalization with respect to progressively richer information, via context and toolsets. (Left) We run teacher sessions using Python Gameplay with increasingly detailed descriptions of PuzzleScript-Narrow games. Performance initially improves both on the same games, and ARC-AGI-3 transfer, however at higher levels of detail transfer plateaus. (Right) We ablate the teacher’s toolset and Gameplay constraints; performance initially improves on both PuzzleScript-t20 and PuzzleScript-t30 with richer toolsets, however declines on PuzzleScript-t30 after adding t20-specific token and turn budgets. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 5: Algorithmically measured behaviors. (Left: Game play and design) Newer models more often use A/B Testing (generated games played with and without teacher-written artifacts) and produce fewer games that have low complexity and low difficulty (optimal solution length < 5 and 100% teacher-observed win rate). (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM, newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. For Opus and GLM, newer models prefer smaller context updates.

Figure 9: Improvements from self-organized learning transfer across benchmarks. Player performance is evaluated at intermediate context updates along the self-learning trajectory on PuzzleScript-t20, PuzzleScript-t30, ARCAGI-L1 and MazeBench. The context optimized under our canonical setting, Gameplay (PS-t20), improves over the unoptimized baseline (dashed line) on PuzzleScript games with both 20- and 30-turn horizons. These gains transfer to different game engines and representations in ARC-AGI-L1 and MazeBench. We also compare progressively richer teacher toolsets, starting from Read/Write, adding Bash, and then PuzzleScript-Gameplay tools. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 4: Recent models self-improve. Results on PuzzleScript-t20 for two models in each family. Newer generations self-improve over the baseline while older generations fail to do so. Error bars are ±1 SD over 3 seeds.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.tldr: Sufficiently capable LLM agents can autonomously devise self-improvement strategies and transfer what they learn across diverse gameplay tasks.

papers.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.
authors: Pranav Gupta, Deepan Muthirayan, Ravi Banavar
bullets: Addresses prediction errors in DDPC caused by nonlinear manipulator dynamics.
Uses a mechanical model to map virtual accelerations to torques, with recorded data capturing residual dynamics.
Robustly optimises prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball around the fitted trajectory subspace.
In planar 2R simulations, it tracks better than double-integrator MPC but requires greater torque effort.
Performance compared with direct regularised DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.

papers.abstract: Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.

papers.abstract: Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.

papers.abstract: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.

papers.abstract: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.

Its advantage over the better kinematic model remained 24–30% for straight motion and turns at every frequency; for pedestrians, CV was more accurate.
A 10 Hz-trained model with interpolation nearly matched frequency-specific training down to 2 Hz but was 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz; hypotheses were only partly supported.

papers.abstract: Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual

papers.abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.
authors: Almog Anschel, Sarah Keren
bullets: Addresses the limitations of symbolic recognizers and methods requiring hard-to-transfer dynamics models.
Learns a trajectory prior and runs a warm-started denoising process for each candidate goal.
Steers samples toward observed motion using a closed-form likelihood gradient, then applies Bayes’ rule to estimate goal posteriors.
Evaluated on simulated robots, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories with four metrics covering distinct failure modes.
Preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs during ambiguous trajectory prefixes, unlike filter- and classifier-based observers that may collapse or become overconfident.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Four metric trade-offs across the five evaluation domains. Each panel scatters one point per (method, domain) for the six methods over the five domains. Colour identifies the method; marker shape identifies the domain (legend below). WORD points carry a thicker outline. The desirable corner is bottom-right in every panel; panel (d) reverses the x-axis so lower Brier still points right.

Figure 2: WORD online inference on a 2-goal synthetic scenario. An agent (green) starts at the bottom of a 10× 10 world and must reach one of two goals separated by a circular obstacle; WORD maintains one denoising chain per candidate goal and updates a posterior as observations arrive. (a) Prior. Before any observation, the score network ϵθ shapes Gaussian noise into two obstacle-aware trajectory clusters, one towards each waypoint, and the goal prior is uniform. (b) Ambiguity. The agent has skirted the lower edge of the obstacle but its heading is still consistent with both goals; both clusters survive and the posterior remains nearly balanced. A filtering baseline would already have collapsed onto one mode here. (c) Observation guidance. Once the agent commits left of the obstacle, the score-guidance term ∇τ log p(Z | τ ) (orange) pins each chain to the observed path; the right cluster must arc awkwardly over the obstacle to remain reachable, and posterior mass shifts toward w1. (d) Commitment. As the agent approaches w1, the surviving chain dominates and the posterior collapses. Pseudocode is in algorithm 1.

At this point, the past path and the current heading remain consistent with two of the exits (green w1, red w2) so a faithful belief over the agent’s goal must keep both alive until later observations rule one out.

papers.title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
papers.tldr: WoRD uses diffusion-based trajectory inference to maintain calibrated, multimodal beliefs about an agent’s goal from partial motion observations.

papers.abstract: Abstracting structured buildings from limited observations is essential for 3D urban modeling and digital twins. Partial point clouds and overhead images of the same building provide incomplete 3D surface measurements and visual cues to its footprint, roof geometry, and rooftop structures, respectively. This motivates a unified framework that aligns geometric and visual cues in 3D and reconstructs buildings from either or both modalities. Building on this connection, we present Any2Building, a unified model for Level of Detail 2 (LoD2) building reconstruction from partial point clouds, overhead images, or both, with optional coarse geometric priors. At its core is an occupancy-grounded shared spatial queries representation that organizes available observations within a common 3D grid. Supervised by complete building surface voxels, these queries connect observational evidence to target geometry, enabling a shared generator to learn structural priors across tasks and providing spatial guidance for recovering missing structure. A trained voxel conditional surface-generation and low-poly remeshing pipeline then converts the predicted structure into compact LoD2 building models. To support this framework, we introduce BuildingWorld-Image, comprising approximately one million paired samples of partial point clouds, overhead images, and LoD2 building models across 18 cities. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Any2Building outperforms existing methods in geometric reconstruction accuracy across unimodal and multimodal point-cloud completion, single-image building generation, and prior-assisted generation, while maintaining detailed and robust recovery when point cloud input modality is degraded.
authors: Hongye Hou, Zhuoxiao Li, Liu Xiangyu, Tengxi Wang, Jing Ou, Dongli Wu, Shuai Zhang, Tongyan Hua, Wufan Zhao
bullets: Addresses incomplete building reconstruction for 3D urban modeling and digital twins.
Uses occupancy-grounded shared spatial queries on a common 3D grid to align geometric and visual cues.
Generates building surfaces with a voxel-conditional pipeline, followed by low-poly remeshing.
Introduces BuildingWorld-Image with about one million paired samples across 18 cities.
Reports improved geometric reconstruction across unimodal, multimodal, and prior-assisted settings, including degraded point-cloud inputs.

papers.abstract: We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI. We release the dataset and code.
authors: Nhi Hoai Doan, Tatsuya Hiraoka, Munachiso Samuel Nwadike, Kentaro Inui
bullets: Proposes the Polarity Composition Hypothesis as a high-level model of negation processing in NLI.
Behavioral evaluations find predictions largely conform to the hypothesis.
Distributed Alignment Search identifies causally effective subspaces aligned with its variables.
These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI.
The dataset and code are released; transfer beyond the tested MNLI subset is limited.

papers.abstract: Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.
authors: Hansang Lee
bullets: Four public preference-optimized checkpoints name fewer object categories and show no significant set-level object F1 improvement on CHAIR.
A positive EOS logit bias makes the base model stop earlier and reproduces 58–86% of three checkpoints’ CHAIRi gains across two COCO sets.
Longer decoding does not restore the categories lost by preference optimization; negative EOS bias recovers little of the lost recall, with most added mentions repeating existing categories.
The proposed base-guided object-category restoration appends high-confidence categories absent from the optimized caption.
With development-set thresholds, restoration approaches base-model recall on held-out COCO while maintaining a lower distinct-object hallucination rate.

The gray curve is the base model with a positive EOS logit bias, and the vertical gap between a star and the curve at the same recall is the stopping-controlled gain. The short colored paths show each PO model with a negative EOS bias of up to 10, dotted where more than 5 percent of the captions reach the 512-token limit. papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and restores object coverage in preference-optimized vision-language models; directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Preference optimization reduces object hallucinations in LLaVA-1.5-7B partly by saying fewer objects, but base-guided restoration can recover missed categories without training while keeping hallucination lower than the base model.

papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.
authors: Mridul Mahajan, Xuezhou Zhang, Aldo Pacchiano
bullets: Inference-time scaling typically samples multiple responses from a single policy and evaluates them collectively.
The proposed approach learns $k$ stratified policies, each contributing one response to a $k$-sample objective.
The policies use separate LoRA adapters over a shared language-model backbone and are optimized for pass@$k$.
Linear analysis shows a policy population can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error even when each individual LoRA has nonzero error.
Experiments across multiple reasoning tasks consistently improve pass@$k$ versus a single-policy baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Pairwise Jaccard similarity between the sets of problems solved by each policy. Lower values indicate that a pair of policies solve mostly disjoint subsets of problems; a value of 1 indicates total overlap. ARITHMETIC, KNIGHTS-&-KNAVES, and SUDOKU show low overlap; the values for GSM-SYMBOLIC remain ≤ 0.9, which still shows non-redundancy in this harder setting.

Figure 7: (a) Scaling the rank of SINGLE by 5× (BIG-SINGLE) to match STRATIFIED’s total trainable parameters still underperforms it. (b) SINGLE is unstable on GSM-SYMBOLIC; the final checkpoint, SINGLE (Final), achieves a substantially lower score than the pre-collapse checkpoint used elsewhere. STRATIFIED does not exhibit this collapse on any seed. (c) An independently trained ensemble (INDEPENDENT) with matched total training compute underperforms STRATIFIED.

Figure 1: An illustrative example of stratification. With a fixed budget of five responses, i.i.d. sampling from a single policy may repeatedly sample the same solution modes (left). For five modes, the probability of covering all modes is at most 5!/55 ≈ 3.84%, which is attained when the policy assigns equal probability to each mode. In contrast, stratified sampling allocates one response to each policy in a learned population, which allows specialized policies to produce complementary responses (right); under perfect specialization, all five modes are covered with probability one.
Figure 3: We evaluate our method on a diverse set of reasoning tasks. These span constructing valid arithmetic expressions, logical deduction, constraint satisfaction, and mathematical word problems.

Figure 8: Comparison with UPSKILL on ARITHMETIC. (a) STRATIFIED outperforms UPSKILL, which uses an explicit diversity reward. (b, c) Operator distribution of each policy. Stratified policies achieve a comparable level of diversity to UPSKILL: different policies focus on different operators.

For ARITHMETIC, KNIGHTS-&KNAVES, and SUDOKU, mass is concentrated at low counts; this indicates that most solved problems are solved by only one or two policies (not the full population). Figure 2: An illustration of Theorem 1. Colored segments represent the regional target maps f⋆(x) = Tjx. A rank-1 population fits every region exactly, whereas the best single linear map Bx has an irreducible gap ε⋆ > 0.

Table 4: Pass@5 accuracy of individual LoRA adapters in our stratified population of five specialized policies, compared to SINGLE and STRATIFIED, with adapters ranked by their pass@5 accuracy. Even the best LoRA adapter in the population underperforms both SINGLE and STRATIFIED.

papers.selection_reason: Stratified LoRA policies for LLM inference-time sampling; relevant to language foundation model reasoning.
papers.title: Learning Stratified Policies for Inference-Time Objectives
papers.tldr: Stratifying inference-time samples across complementary LoRA policies improves pass@$k$ over repeatedly sampling one policy.

papers.abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.
authors: Chengqian Ma, Yuanze Zeng, Hongyu Wang, Mingfeng Lin, YiCheng Xiao, Yu Chen, Pengyu Li, WenHao Wang, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
bullets: Addresses spatial dilution of small moving objects and temporal loss of motion direction, speed, and event order.
Uses Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning to select anchors, while Patch Diffs encode changes between neighboring frames.
Dual-Road Change Memory, active motion ROIs, and Entity State Chains form dynamic, temporally ordered representations.
With only 0.22% trainable parameters on a frozen 27B backbone, VIVID-Small outperforms eleven baselines overall across 8,083 questions.
VIVID-Large achieves the strongest results on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass; the method is evaluated under limited-data settings.

Table 3. Component ablation of VIVID across MotionBench (MB), Video-MME (VMME), and TempCompass (TC), in accuracy (%) on the shared Qwen3.8 27B backbone (Kf = 8 reader frames; Overall pools all 8,083 questions).

papers.title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
papers.tldr: VIVID improves video MLLM reasoning under limited frame budgets by preserving localized visual changes and chronological entity dynamics beyond static keyframes.

papers.abstract: $\pi^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $\pi^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
authors: Yifan Wang, Weiguang Zhao, Ni Yang, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
bullets: Recovers dense geometry, camera poses, metric scale, point tracks, and moving-object masks from single- or multi-image inputs.
Uses a geometry branch plus a geometry-conditioned motion branch that lifts image correspondences into 3D.
Achieves the best overall average rank on geometry benchmarks and competitive 2D/3D tracking and segmentation performance.
The full system has about 0.5B parameters and can process scenes with thousands of images despite training on at most 64 views.
The paper also describes its data and training recipe, design studies, and releases code and models.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.
authors: Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, Yufeng Zhan, Wenchao Xu
bullets: Recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3), gripper states, scene geometry, and camera parameters from RGB videos with initial 2D TCP queries.
Uses a shared 4D scene representation for both tracking observed motion and generating future TCP trajectories conditioned on robot observations and language.
Introduces cross-embodiment augmentation by retargeting recovered motions and synthesizing observations without source-robot state recordings.
Reports 7.60 mm and 16.07 mm absolute trajectory errors on DROID and RoboLab, respectively, and 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin.
Joint training with source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

papers.title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: TCP4D unifies TCP tracking and future trajectory generation from monocular robot videos, enabling cross-embodiment data augmentation and strong manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.
authors: Dewu Zheng, Yang Ye, Hongyu Zhang, Jun Yu, Yanlin Wang
bullets: Introduces a dataset of 350 complete training-experiment trajectories spanning seven task categories.
Annotates individual experimental decisions for quality and masks supervision on low-quality behavior.
Evaluated with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench for autonomous post-training.
Training on RSI-Prime produces a 31.95% relative improvement over the original GLM-5.3.
The work focuses on developing model-training capability as a foundation for future RSI systems.

papers.title: RSI-Prime: Training Models to Train Models
papers.tldr: RSI-Prime trains LLMs to make better model-training decisions, improving autonomous post-training performance and supporting recursive self-improvement.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.
authors: Basavaraj R M, Harshal Chandel
bullets: Introduces GIB-200K, a benchmark of controlled retrieval noise, image degradation, and cross-modal conflicts.
Derives measures for text over-weighting (Knowledge Inertia), image over-weighting (Sensory Capture), and ungrounded clean accuracy (Grounding Illusion Score).
Evaluates four open models using measurement-error-corrected regression and counterfactual flip analysis.
Clean accuracy is high (92.5%–94.2%) but drops substantially under adverse conditions (41.3%–59.9%).
A retrieval consistency check improves reliability under misleading documents at the cost of coverage; image fallback is unreliable when images are degraded.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and quantifies grounding and modality weighting in retrieval-augmented VLMs, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model behavior.
papers.title: The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?
papers.tldr: The study shows that vision-language models often combine retrieved text and images non-ideally, becoming over-reliant on one modality when the other is noisy or contradictory.

papers.abstract: GRPO has become the dominant reinforcement learning method for eliciting reasoning capability in LLMs using verifiable rewards. However, it suffers from a fundamental failure mode: when a training question exceeds the base model's current capability, all generated responses fail and receive zero reward, yielding no gradient signal and stalling further capability expansion. An emerging class of GRPO extensions, termed Hint-Augmented GRPO (HA-GRPO), adds a "hint" to the context to reduce the difficulty of the question, thereby producing a usable gradient signal. Nevertheless, existing HA-GRPO methods share a key issue: no hint is available at inference time to append to the question, creating a training-inference context mismatch that leads to inconsistent performance gains. In this work, we reinterpret the function of hinting -- not as reducing question difficulty, but as steering model behavior -- and propose ASH (Activation Steering for Hinting), a novel HA-GRPO method built on this view. During training, the model is presented with both hinted and plain questions, while a trainable steering vector is optimized to widen the margins between the model's generation probabilities for responses to the hinted version relative to the plain version, thereby capturing the question-agnostic component of the behavioral shift induced by the hint. During inference, the trained steering vector is directly injected into the model's activation, reproducing the hint-conditioned behavior without requiring any hint in the context. Experiments with four LLMs (Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base, Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct) show that ASH consistently improves pass@$k$ on competition-level mathematics benchmarks (AMC, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AIME25) and out-of-distribution benchmarks (Minerva, GPQA-Diamond). Notably, it improves average pass@8 of Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base by \textbf{2.60}\% and \textbf{2.21}\%.
authors: Khiem Le, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla
bullets: GRPO can stall when all answers to difficult training questions receive zero reward, providing no learning signal.
Existing hint-based methods create a training–inference mismatch because hints are unavailable at deployment.
ASH trains on both hinted and plain questions and learns a steering vector that captures the hint-driven behavioral shift.
At inference, the vector is injected into model activations to induce hint-conditioned behavior without modifying the prompt.

Across four LLMs, ASH improves pass@k on competition-level math and out-of-distribution reasoning benchmarks; average pass@8 gains of 2.60% and 2.21% are reported for Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base.

(b) pass@k of ASH-trained models drops sharply without the hint at inference time. However, activation steering significantly restores it.

papers.title: Get Hint-Augmented GRPO Done Right Through Activation Steering
papers.tldr: ASH makes hint-augmented GRPO usable without inference-time hints by learning to reproduce hint-induced behavior through activation steering.

papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.
authors: Giovanni Adorni, Daniele Grosso
bullets: Recasts traditional NLP: language is not only analyzed or generated but also used to structure reasoning and orchestrate workflows.
Defines Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical extension centered on prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts.
Introduces Dialogic Working Memory, where prompts and conversational states temporarily externalize goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and reasoning states.
Relates memory architectures such as BTMA, SKGE, and RMR to episodic, semantic, and metacognitive support for long-horizon dialogue.
Argues for a post-symbolic, post-interface view of AI systems in which natural language combines communication, specification, cognitive scaffolding, and distributed memory.

papers.selection_reason: Conceptual framework for prompts as external memory and dialogic working memory; relevant to LLM memory architectures.
papers.title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
papers.tldr: The paper frames prompting as a form of natural-language programming in which language serves as an executable cognitive medium, reasoning scaffold, and distributed memory for human–AI collaboration.

papers.abstract: Model-based quadruped controllers usually step on a cyclic gait, which lifts the legs in a fixed order on a fixed period, wherever the safe footholds are. We present CADENCE, a learned step planner with a small action space. Every 40 ms, it picks one of at most 65 discrete choices: no step, or one leg's step to a safe foothold. It also predicts a swing time. We train CADENCE by reinforcement learning on top of a convex model predictive controller (MPC). Nothing prescribes a gait: there is no gait schedule, and the reward has no gait term, only a cost per step. The one structural constraint is that at most two legs may swing at once. The policy we analyzed developed an acyclic gait, with no fixed period or stepping order, yet it still paired diagonal legs. An inverse footstep model (IFM), fitted on a controller's logged steps, turns each foothold into a command. With only the IFM refitted, on fewer than 20,000 steps, CADENCE ran frozen on OCS2's nonlinear MPC. In simulated trials on a range of terrains (26% to 49% voids) and speeds (0.1 m/s and 0.2 m/s), it succeeded in 85.1% (mean of five seeds), against 67.8% for OCS2-Trot, 65.5% for OCS2-Single, and 39.6% in a static walk ablation of CADENCE. At 49% voids, it succeeded in 72.9%, against 43.0% for OCS2-Trot.
authors: Owen Sullivan, Sourav Selvaraj, Mahdi Agheli
bullets: Replaces fixed-period cyclic gaits with per-step decisions over at most 65 actions, including no step or stepping one leg to a safe foothold.
Uses reinforcement learning on top of a convex MPC, predicting both the selected foothold and swing time.
Imposes only a two-leg maximum on simultaneous swings; the learned policy nevertheless develops diagonal-leg pairing without an explicit gait objective.
An inverse footstep model enables deployment with a nonlinear MPC after refitting on fewer than 20,000 logged steps.
Across simulated terrains and speeds, CADENCE achieved 85.1% mean success, including 72.9% on terrains with 49% voids.

papers.title: CADENCE: Learning Acyclic Gaits for Model-Based Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: CADENCE learns an adaptive, acyclic quadruped gait that selects safe footholds without a predefined stepping schedule and improves simulated locomotion success across challenging terrains.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.
authors: Rose N. Kwon, Samy Mammeri, Sabyasachi Sahoo, Christian Gagn\'e, Thomas Jiralerspong
bullets: Narrow harmful-task fine-tuning can produce harmful behavior beyond the training distribution.
Inoculation prompting reduces this emergent misalignment but may leave the behavior conditionally accessible.
Textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete trigger predictor.
Prompts that induce activation states resembling the inoculation context are more likely to restore suppressed behavior.
Activation-space analysis may help detect residual vulnerability during evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Studies the re-emergence of misalignment after inoculation prompting, focusing on activation states. This contributes to understanding test-time behavior and alignment in LLMs.
papers.title: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting

papers.abstract: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.
authors: Qitong Wang, Jihui Jin, Divya Kothandaraman, Vishnu Raj, Christopher Rasmussen
bullets: Targets the cost of transferring and processing full multimodal representations on lightweight devices.
Estimates the importance of spatio-temporal video blocks and aligned audio windows using Monte Carlo Shapley valuation.
Uses query-agnostic embedding coverage to balance utility, cross-modal redundancy, and unimodal diversity under a token budget.
Retains original embeddings for reuse across multiple local questions, avoiding repeated media transmission.
Across three benchmarks and two models, it matches or exceeds competing compression methods; in one setting, it improves accuracy by 12.86–14.62 points and reaches up to 1.92× decoding speedup.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A server processes video and audio into a compact memory and transfers it once to a personal device. The device reuses this memory to answer multiple questions locally, keeping user queries on the device. To construct the compact memory, we propose a novel token selection method. Fig. 2 provides an overview of our framework and the proposed method.

Figure 2. (a) The server encodes audio-visual content, constructs token groups as players, and performs query-agnostic selection to build a compact multimodal memory. The memory is transferred once to a lightweight device and reused to answer subsequent questions locally. Selection considers unimodal utility, intra-modal diversity, and cross-modal redundancy. (b) Video players are formed from spatio-temporal token blocks, while audio players group tokens aligned with the corresponding temporal intervals. Colors illustrate example groups in each modality. (c) We estimate each player’s Shapley value by Monte Carlo sampling of player permutations using a weighted coverage function that captures intra-modal diversity through cosine similarity of embeddings (i.e., e). The weights incorporate unimodal utility, derived from token-embedding L2 norms as a proxy for semantic informativeness, and cross-modal redundancy, measured by cosine similarity between players from different modalities. Players with higher estimated Shapley values are retained, while lower-scoring players are pruned.

Figure 3. Each row shows the same sampled frames for a different method, with retained regions highlighted and pruned regions darkened. Our method better preserves key objects and complementary action-related cues across the displayed frames, including the skateboard, foot placement, and the demonstrator’s body. “Q” and “A” denote the question about the video content and its corresponding ground-truth answer, respectively.

papers.title: Transfer Once, Ask Locally: Compact Audio-Visual Memory for On-Device Question Answering
papers.tldr: A training-free method prunes audio-visual tokens into a compact memory that is transferred once and reused for fast, private on-device question answering.

papers.abstract: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. We theoretically justify the algorithm by analyzing the setting when the undo map is linear and the source is linearly-$Q^\star$ realizable, where our approach has strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the target MDP. Empirically, we demonstrate that these benefits extend beyond this regime: on challenging continuous control tasks and Atari games, our method achieves significantly better sample efficiency. Overall, our results highlight how shared structure between tasks can be leveraged for efficient transfer of policies across environments.
authors: Mridul Mahajan, Aldo Pacchiano, Xuezhou Zhang
bullets: Studies when transfer between source and target MDPs is provably beneficial under an exact state-space undo map.
Learns the undo map by matching state-feature statistics from both MDPs.
Transfers the source policy after recovering the source representation in the target.
For linear undo maps with linearly-$Q^\star$-realizable sources, achieves better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL theoretically.
Shows improved sample efficiency on continuous-control tasks and Atari games beyond the analyzed setting.

papers.abstract: Household robots often need to operate appliances, and smart appliances offer both control panels and device APIs. Existing embodied AI simulation environments, however, model appliances solely as physical objects. We introduce PAIR, a smart-home simulation environment grounded in the Matter protocol~\footnote{https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/matter/}, the industry standard for smart-home devices. PAIR provides 84 smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. From a survey of 1,443 requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that all require object manipulation yet remain solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Robots rarely get far enough to use the API: even with oracle plans and API access, over 90\% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3\% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency.\footnote{We will release our code and data upon publication.}
authors: Junseong Pyo, Hyeongjin Kim, Jongwook Han, Seungwon Kook, Sungjib Lim, Yohan Jo
bullets: Existing embodied-AI environments treat appliances only as physical objects, overlooking device APIs and functional control panels.
PAIR includes 84 smart-device assets with shared physical/API state and evolving ambient conditions.
It provides 40 manipulation-required tasks derived from 1,443 requests, plus 340 human demonstrations for policy training.
Two fine-tuned VLA policies completed none of 120 evaluation episodes; most failures occurred during navigation, grasping, or door operation.
Even with oracle robot control, the best planner completed only 57.3% of plans, and planners often chose API use based on panel readability rather than latency.

papers.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
authors: Yuanhao Zeng, Shaocheng Lan, Ao Lu, Kuang Yan, Heng Lin, Xinang Xu, Yuan Luo, Yueting Wang, Yexin Li, Ruo Shan, Kan Ren
bullets: The Resolution Hypothesis attributes evolution failures and inconsistent results to unreliable improvement identification.
At the candidate level, useful artifacts exist, but selection is roughly no better than random at distinguishing them from harmful artifacts.
Selection errors accumulate across evolution rounds, preventing reliable bootstrapping on some tasks.
At the method level, typical performance gaps are smaller than run-to-run variation, making rankings unstable.
The findings motivate evaluation systems that make genuine improvements detectable and accumulable.
