papers.selection_reason: Addresses the bottleneck of evaluation noise in self-improving agents. This is highly relevant to LLM agent evolution and test-time evaluation, offering insights into improving agent self-improvement loops.
papers.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
papers.tldr: Agent evolution is often limited less by generating improvements than by noisy evaluation that cannot reliably recognize and preserve them.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.
authors: Jason Liang, Dylan Waldner, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: The study tests four Schwartz value types across diverse coding tasks and repeated self-improvement iterations.
Openness-to-change values improve held-out performance, while conservation values can underperform having no value guidance.
Values alter the algorithms agents build, including their size, complexity, and overall approach.
Allowing agents to revise their own values reduces behavioral differences; values distilled from AI literature show no detectable benefit over none.
The findings support values as a way to shape agent behavior, with effects depending on task and value design.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of value statements on self-improving coding agents, relevant to LLM behavior and test-time adaptation. The findings on how values shape agent output are transferable to agent design and alignment.
papers.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
papers.tldr: Value statements in persistent instructions can steer self-improving coding agents toward different solution strategies and performance levels, but designing those values still requires human oversight.

papers.abstract: Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.
authors: Jiarui Guo, Saining Zhang, Jiaying Wan, Jiawei Weng, Junhao Chen, Rui Zhang, Yuanbo Lyu, Zhiheng Lee, Peishuo Li, Jingrun Du, Weiqing Xiao, Weiyi Lin, Zenan Meng, Hu Wei, Lin Qu, Zongzheng Zhang, Hao Zhao, Chaojian Li
bullets: Contains 83,365 assets across 485 categories and five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags.
Combines reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration.
Uses independent simulation verification with interaction conditions distinct from calibration to assess physical reliability.
Evaluates deformable responses, robotic grasping with object integrity, and sim-to-real replay for fragile-object manipulation.
Provides a scalable foundation for embodied robotic learning with physically realistic deformable objects.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a large-scale simulation-verified deformable object dataset and pipeline for embodied robotic learning and grasping.
papers.title: RFW-S: Everyday Deformable Objects with Independent Simulation Verification
papers.tldr: RFW-S is a large-scale, simulation-verified dataset of everyday deformable objects designed for physically grounded robotic simulation and learning.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.
authors: Bingjun Luo, Jialin Guo, Siqi Li
bullets: Uniform frame budgets overlook variation in how much visual evidence different questions require.
The authors find that question subsets favor different frozen frame-sampling policies, and more frames do not consistently improve every metric.
FrameRouter is a training-free test-time framework with an evidence-demand router, budget-constrained allocation, and frozen sampling-policy bank.
It keeps the average visual budget equal to a uniform reference while reallocating frames selectively across questions.
Experiments on Video-MME-v2 and other long-video benchmarks show improved QA performance without changing the underlying samplers.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models predict dense point maps from multiple images in a single pass. Without explicit geometric constraints, however, their predictions are often inconsistent across views and lack fine-grained precision. Recent methods incorporate geometric priors such as camera pose or depth, but use them merely as auxiliary inputs, process each view independently, or refine the geometry only where the priors are available. We present Refin3R, which refines feed-forward point maps with Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, propagating SfM geometry over the image grid. In its dual-branch architecture, a 2D branch extends SfM geometry beyond its coverage using geometry-aware backbone features, while a 3D branch reasons over the SfM points of all views, capturing multi-view structure that the image grid alone cannot represent. The two branches exchange information bidirectionally to jointly refine each view, yielding dense and accurate point maps. Across ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks\&Temples, and out-of-domain human and surgical scenes, Refin3R consistently outperforms feed-forward and geometry-guided methods in point map accuracy while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.
authors: Jongmin Lee, Jaeyeong Kim, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses cross-view inconsistency and limited fine-grained precision in dense point maps.
Uses SfM points as geometric guidance, extending them across image grids rather than treating them only as auxiliary inputs.
Combines a geometry-aware 2D branch with a multi-view 3D branch that reasons over SfM points.
Bidirectional information exchange jointly refines point maps for each view.
Reports higher point-map accuracy than feed-forward and geometry-guided methods across multiple in- and out-of-domain scenes, while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Refin3R. A feed-forward model provides dense depth Dff and geometry-aware features F, and SfM provides partial but accurate depth Dsfm (Sec. 3.2). For each view, a 2D U-Net refines the dense depth on the image grid, while a sparse 3D U-Net refines the SfM points of all views that project into its image, with both branches exchanging information (Secs. 3.3 and 3.4). A spatial propagation network (SPN) fuses their estimates into the refined depth (Sec. 3.5), which is back-projected into the final point map.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Each row shows one example from ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks&Temples, 4D-DRESS, and MVdVRK, with only one input view visualized. We compare a feed-forward model using only images (DA3), monocular depth completion (Any2Full), a geometry-conditioned model (Pi3X), and feed-forward methods with multi-view geometry (BLASt3R, GGPT), where Any2Full, Pi3X, and GGPT use the same SfM prior as ours. AUC@10 (cm; mm for MV-dVRK) is shown in each reconstruction.

Figure 3. Bidirectional 2D–3D interaction. The 2D feature map of each view and the voxel features of its grid exchange information along pixel columns. Top: In 2D→3D injection, the image feature of each pixel is broadcast to all occupied voxels in its column, providing the 3D branch with image context. Bottom: In 3D→2D gathering, the voxel features in each column are averagepooled along the depth axis and fused into the image feature map, providing multi-view evidence back to the 2D branch. Only voxels containing points of the current view (blue) are pooled, while those formed solely by points of other views (red) are excluded.

papers.title: Refin3R: Geometry-Guided Refinement for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Refin3R improves feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction by propagating SfM geometry through a bidirectional 2D–3D refinement network.

papers.abstract: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.
authors: Evgeny Alves Limarenko
bullets: CBCT typically obscures non-calcified abnormalities, which are usually assessed with MRI.
A two-stage pipeline combines anatomy-focused 3D masked-autoencoder pretraining with automated, targeted cropping of the temporomandibular joint.
In 212 paired CBCT–MRI joints, the approach detected synovial effusion with ROC AUC 0.793 using patient-isolated cross-validation.
The signal emerged only with the proposed physics-guided pretraining and captured 3D anatomical chirality and intra-patient consistency.
The study supports opportunistic screening of occult soft-tissue disease from routine radiographic scans, demonstrated in the TMJ.

papers.title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning

papers.abstract: Analytic continual learning replaces iterative gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pre-trained representations, summarizing all past sessions in two running sufficient statistics: the feature autocorrelation matrix $\Sigma_t$ and the class cross-correlation matrix $\Gamma_t$. Lifting backbone features into a wide random code of dimension $M \gg D$ substantially improves linear separability across tasks, but forces $\Sigma_t$ to grow quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Under a fixed persistent memory envelope $\Bcal$, a learner faces a fundamental structural trade-off: store exact pairwise co-activations inside a narrower feature code, or expand to a wide code while compressing cross-coordinate interactions. We observe that the coordinate self-variances $v_t = \diag(\Sigma_t)$ and class statistics $\Gamma_t$ grow only linearly with $M$, whereas off-diagonal interactions dominate memory. We introduce \method (\textbf{Co}ordinate-\textbf{Re}stored \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning), which retains $(v_t, \Gamma_t)$ exactly, maintains off-diagonal co-activations through a streaming rank-$q$ factor $F_t$, restores exact diagonal variances via $\Sighat_t = F_t^\top F_t + \Diag(v_t - \diag(F_t^\top F_t))$, and solves the full $M\times C$ normal equations via the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, \method matches dense full-covariance readouts within $0.09$ points while cutting persistent state by $90.7\%$ ($35.9$ vs.\ $385.3$ MiB). Under equal memory envelopes of $16$--$80$ MiB, prioritizing expansion width $M$ over covariance rank $q$ outperforms exact narrow readouts in $17$ of $18$ configurations by up to $+2.19$ points.
authors: Elena Voss, Pixel Nomand, Marcus Hale, Sofia Reyes
bullets: Analytic continual learning stores feature and class sufficient statistics, but wide random codes make covariance storage quadratic in feature width.
CoReACL retains feature variances and class statistics exactly while approximating off-diagonal covariance with a streaming rank-q factor.
A diagonal correction restores exact variances, and Woodbury identities solve the resulting full-width readout efficiently.
Across five benchmarks, it matches dense covariance readouts within 0.09 points while reducing persistent memory by 90.7%.
With equal 16–80 MiB budgets, wider feature codes beat exact narrower readouts in 17 of 18 configurations, by up to 2.19 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CORE-ACL at session t. I. Frozen backbone features are lifted into a wide sparse random code Φt ∈ Rnt×M . II. III. Exact diagonal variance restoration repairs the truncated covariance into Σ̂t, and a Woodbury normal-equation solve yields the full-width classifier Wt ∈ RM×C .

papers.abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

papers.abstract: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.
authors: Nguyen Quang Trung, Hoang Phan, Shuo Sun, Longyin Zhang, AiTi Aw
bullets: Targets multimodal reasoning across image STEM, image perception, and video domains.
Uses domain-specific GSPO-trained teachers and Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to merge their capabilities into one student.
Introduces M3OPD-SFT-1.35M and M3OPD-RL-193K, with verifiable rewards, and evaluates on 21 decontaminated benchmarks.
MOPD outperforms mixed-training baselines on average while closely matching each teacher in its specialized domain.
A subsequent MixRL stage further improves the MOPD student without collapse, producing M3OPD-Reasoner-9B; data, code, and checkpoints are released.

papers.abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.
authors: Hoang Pham Cong, Long D. Nguyen, Ho Viet Duc Luong, Nguyen Tran Minh Nhat, Binh P. Nguyen
bullets: Targets decision-relevant missed objects rather than relying only on image cues or uniformly increasing resolution.
Builds a decision-sensitivity field by testing how hypothetical objects at different locations would affect the planner’s draft action.
Repeatedly verifies the sensitivity field and the detections supporting the current action until the action stabilizes.
For two planner classes, it is theoretically equivalent to whole-frame high-resolution perception when crop detections and coverage conditions hold.

Across three driving datasets, it matches the full-resolution action on about 98% of frames using about one-quarter of the pixels, while reducing false braking and recovering more relevant missed objects.

papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
authors: Xinying Hu, You Wu, Haoyi Wu, Jianchao Tan, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Kewei Tu
bullets: mHC scales poorly beyond four streams because each sublayer broadcasts one output to every stream.
TPHC routes different mixtures of streams to each tensor-parallel shard and keeps shard outputs separate during write-back.
The method adds no parameters or FLOPs to attention or FFN sublayers.
On an 8B model, training takes 9% longer with four streams; increasing to sixteen streams adds 19% training time.
On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC lowers validation loss by 0.7–1.0% and improves six-benchmark zero-shot accuracy by 0.3–0.7 percentage points versus mHC.

papers.abstract: When a text-to-video diffusion model ignores part of a prompt, the usual first fix is to raise the classifier-free guidance scale. This paper is a measurement study of when that fix works. On Mochi, the same increase repairs failures on rare compositions ("a snowy beach") beyond what generating again does, does not repair negations ("a highway with no vehicles"), where it fixes fewer failures than generating again does, and changes nothing for events that must happen late in a clip ("a sandcastle that a wave washes flat"). Which of these happens can be known in advance, from the prompt and one inexpensive score. The score, which we call demand, measures how strongly the denoiser reacts to the part of the prompt that the failed video leaves out, and it is read from the first quarter of denoising, before any video exists. Our main finding is a condition: raising the scale is effective only when the prompt contains no negation and no event tied to a specific time, and when demand is sufficiently high, with recovery clearly higher above a fitted threshold than below it. Published corrections for the three failure types, used as fixed probes, behave as this account predicts. A short decision rule follows: before generating again, a user can tell whether the most common fix is worth trying, and what to use when it is not.
authors: Taewon Kang, Matthias Zwicker
bullets: On Mochi, stronger guidance helps rare compositions such as “a snowy beach” more than regenerating.
It helps fewer negation failures, such as “a highway with no vehicles,” than generating again, and does not fix events that occur late in a clip.
A demand score, computed from the first quarter of denoising, measures the denoiser’s response to omitted prompt content before video generation finishes.
Guidance is effective when the prompt has no negation or time-specific event and demand exceeds a fitted threshold.
The study provides a decision rule for choosing between increasing guidance and generating again.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.
authors: Haoyang Liu, Kecheng Liang, Xinyu Li, Weixing Chen, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses premise errors caused by applying physical constraints beyond their valid states or conditions.
Uses an inference-time visual harness that links scopes to observations and creates derived views for reasoning.
Maintains scope-aware working memory by checking revisions against sources and invalidating dependent conclusions.
Outperforms direct solving across six VLMs on PhysAlign; with Gemini-3.8-flash, it exceeds Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points.
Improves OOD performance on PhysUniBench, with ablations supporting explicit scope and dependency management.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models (WAMs) drop future prediction at inference, assuming that representations learned through auxiliary future supervision still benefit action generation. However, our layerwise analysis of Fast-WAM reveals a depth-dependent mismatch: while probes decode future state transitions more accurately from deeper visual layers, the gradients and visual focuses of the future and action objectives increasingly diverge with depth, leaving much of this predictive information unused by the action pathway. To address this issue, we introduce RelayWAM, which adds an explicit transition space between the video and action backbones. Conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, and current action estimate, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant predictive cues across depth and relay them directly into the action attention, without generating future frames at inference. Experiments show that RelayWAM substantially amplifies the benefit of future supervision, translating into stronger generalization under distribution shifts in both simulation and real-world robot tasks. On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM achieves 72.03% mean success, compared to 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.
authors: Fangchuan Wang, Hao Zhang, Qiyan Zhao, Huanqi Zhao, Guanting Ye, Xu-Yao Zhang, Yuqing Gao
bullets: Future information becomes more decodable in deeper visual layers, but its gradients and visual focus increasingly diverge from the action objective.
RelayWAM inserts instruction-, robot-state-, and action-conditioned recurrent transition layers between video and action backbones.
These layers extract predictive cues across depth and feed them into action attention without predicting future frames at inference.
The method strengthens the practical value of future supervision in simulated and real-world robot tasks.
On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM reaches 72.03% mean success, versus 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of RelayWAM and the representation–utilization gap. Left: Training-focus attribution reveals that existing futuresupervised WAMs suffer from an objective mismatch—action relies on local gripper–object regions while future prediction attends to the whole scene—whereas RelayWAM aligns both focuses. Top right: Linear probing shows that future supervision writes rich predictive cues (∆R2) into deeper Video DiT layers. Bottom right: RelayWAM introduces an explicit transition space to relay these cues to the Action DiT without test-time future generation, reaching 72.03% success on LIBERO-Plus.

Figure 4. Architecture of RelayWAM. Attached to selected intermediate and deep layers of the Video DiT, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant future information from visual representations conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, current action estimate, and flow time. The extracted cues are progressively accumulated across depth into action-aligned transition tokens Tl, projected into transition keys and values (K̂l, V̂l), and injected directly into the native Action DiT attention. This enables action generation to leverage multi-depth predictive representations without generating future observations at inference time.

Figure 3. Action and future supervision diverge across depth in Fast-WAM. Top left: gradient energy projected onto top-k action and future directions shows that the two objectives share subspaces in shallow layers (layer 4) but become nearly orthogonal in deep layers (layer 28). Top right: held-out future R2 decoded from action-sensitive subspaces drops well below random subspaces of equal dimension as depth increases. Bottom: training-focus maps on “open the middle drawer” and top-10% focus concentration averaged over five tasks. Unlike Fast-WAM (solid), RelayWAM (dashed) keeps both objectives focused on task-relevant regions.

Figure 5. Real-world apple picking on a Piper robotic arm. Left: qualitative rollouts under out-of-distribution apple placements with leaf occlusion (top) and colored ambient lighting perturbations (bottom). Right: success rates (%) across 20 trials per setting. Without any large-scale embodied pretraining (unlike DM0.5), RelayWAM outperforms Fast-WAM across all settings and maintains strong robustness under severe illumination shifts (70% vs. 15%).

Figure 6. Controlled 2×2 ablation of future supervision and the transition space. LIBERO-Plus success rate (%) versus layer20 future predictability (R2) across all four controlled variants. Adding future supervision alone (w/o transition space) raises R2 but yields only a +5.2-point success gain over the base model (w/o both), whereas introducing the transition space unlocks the utility of predictive features and amplifies the gain to +15.6 points (72.03% overall).

Figure 2. Causal erasure of future information in Fast-WAM vs. RelayWAM. We erase residual future directions from a sliding window of 4 consecutive Video DiT layers read by the action pathway, leaving the video backbone unchanged. Top: held-out R2 of the residual future decoded after future erasure (solid red) versus variance-matched random erasure of the same rank (dashed blue). Bottom: resulting action shift normalized by noise-resampling variance, plotted at the center of each erased window. While FastWAM (left) is insensitive to future erasure, RelayWAM (right) shows a pronounced action shift across intermediate-to-deep layers (layers 12–20), confirming active utilization of predictive cues. Shaded bands indicate 95% confidence intervals over episodes.

papers.abstract: Accurate shape estimation of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is a fundamental challenge in robotic manipulation, often hindered by visual occlusions and the high-dimensional configuration space of flexible materials. While Force/Torque (F/T) and vision-centric methods have been proposed, they frequently struggle with grasp-site ambiguities and environmental interference. In this letter, we investigate the hypothesis that global shape estimation can be achieved through tactile sensing and proprioception, without any visual perception. We contend that dense, high-resolution tactile imprints capture critical boundary conditions and contact gradients that are sufficient to resolve the high-dimensional configuration of the DLO. To prove this, we introduce a Physics-Informed Vision Transformer (ViT) framework that maps tactile images to a 3D vertex chain. By leveraging self-attention mechanisms and a physics-weighted loss function, our model enforces structural priors to ensure that the predicted geometry adheres to the object's physical manifold. Experimental results demonstrate that our tactile-based approach achieves superior reconstruction accuracy across Euclidean and Chamfer metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficiency of this modality, achieving model transfer to novel DLO materials and geometries. Our findings suggest that tactile feedback provides a robust and computationally efficient alternative for DLO state estimation in visually degraded or occluded environments.
authors: Rotem Atari, Stav Ashur, Avishai Sintov
bullets: Addresses visual occlusion, grasp-site ambiguity, and environmental interference in DLO shape estimation.
Maps dense tactile images to a 3D vertex chain using self-attention.
Uses a physics-weighted loss to enforce physically plausible geometry.
Reports superior reconstruction accuracy on Euclidean and Chamfer metrics.
Transfers to novel DLO materials and geometries, supporting use in visually degraded environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Architecture of the proposed ViT-Sparsh (ViT-S) -based shape estimation model. The system processes synchronous inputs from two grippers, each providing tactile images and gripper pose data. A ViT-based encoder extracts high-dimensional tactile features which are concatenated with proprioceptive embeddings to form input tokens. These tokens are processed by a cross-attention decoder to capture long-range spatial correlations between the two contact sites. Finally, a differentiable B-spline layer enforces geometric smoothness. The output is a spatial vertex chain representing the DLO configuration.

papers.abstract: Goal-conditioned planning with image observations and goals requires predictions that distinguish visual states and action consequences. Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and merge actions with different physical outcomes. We propose the Spiking Latent World Model (SpikWM), an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with one simulation step per image and one neural update per latent position. Spiking Regional Encoding retains spatial cues through regional pooling. Bi-Spike Action Encoding combines positive and negative binary responses, while Causal Membrane Prediction carries subthreshold evidence across the latent history with learned group-wise time constants. The encoder and predictor are trained jointly on reward-free image--action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg. With a common planner, SpikWM achieves mean success rates of $88.67\%$, $97.33\%$, $99.33\%$, and $86.67\%$ on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, respectively, outperforming two spiking baselines. Push-T ablations support each module, and controlled replays examine responses to appearance and physical state changes. Under a matched planning budget, SpikWM reduces estimated arithmetic energy by $75.6\%$ relative to LeWM. Code will be released at https://github.com/ShawnYE618/SpikWM.
authors: Shuhan Ye, Hongbin Yu, Chong Wang, Hui Lu, Jiaming He, Yi Yu, Jiangbo Qian, Xudong Jiang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting visually distinct states and differing physical outcomes from image–action sequences.
Uses a joint-embedding predictive architecture with regional spatial encoding, bidirectional spike action encoding, and causal membrane memory.
Trains end-to-end on reward-free image–action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg.
With a common planner, reports 86.67%–99.33% mean success across four benchmarks and outperforms two spiking baselines.
Reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 75.6% versus LeWM under a matched planning budget.

papers.abstract: Ensembles of diverse Large Vision Language Models have demonstrated performance beyond that of single models across multiple datasets and tasks. However, the necessary aggregation process usually relies on training, parameter fitting, or complex task-specific pipelines. Furthermore, evaluation is limited, making a fair comparison difficult. We create a unified pipeline where we perform candidate response selection: we build an ensemble by selecting the best answer from a set provided by different models. We comprehensively evaluate across 34 different means of confidence estimation, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. We show that simple training and parameter-free approaches can be sufficient, even for ensembles of different architectures. These simple self-assessment approaches rely solely on each constituent model's confidence, without explicit calibration, yet are able to perform better than said constituent models. They are also competitive with more involved alternatives on standard metrics such as accuracy, including on open-ended problems. However, we also discover that dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording are key confounding variables insufficiently explored by prior work that significantly affect ensemble performance, such that the ensemble can perform worse than its best constituent model. These must be optimized for to get the most out of ensembles, at the cost of limiting their generalizability. We recommend that practitioners consider training-free ensembles only if deployment conditions can be precisely characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models being a good starting point.
authors: Michael Smith, Frank P. Ferrie
bullets: The study uses candidate response selection to choose the best answer from responses generated by multiple LVLMs.
It evaluates 34 confidence-estimation methods, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications.
Training-free, parameter-free self-assessment can outperform individual constituent models and remain competitive with more complex methods, including on open-ended tasks.
Ensembles may underperform their best constituent model when dataset, model composition, or prompt conditions are poorly matched.
The authors recommend training-free ensembles when deployment conditions are well characterized, with Best-of-N strong-model setups as a starting point.

papers.abstract: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.
authors: Katarzyna Fojcik, Aidas Mikalauskas, Matthias Kampa, Renaldas Zioma, Jogundas Armaitis
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training deep logic networks and learning their connectivity.
Distills a trained ResNet layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving multi-bit residual streams and BatchNorm.
Uses hard LUT decisions during both training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap.
Reports strong results across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and 64px ImageNet, demonstrating improved depth scalability for LUT networks.
An optimized FPGA model achieves 90.04% on CIFAR-10 at 189k images/s; results depend on tree budget and shape.

papers.abstract: Failure avoidance in complex robot-environment interactions is challenging because the underlying dynamics are difficult to model accurately, and available predictive models may not provide reliable derivatives. We present Sim2CBF, a failure-avoidance framework that solves the Control Barrier Function (CBF)-Safety Filter (SF) optimization problem using only forward-model evaluations, thereby avoiding differentiation of the predictive model. Specifically, we approximate the CBF constraint using finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled control inputs while preserving failure-avoidance guarantees. The underlying CBF is implicit and constructed from backup-policy rollouts, enabling the use of expressive predictive models such as physics-based simulators and learned world models. Compared with purely sampling-based SFs, our formulation requires fewer control samples and yields less conservative behavior than direct nominal-backup blending. We evaluate Sim2CBF in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, demonstrating its applicability to contact-rich and learned dynamics, as well as its adaptability to changes in the predictive model.
authors: Luzia Knoedler, Yihan Liu, Shaohang Han, Yifei Dong, Jana Tumova
bullets: Targets safety filtering when complex or learned dynamics lack reliable derivatives.
Approximates CBF constraints with finite differences and local interpolation over sampled controls.
Builds an implicit CBF from backup-policy rollouts, supporting physics simulators and learned world models.
Uses fewer control samples and is less conservative than purely sampling-based filtering or nominal-backup blending.
Demonstrated in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, including contact-rich settings.

papers.abstract: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026
authors: F{\i}rat \"Oncel, Cem Subakan, Mirco Ravanelli, \c{C}a\u{g}atay Y{\i}ld{\i}z
bullets: Existing efficiency claims for kernelized attention often fail to reproduce against modern baselines.
FlashAttention generally uses less memory and runs faster during training and in vision transformers; causal-language-model inference is the main exception.
Under a unified distillation protocol, current kernelized methods lag softmax by 2–10 points, and scaling alone does not eliminate the gap.
LARA++, using importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy.
The remaining computational overhead means improved quality does not resolve kernelized attention’s efficiency disadvantage.

papers.abstract: Drifting, the deliberate control of a vehicle at large sideslip angles, is relevant to both motorsport and recovery from unexpected oversteer. Existing autonomous drifting methods typically determine drift intensity through predefined reference trajectories, optimization objectives, or learned policy rewards, rather than accepting a desired sideslip angle as an explicit input. We propose, to the best of our knowledge, the first generative drift trajectory planner explicitly conditioned on a requested peak sideslip angle. A conditional flow matching model is trained on demonstrated drift laps with hindsight-derived sideslip labels and refined through reinforcement fine-tuning. A control barrier function (CBF) correction is then applied to satisfy model-based road, tire friction, and actuator constraints at the planning waypoints. In closed-loop experiments in the racing simulator Assetto Corsa, a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks the generated plans for six requested sideslip angles from 20 deg to 45 deg, with 30 laps (approximately 75 km) per request. The median peak sideslip angle measured across drift-corner passes follows the requested angle, with a mean absolute error of 1.2 deg across the six conditions. Ablation experiments show that reinforcement fine-tuning improves conditioning accuracy, while CBF correction substantially reduces off-road and spin events.

papers.abstract: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Hao Zhong, Yanming Yang, Jiahao Tian, Lin Liu, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Yiding Tian, Chunhua Shen, Zhenzhong Lan, Chi Zhang

Supports adaptive control detail, plausible motion under coarse proxies, diverse camera paths, and efficient pipelined streaming.
Reports consistent gains over recent streaming baselines and stable 30-minute racing rollouts preserving scene and subject appearance.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) provide joint multimodal understanding and generation capabilities, making them well-suited to complex environments and promising backbones for next-generation AI. Despite these advances, the harmful stereotypes encoded in such models manifest in increasingly diverse forms, leading to broader and more severe societal consequences. Existing debiasing methods typically impose separate fairness objectives for each sensitive attribute and modality to minimise demographic-dependent variations. However, in omni-modal settings, this attribute-centric paradigm struggles to jointly address diverse social biases with distinct fairness objectives and to generalise beyond predefined attributes. To this end, we propose OmniDebias, one of the first methods for promoting fairness in OLLMs, which employs a bias-centric formulation to extract and mitigate a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities while preserving attribute-related knowledge. Specifically, we exploit activation inconsistencies of a given attribute (e.g., gender) across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate knowledge. We further consolidate multiple extracted biases into a shared representation, formulating a unified objective that captures the underlying structure across social biases and generalises to unseen attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eliminating unified bias with both post-hoc editing and fine-tuning can consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities in OLLMs while maintaining favourable utility.
authors: Runqi Lin, Suqin Yuan, Zihao Fu, Chris Russell
bullets: Existing attribute- and modality-specific debiasing struggles with diverse biases and unseen sensitive attributes.
OmniDebias extracts bias from activation inconsistencies across semantic contexts while retaining legitimate attribute-related knowledge.
It consolidates multiple biases into a unified representation and objective spanning attributes and modalities.
Post-hoc editing and fine-tuning consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities while maintaining favourable utility.

Bias-centric methods instead disentangle and mitigate shared bias while preserving legitimate attribute-related knowledge, enabling unified debiasing across attributes and modalities and facilitating generalisation to unseen attributes.

papers.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
authors: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
bullets: ExploitBench agents frequently stop with execution budget remaining, leaving their ultimate exploitation capability unclear.

SCoRe compacts context during stop bursts and marks such judgments as unproven, improving verified capability over evaluated continuation baselines.

papers.abstract: Natural language-guided UAV navigation enables intuitive human-robot interaction and flexible autonomous flight in complex environments. However, reliable navigation requires accurate instruction following, continuous task progress tracking, and safe obstacle avoidance, which remain challenging for existing world-action models that primarily focus on action prediction. To address these limitations, we propose a world-action learning framework that integrates three complementary mechanisms: a language-conditioned action interface with targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion, recurrent instruction-consumption prediction to track task progress and determine termination, and Gaussian-scene post-training to enhance obstacle avoidance through trajectory imitation and differentiable geometric feedback. Closed-loop evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate improvements in sequential task completion, safe goal reaching, and timely termination. Furthermore, direct one-step denoising reduces inference overhead, and real-world indoor and outdoor flights validate the framework's effectiveness.

bullets: Targets limitations of action-focused world-action models in reliable, safe language-guided UAV navigation.
Uses a language-conditioned action interface with targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion.

Applies Gaussian-scene post-training with trajectory imitation and differentiable geometric feedback for obstacle avoidance.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables post-training of flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies by optimizing expected task return through environment interaction. However, this optimization raises two challenges: policy updates can alter the velocity-field geometry underlying the score approximation used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts can yield uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs. We introduce an RL framework that combines Outcome-Balanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with policy-induced flow rectification. Outcome-Balanced PPO reweights positive advantages using task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while preserving their signs. Policy-induced rectification periodically fits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs generated by the current policy, refreshing the representation used in subsequent stochastic optimization. We evaluate the framework on simulated manipulation benchmarks and additionally study a component combination in a Real2Sim2Real task, examining task performance, optimization behavior, and flow consistency. The proposed framework improves success rates over the evaluated baselines across the simulated benchmarks.
authors: Yuhan Wang, Ruiyang Wang, Jiaguan Zhu
bullets: Addresses uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs in sparse multi-task rollouts.

papers.abstract: Our aim is to advance the understanding of genuine audio-visual coordination in joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation, with particular emphasis on semantic consistency. Evaluating audio-visual consistency in T2AV generation is nontrivial, as detailed text prompts obscure whether such consistency stems from genuine cross-modal coordination or merely from independent text following. To isolate the former, we introduce intrinsic jointness: the ability of audio and video to produce the same realization for details left underspecified by the prompt. Using semantically underspecified prompts (e.g., "musical instrument playing" rather than "electric guitar playing"), we investigate four recent models and reveal their limited intrinsic jointness. To address this limitation, we propose JointREPA, a simple representation alignment-based post-training method to facilitate cross-modal coordination. Since existing benchmarks use semantically detailed prompts, we introduce UNSAIDBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate intrinsic jointness under semantic underspecification. Experiments across two distinct models and three benchmarks, including UNSAIDBench, demonstrate that JointREPA consistently improves semantic consistency.
authors: Jihoo Jung, Ji-Hoon Kim, Suyeon Lee, Gia Thinh Pham, Joon Son Chung
bullets: Detailed prompts can hide whether audio and video coordinate or merely follow the same text.
Intrinsic jointness tests whether both modalities agree on details omitted from the prompt.
Evaluation of four recent models reveals limited intrinsic jointness.
JointREPA uses representation alignment during post-training to strengthen cross-modal coordination.
UNSAIDBench evaluates intrinsic jointness, and experiments show consistent semantic-consistency gains across two models and three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Detecting multiple reflection symmetries in 3D shapes requires aggregating geometric evidence over a large space of candidate planes, making traditional voting approaches computationally expensive. We introduce the Fourier Accelerated Symmetry Transform (FAST), a training-free framework that combines geometric pair voting with efficient spectral computation. Exploiting the fact that global reflection planes pass through the shape centroid, we reduce the search to plane orientations, while geometric consistency filtering and independent witnesses suppress unreliable pair hypotheses. Our key insight is to represent these votes as a signal over plane orientations and efficiently compute a continuous, smoothed symmetry field in the spherical-harmonic domain. Specifically, we exploit the Funk-Hecke theorem, the spherical counterpart of the Fourier convolution theorem for rotationally symmetric kernels, to transform Gaussian smoothing into multiplication of harmonic coefficients. This enables efficient field evaluation, from which symmetry candidates are extracted, refined, and geometrically verified. Across two benchmarks, including a new benchmark of highly symmetric shapes, FAST achieves the highest clean multi-plane detection $F_1$ scores among evaluated methods (0.861 and 0.947), with GPU inference below 4 ms per shape: over $100\times$ faster than the next-fastest evaluated multi-plane GPU baseline. FAST also demonstrates strong robustness to geometric noise and competitive single-plane detection, achieving 94.9% success on clean single-plane shapes.

papers.abstract: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.
authors: Steven Yu Tung, Shubham Vaijanath Phoolari, Christoph Lauer, Abhinav Valada, Steven Peters
bullets: Identifies intent leakage: uninstructed agents may react before an instructed maneuver becomes publicly observable.
Introduces a paired intervention test that holds the instructed agent’s trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction.

Presents CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator that limits interactions to publicly available beliefs.
Existing designs displace 23–83% of nearby agents through leakage; CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while achieving comparable WOSAC realism (0.763).

figures.caption: Figure 3. CaFe. The private stream conditions each agent on its own instruction, while a language-blind pass of the frozen backbone predicts public beliefs from committed motion. In inter-agent attention, an agent reads its own private features and the public beliefs of others, never their private futures or instructions. After each one-second commit, both streams update from the new observable history. The example on the right shows how public beliefs change as an agent’s motion reveals its intention.

Figure 2. Measuring intent leakage. We replay the instructed agent’s motion without its private instruction, compare surrounding agents across rollouts, and quantify leakage along two dimensions: the fraction of affected agents and their mean displacement.
Table 4. Effect of guidance. WOSAC 2025 realism, collision and off-road rates without and with guidance. Guided CaFe has 0.0% affected agents at 8 s.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' mobile manipulator robot, developed at the Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Shahid Beheshti University. Hereafter, this platform is referred to as the @Work Robot. The robot targets industrial tasks, with an emphasis on improving efficiency in repetitive or hazardous work environments. It uses a 4-wheel Mecanum drive for omnidirectional movement and a 5-degree-of-freedom manipulator arm with a 3D-printed gripper for object handling and navigation. The electronics consist of custom PCB boards built around ESP32 microcontrollers, together with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX that handles high-level processing and real-time system control. On the software side, Hector SLAM provides mapping and localization, A* handles path planning, and YOLO performs real-time object detection. These modules draw on fused sensor data to deliver robust navigation and reliable collision avoidance. Overall, the system shows effective hardware-software integration, with consistent performance in autonomous navigation, object handling, and task execution in industrial-like settings.

papers.abstract: Scientific document reasoning requires an agent to acquire and integrate evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables. Retrieval can identify relevant sources while missing complementary support, and answer-level feedback alone does not reveal whether an error stems from evidence acquisition or evidence use. We present an agentic Retriever--Perceiver--Reasoner framework for multimodal scientific document reasoning. The Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget. Given the selected evidence and question, the Perceiver constructs a question-conditioned latent ontology, an implicit organization of multimodal evidence in a shared continuous space. The Reasoner combines this latent guidance with the original sources to produce grounded answers. We train the three components through diagnostic-guided co-evolution: alternating updates optimize them with a shared answering reward, while Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) identify questions that need better retrieval or latent guidance and direct targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, our framework obtains average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.
authors: Frank Nie, Ethan B. Liu, Yuan Zhu, Jindong Han
bullets: Targets reasoning over evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables, where retrieval and evidence use can fail separately.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Motivation and overview of our agentic framework. Diagnostic-guided co-evolution further coordinates evidence acquisition and utilization through a shared answering reward and paired diagnostics.

Figure 2. Overview of diagnostic-guided co-evolution. (1) Diagnostic-guided resampling combines regular questions with RPF- or LEFselected questions for component-specific training. (2) Alternating component co-adaptation sequentially updates the Perceiver, Retriever, and Reasoner under a shared answering reward, keeping the other two components fixed at each update. (3) Paired diagnostic feedback uses RPF to compare responses based on retrieved and annotated evidence, and LEF to compare responses with and without latent guidance. Positive score gaps determine the feedback pools for the next training cycle.

papers.abstract: Conventional balance formulations often assume a rigid, stationary support, decoupling body stabilization from support motion. This assumption becomes inadequate on mechanically responsive supports, creating a coupled control challenge: corrective body motions intended to restore equilibrium can also excite support motion. We formulate sustained balance as a coupled regulation problem that coordinates equilibrium restoration with suppression of motion induced by the robot's own corrections. We introduce LISST (Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Stabilization), a learning framework that accounts for how earlier actions shape the conditions for subsequent corrections. It uses recent observations to support immediate adjustments and longer histories to characterize persistent motion, with physical supervision relating the learned representation to robot-support behavior. To evaluate corrective actions, LISST uses coupled dynamics to assess both imbalance and the direction of motion. A Lyapunov-inspired criterion measures progress over finite windows, accommodating the transients required to restore balance. This physical evaluation guides joint-level policy learning through backpropagation through differentiable model rollouts. Privileged guidance focuses training on difficult states reached by the deployment policy and is transferred through distillation. The resulting policy operates using only onboard proprioception. Real-world experiments demonstrate that LISST maintains balance while limiting residual oscillations during continuous interaction with a dynamically responsive support. Video: youtu.be/iGHU7S4wPyw.

papers.abstract: An agent or robot in a scanned building must locate its camera in rooms that no model saw during training. Point cloud registration methods can align each RGB-D frame with the building's colored point cloud, accurately but at a high cost. We observe that geometric refinement brings nearby initial poses to the same final pose, so the learned component only needs to find the place. Kolibri does this with a graph network of 55,712 parameters that describes 10 cm cubes of points, called cells, by their color, local shape and neighbors. With the same refinement, it matches GeDi on 96 unseen ScanNet rooms (81.4% against 80.3% within 5 cm and 5{\deg}) and on a held-out test of 10 further rooms, in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti. The saved time allows for search without a room label. In one point cloud of 100 rooms, Kolibri loses 1.3 points against knowing the room, while retrieving the room first loses 56.0. In a hospital emergency department scene from a real scan, it localizes 86.5% of the frames rendered from the scan in 384 ms each, where GeDi needs 91 minutes per frame on cubes of the scan for a similar recall. The method needs colors that agree between the frame and the point cloud. On gray frames and across cameras with different color responses, point cloud registration methods keep the lead.
authors: Leonel Aguilar, Bartu Tuncay, Christoph Hoelscher

Efficient search largely removes the need for a known room label, losing only 1.3 points versus room-aware retrieval in a 100-room cloud.
Performance depends on consistent colors between the RGB-D frame and point cloud; gray frames and cross-camera color differences favor registration methods.

papers.abstract: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.
authors: Elif Dorukba\c{s}{\i}, \.Ilker T\"urker
bullets: Encodes eight independent ECG leads with amplitude letters and exact time gaps; derives the remaining four algebraically.
Uses cardiac-cycle-dependent key-point selection, a learned 26-letter logarithmic codebook, and a 10-step tolerance schedule under a fixed token budget.
Applied to 21,388 PTB-XL records, all fit within 4,080 tokens and stored lead strings were exactly recoverable.
Decoded signals correlated 0.982 with references; classifier macro-AUROC was 0.9157 versus 0.9167 for original signals, meeting the stated non-inferiority margin.
The result is not confirmatory because the test fold informed encoder development, and LLM ability to interpret the encoding remains untested.

papers.abstract: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.
authors: Jie Chu, Haoting Shi, Fucheng Zhang, Jiawei Liu, Junwei Liao, Ying Wen, Muning Wen
bullets: Existing multimodal generators generally cannot perform symbolic reasoning over canvas text without an underlying text module or prompt rewriter.
The study trains generative models from scratch using only images as input and output, with no text pathway.
Models answer questions by writing intermediate reasoning steps frame by frame, which outperforms single-frame answering.
Scaling follows a predictable power law, and reinforcement-learning post-training further improves reasoning.
A shared canvas enables cross-modal reasoning, which text-only language models cannot provide.

papers.abstract: We show that an appropriate visual harness can substantially improve the performance of general vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse medical imaging tasks. We introduce \ours, a medical visual harness that equips general VLMs with interactive visual tools and systematic diagnostic evidence management. With \ours, general VLMs interactively explore medical images and progressively acquire diagnostic evidence, which is preserved in a lossless memory for subsequent retrieval and use. After submitting an initial answer, the VLM receives an assessment of potential omissions and the reliability of identified findings. This assessment guides further image inspection and measurement, followed by answer revision in an iterative agentic loop until sufficient evidence is obtained. Across 11 tasks and four imaging modalities, \ours improves performance on all tasks with Qwen3.8-27B, with notable gains in spleen measurement (63.3\% to 98.3\%), renal search (57.5\% to 71.2\%), and pulmonary nodule detection (0.0\% to 28.2\%). High-capability API-based VLMs achieve even higher performance with \ours. For example, GPT-6.1 Sol improves pulmonary nodule detection from 10.8\% to 69.2\% with \ours, demonstrating the complementary benefits of stronger model capabilities and an effective medical visual harness. Our results highlight the potential of visual harnesses as a new paradigm for scaling general VLMs to medical imaging tasks.
authors: Shaowen Wan, Hanqi Jiang, Zihao Wu, Junhao Chen, Weihang You, Ruiyu Yan, Bowen Chen, Tianming Liu, Lin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting general VLMs to diverse medical image analysis tasks.

Higher-capability API-based VLMs also benefit, suggesting complementary effects between model strength and the visual harness.
