papers.abstract: Existing agentic manipulation systems treat pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies as opaque, language-only primitives: when a policy call fails under unfamiliar instructions or scene perturbations, the agent cannot steer its behavior and is forced into futile retries or costly manual takeover. We present InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable and inspectable tools through a bidirectional geometric interface with vision-language agents. In the forward direction, test-time geometric guidance translates an agent-specified end-effector target into input gradients through the action expert via a differentiable command-to-pose mapping, while soft-time target alignment treats arrival time as a latent execution index to match the target pose without distorting the policy's approach motion. In the reverse direction, action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks and calibrated camera reprojections back to the agent, allowing it to diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise targets for subsequent VLA calls, or locally adjust motion segments on top of the guided trajectory. Making the VLA controllable not only boosts online agentic tool use, but also unlocks effective recursive self-improvement (RSI), achieving state-of-the-art performance of 99.4\% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62\% on RoboDojo, and 89.4\% on RoboCasa365. Project page: https://lingwupro.github.io/InteractVLA/.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Shifeng Bao, Yihan Lin, Haitao Shen, Yining Luo, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of treating VLAs as opaque, language-only tools under unfamiliar instructions or scene changes.
Uses bidirectional geometric interaction: agents guide VLA actions toward target poses and inspect action chunks with camera reprojections.
Soft-time target alignment matches target poses while preserving the policy’s natural approach motion.
Supports agentic diagnosis, target revision, local trajectory adjustment, and recursive self-improvement.
Reports 99.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62% on RoboDojo, and 89.4% on RoboCasa365.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. Across eight benchmarks spanning object detection, referring object detection, and document layout grounding, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIou among compared MLLMs on six benchmarks. It also delivers $2.07\times$ and $1.25\times$ the mean box-generation throughput of representative grounding baselines under vLLM and Transformers, respectively, while achieving higher accuracy in both comparisons.
authors: Zhaojie Chen, Junyan Yang, Le Yang, Qi Dang, Yucheng Huang, Qianyi Che, Zhaoqiang Chen, Xinqi Zhu, Qiang Zhao
bullets: Autoregressive coordinate generation is costly because each box requires multiple sequential decoding steps.
SemGeo uses a single grid token for coarse instance localization, then a geometric decoder recovers precise discrete box coordinates in parallel.
Gaussian soft labels encode coordinate distances to jointly train proposal generation and localization.
Reinforcement post-training uses model-generated proposals with box-set rewards and coordinate supervision to reduce the teacher-forcing mismatch.
Across eight benchmarks, SemGeo leads in F1@mIoU on six and achieves higher accuracy with 2.07× and 1.25× the mean throughput of representative baselines under vLLM and Transformers.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.
authors: Egor Shibaev, Danila Biktimirov, Ivan Klimov, Artem Makoian, Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Dmitry Vetrov

papers.abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.
authors: Irene Gos\'alvez-White, Roberto Mag\'an-Carri\'on, Carlota de la Vega-Soriano, Pedro Garc\'ia-Teodoro
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs can reliably extract packet-level fields and reconstruct flow-level sequences.
Introduces a reproducible question-answering methodology using human-generated ground truth.
Compares LLM performance on raw and protocol-filtered traffic representations from benign CICIDS2017 traffic.
Uses an automated LLM-as-a-judge pipeline validated against human evaluations.
Finds that filtering reduces prompt overhead and incorrect answers, highlighting its value for LLM-assisted network management.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are widely used as zero-shot image quality assessors, yet their good-vs-poor answers agree only moderately with human opinion. We ask whether these models fail to see quality or fail to say it. Layer-wise probes on five VLMs point to the second: quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and still from the last language layer, far better than the answer reveals, and about a hundred labels recover most of it. The loss lies mainly in the final read-out, which partly reads something else: relative to human opinion, it over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness on all five models. We test this by intervention: if the read-out is at fault, a closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron, fitted to many prompts at once, should close the gap and no more. Both hold. Under prompts never used for fitting, the edit recovers 86--100\% of what a ridge head on the last-layer state, fitted under the same prompts, finds beyond the answer on KonIQ. Where that gap is small, it gains little, too little for our transfer criterion on the two largest models; where the head itself is below the answer, it lowers the score; and it works only when written from the middle of the language model on. Unlike unconstrained fine-tuning, the edit leaves perception question answering intact. It does not carry over to yes-or-no or rating questions, and it reverses the good--poor contrast after sentiment-laden sentences. Code will be made available.
authors: Zhuangzi Li, Shilv Cai, Jian Jin, Zhiyi Pan, Haihong Xiao, Weisi Lin
bullets: VLMs encode image quality well internally, yet their good-vs-poor answers align only moderately with human opinion.

The method edits a single last-layer neuron using multiple prompts, without unconstrained fine-tuning.
On unseen prompts for KonIQ, the edit recovers 86–100% of the improvement available from a ridge head on the last-layer state.
The edit is prompt- and layer-sensitive: it does not transfer to yes/no or rating questions and can reverse judgments after sentiment-laden sentences.

papers.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
authors: Oleg Pavlov, Nikita Gavrilov, Soslan Kabisov, Gennadii Savrasov, Andrey Kuznetsov, Anton Konushin, Dmitrii Zhemchuzhnikov
bullets: Targets privacy and affordability challenges for practitioners handling proprietary CAD parts.
Decomposes reconstruction into sequential visual decisions about what to build and correct.
Uses geometric tools for precise construction while focusing the agent on visual reasoning.
Runs on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops and integrates with FreeCAD.
The authors report higher reconstruction quality than prior approaches across the main benchmarks, including frontier-model-based systems.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as world models for planning, yet a world model that makes plausible, realistic-looking videos that are consistent with the training data can produce poor decisions. We address two key questions: (1) when can we trust a world model for planning, and (2) what should we do when we cannot? We introduce CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore), a certificate-guided technique that assesses whether a world model can be trusted for planning and determines what to do next: whether to upweight the training data to debias the model; roll out more samples at test time; or explore by collecting new data where support (how well the training data cover the planner's decisions) is missing. We deploy CURE across multiple domains, spanning simulated physics based on PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table pushing in simulation and on real videos. The decisions our certificate trusts have lower regret than those it does not (e.g., 0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim and 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), whereas video perceptual quality does not identify good decisions. By focusing on decision quality rather than perceptual quality, CURE lowers regret over the best pessimistic decision rule by 10-25% across support levels, and over world-action models, search and policy learning by 41-64%, given the same data.
authors: Raphael C. Kim, Michele Santacatterina, Jingsen Zhu, Ramin Zabih
bullets: Realistic-looking, training-consistent videos do not guarantee good planning decisions.
CURE uses certificates to assess whether the model’s support covers the planner’s decisions.
Depending on the diagnosis, it upweights data, rolls out more samples, or explores unsupported regions.
Across physics, robotic control, and pushing tasks in simulation and real videos, trusted decisions had lower regret than untrusted ones.
Focusing on decision quality reduced regret by 10–25% versus a pessimistic rule and 41–64% versus several alternative methods under equal data.

figures.caption: Figure 3. CURE in action. Top: MuJoCo contact. Bottom: Language-Table sim. Left: the standard world model’s chosen action misses the goal in the real rollout (true outcome shown). Middle: CURE’s certificate decides the fix. Top: the certificate is below zero because the training data has too little support for the needed action, so CURE collects new clips (Explore). Bottom: the certificate passes, so CURE acts, with the upweighted model and more rollouts per action (Upweight, Rollout). Right: CURE’s chosen action reaches the goal. The regret numbers are normalized such that 0 is the best action in the bank, and 1 is a random action on average.

Figure 2. CURE. We estimate the behavior policy π̂b and the weights α̂ on the training data, and the model error ε̂ on a validation set. We then train the candidate models (standard, debiased, retargeted) and certify each one (D1). If none passes, we collect new clips where the certificate fails and re-certify, until the clip budget is spent (D2). We keep the model with the largest certificate margin (D3), and spend extra rollouts only on contended actions, those too close to the top score to tell apart, that have support (D4). Full procedure in the supplementary material.
Figure 5. Test-time compute helps only where the model has support. Regret against number of candidates scored K. Hollow: low; filled: partial; dotted: high support.

Figure 1. Convincing video does not mean a better action. World models make decisions by generating videos as imagined rollouts, predicting the regret from the videos, and picking the action with the lowest predicted regret. A more convincing video may still predict regret badly, and choose an action that fails in the true rollout (top). A less convincing video, despite the visible artifacts (ghosting, blurring and smearing of the arm), can predict accurately and select a better action (bottom).

papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world models for planning with certificate-guided trust and data-support diagnosis.
papers.title: Plausible Videos Can Lead to Poor Decisions: Diagnosing and CURE-ing World Models for Planning
papers.tldr: CURE diagnoses when video world models are reliable for planning and chooses whether to debias training data, sample more rollouts, or collect new data to reduce decision regret.

papers.abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.
authors: Tian Lyu, Yichen Jiang, Ziyuan Cheng, Yunda Yan, Xiangyu Pan, Junjie Jiang, Jialin Yu, Boyu Ning, Pietro Li\`o, Fan Mo
bullets: Addresses recursive drift in entity poses and spatial relations during long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control.
Rolls out a scene graph alongside the visual model, couples graph and visual changes, and applies a bounded residual using graph-motion context and node positions.
Acts as a plug-in for DINO-WM and DreamerV3 without backpropagating graph-learning or correction gradients into the original visual dynamics.
Across 32-step rollouts, reduces joint-position error by 11–28%; on real inverted-pendulum sequences, lowers DINO-WM pole-angle error from 12.56° to 6.69°.
In simulated inverted-pendulum control, JointGV-corrected rollouts enable 46/50 successful episodes versus none with original rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of JointGV. Given the current RGB observation and action, the original visual world model (yellow) predicts the uncorrected next visual state Zt+1 and its change ∆Zt. In parallel, JointGV (blue) uses Relation Transformer (RelTR) features to construct a task-conditioned scene graph and predicts the node-feature change ∆N̂t. For the spatial-token case shown here, learned projections map the visual-token and graph-node changes into a shared space, where a change-alignment adapter produces the graph-motion context. The predicted node positions provide a complementary position context. A bounded, gated correction combines these contexts with the original visual prediction to produce Ẑt+1 = Zt+1 + Ct. Setting Ct = 0 recovers the original prediction. Decoded images are shown only for visualization; the global-state adapter is described in Sec. 3.4.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of DINO-WM and JointGV on a held-out DMC Cheetah Run sequence. Columns show rollout steps 2, 8, 16, 24, and 32; adjacent maps show absolute RGB error amplified by four using the shared decoder. Red arrows mark representative structural differences. Kv denotes the self-fed visual training horizon and ω the propagated correction-gradient fraction. Additional episodes and videos are provided in Sec. S8.

Figure 1. Motivation. (a) DINO-WM open-loop predictions initialized from real-robot inverted-pendulum observations increasingly deviate from the observed pole. (b) Pole-angle error rises with rollout horizon for all three models, while JointGV reduces this structural drift.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on a held-out DMC Walker Walk validation sequence. Columns show rollout steps 2, 8, 16, 24, and 32, with absolute RGB error amplified by a factor of four. JointGV uses the DreamerV3 global-state change to pool the graph-node changes and applies the result as a bounded global correction. The corrected rollout better preserves the articulated pose at later steps.

Figure 6. Preliminary physical RM65-B control trial. The two actors start from comparable pole angles. At 1.27 seconds, the pole controlled using the original visual-world-model rollout has fallen to −83.3◦, whereas the actor using the JointGV-corrected rollout keeps it near upright at −2.7◦. This trial demonstrates short-duration physical deployment rather than stable six-second balancing.

Figure 5. Per-window effect across four model–task pairings. Each value is the relative change in 32-step average joint-position error from the original prediction to JointGV; values below zero indicate improvement. JointGV improves 99%, 66%, 89%, and 83% of the respective test windows, showing that the aggregate gains are not produced by a small subset of rollouts.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.
authors: Jiachun Li, Zhuoran Jin, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces MentalGrid, a benchmark for spatial reasoning without intermediate visual feedback.
Finds that simple simulations are limited by perception, while complex ones suffer from weak multi-step reasoning.
Proposes a three-stage curriculum trained on 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples.
SpatialWalker achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model and outperforms Gemini-3-Flash on spatial simulation.
Generalizes to out-of-domain benchmarks with a 4.9% average gain.

papers.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.
authors: Yoonho Choi, Taehyeon Han, Seonghyeon Lee
bullets: Problem: Agents often over-explore repositories and continue calling tools after sufficient evidence has been gathered; standard SFT can reproduce this behavior.
Method: Truncate training trajectories at the earliest sufficient-answer step, add a rationale explaining why stopping is appropriate, and emphasize that rationale during fine-tuning.
Results: JET reduces tool calls by 11–33% on self-generated trajectories and 18–28% versus SFT on expert trajectories.
Across two repository-QA benchmarks and two open-weight 8B models, JET largely preserves performance and lowers inference cost.

papers.abstract: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.
authors: Mohammad Nomaan Husain, Tanja Katharina Kaiser
bullets: Addresses collective estimation when robot observations are noisy and sensor faults vary over time.
Extends the DeGroot-Friedkin model by weighting peers according to retrospective predictive performance.
Supports decentralized, asynchronous communication without requiring sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models.
In simulated collective navigation, it produced more stable estimates and sustained decision criteria more reliably than three baselines, but required longer decision times.
Performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection.

papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

papers.abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.
authors: Teng Lin, Nan Tang
bullets: Covers 386 tasks drawn from 185 real-world tables, with expert-curated reports, standardized structures, and verifiable key insights.
Uses dual judges: a text evaluator checks structure, numerical grounding, and novelty, while a visualization evaluator assesses fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and correctness.
Also measures consistency between generated narratives and visualizations.
Evaluation of 20 state-of-the-art models finds persistent weaknesses, including numerical hallucinations and few genuinely novel insights.
Single-judge evaluation overestimates performance by 8–12 points, supporting complementary multi-faceted evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and dual-judge evaluation for multimodal report generation from tables, directly relevant to multimodal LLM capabilities.
papers.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
papers.tldr: MM-ReportBench is a 386-task benchmark for evaluating whether models can generate faithful, insightful text-and-visualization reports from tables.

papers.abstract: Triangle Splatting represents scenes using semi-transparent triangles, but it evaluates each triangle at the pixel center and culls any triangle with an inradius smaller than one pixel. The former causes severe aliasing, while the latter culls most of the scene at lower resolutions. We show that the integral of the Triangle Splatting window over a pixel admits an exact closed-form solution. The angle bisectors split the triangle into three sub-triangles, in each of which the window is a power of the distance to one edge. Each piece therefore has a closed-form antiderivative, and Green's theorem reduces the integral and its gradients to one term per side of the sub-triangle clipped against the pixel. The integral over the whole triangle, which we show has a closed form, then allows conservative culling, removing only triangles that cannot meet the renderer's alpha cutoff at any pixel. This exact formulation anti-aliases existing models without retraining, exhibits less temporal aliasing than 2x2 supersampling, and enables multi-scale training, matching or outperforming supersampled training at reduced resolutions.
authors: Brent Zoomers, Joni Vanherck, Leander Winters, Jeroen Put, Lode Jorissen, Nick Michiels
bullets: Addresses severe aliasing and excessive low-resolution culling in Triangle Splatting.
Derives a closed-form pixel integral by decomposing each triangle into edge-distance-based sub-triangles and applying Green’s theorem.
Uses the exact whole-triangle integral for conservative alpha-based culling.
Anti-aliases existing models without retraining and shows less temporal aliasing than 2×2 supersampling.
Supports multi-scale training, matching or outperforming supersampled training at reduced resolutions.

papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
authors: Wei Hou, Jingxin Geng, Xin Chen, Zheqing Jiang
bullets: Uses calibrated lineage metadata to attribute output sentences to input spans across multi-source, multi-turn contexts.
Detects concept drift and compacts only no-longer-referenced documents while preserving user instructions verbatim.
Window-level embedding similarity better captures paraphrased support than whole-document or lexical matching.
A greedy-window method is faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line matching; attribution remains stable through 40 turns and completes in about 1 second per turn on one GPU.
Drift compaction is conservative, reporting 0% false compaction, with recall limited by attribution accuracy.

papers.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) faces critical challenges in handling extreme environmental variations while meeting the computational constraints of practical applications. Current methods predominantly address these challenges by either scaling up model capacity or employing computationally intensive reranking stages, creating a significant efficiency bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, we propose EfficientVPR, a lightweight one-stage framework that achieves speed-accuracy trade-offs through two key innovations: i) a scene-aware visual prompt tuning method which adapts pretrained features with less parameters while dynamically adjusting to sample-specific characteristics, and ii) an instance-dependent key local feature enhancement module that further reinforces discriminative regions. Comprehensive evaluations on Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime and SVOX demonstrate that our method establishes a new SOTA for DINOv2-small models by outperforming all same-scale competitors, and delivers a $73\times$ speedup with 60\% lower-dimensional features while maintaining competitive (within 2.5% average R@1 gap) against the SOTA DINOv2-large-based two-stage method. Our code will be available at https://github.com/WiniTang/EfficientVPR.
authors: Wenjing Tang, Chuanguang Yang, Zhulin An, Libo Huang, Yongjun Xu
bullets: Targets the accuracy–efficiency bottleneck of VPR methods that rely on larger models or costly reranking.
Uses scene-aware visual prompt tuning to adapt pretrained features with fewer parameters and sample-specific adjustments.
Enhances discriminative regions with an instance-dependent key local feature module.
Evaluated on Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime, and SVOX; achieves state-of-the-art results among DINOv2-small models.
Compared with a DINOv2-large two-stage method, provides a 73× speedup and 60% lower-dimensional features while staying within a 2.5% average R@1 gap.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The overall architecture of our one-stage method. To maintain strong discriminative power while ensuring lightweight efficiency, we employ DINOv2-small as the backbone with SceneVPT for fine-tuning, preserving generalizable features while adapting to instance-specific characteristics. During feature enhancement, EfficientVPR uses MsIA and OLE to extract multi-scale global features and orientation-aware local features respectively, while SGFS performs instance-specific local feature enhancement of key regions based on sample-dependent semantic cues obtained from backbone.

The core discriminative features lie in the smaller objects, such as street lamps, signs, and building details. Fine-tuned by SceneVPT, the backbone effectively learns to focus on image-specific discriminative regions, such as the signs and street lamps in the first query and the architectural details in the second, while suppressing interference from irrelevant areas like the clouds. In contrast, with other approaches the backbone is prone to either missing the core discriminative features or paying excessive attention to non-essential parts of the image.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight visual place recognition with prompt tuning and feature enhancement; directly targets efficiency.
papers.title: EfficientVPR: Toward Efficient Visual Place Recognition via Scene-Aware Prompt Tuning and Adaptive Feature Enhancement
papers.tldr: EfficientVPR is a lightweight one-stage VPR framework that improves efficiency under environmental variation through scene-aware prompt tuning and adaptive local-feature enhancement.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
authors: Raluca Stevenson, David Bignell, Jennifer C. White, Tabish Rashid, Emanuele Aiello, Mariya Hendriksen, Junha Hyung, Sadegh Aliakbarian, Abdelhak Lemkhenter, Marko Tot, Katja Hofmann, Sarah Parisot

Demonstrates high-quality, consistent gameplay training using approximately one day of gameplay data.
Scope: the speed–quality trade-off and data-efficiency claims are demonstrated for gameplay generation.

papers.abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.
authors: Li Li, Xiangbo Gao, Bo Ni, Samyadeep Basu, Viet Dac Lai, Jing Shi, Seunghyun Yoon, Gang Wu, Yu Wang, Thien Huu Nguyen, Tyler Derr, Franck Dernoncourt, Zhengzhong Tu, Yue Zhao
bullets: The study identifies “motion collapse,” where reward models prefer motion-suppressed edits; the baseline does so in 97% of VE-Bench cases.
Learned video rewards, a VLM judge, latent optimization, and reward-guided fine-tuning all show vulnerability to motion suppression.
The proposed model adds an RGB frame-difference stream and trains on motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives, with a human-quality distillation anchor.

It selects motion-suppressed candidates in 0% of motion-ladder cases, reaches 0.57 Spearman correlation with human ratings, detects unseen suppression variants, and preserves motion during fine-tuning.
Scope: the method is evaluated on VE-Bench and two editing pipelines.

papers.abstract: A task specifies how the world should change, while a policy specifies what the robot should do. We introduce Progress Predicts Policy (PPP), which learns a language-conditioned scalar field through the commands induced by its differential. We obtain action conditioning by composing a latent progress field with a shared world model and read its action gradient at a fixed reference command. Continuous commands scale this gradient by a learned positive gain, while discrete commands use finite differences of the same scalar. This yields a hybrid policy without a separate action head or iterative search. Fitting demonstration progress values alone does not ensure that action gradients align with expert commands. PPP trains the induced commands by imitation and uses double backpropagation for the continuous gradient readout to shape the field's local control geometry. Demonstration timing calibrates field values on observed states without additional annotation. The continuous readout remains learnable without progress labels but these timing-derived targets support progress monitoring during execution. Experiments in simulated and real robot manipulation show that PPP outperforms behavioral cloning under a shared architecture.
authors: Licheng Zhong, Gim Hee Lee
bullets: Represents task progress as a scalar field whose differential induces robot commands.
Composes the progress field with a shared world model and uses gradient-based continuous actions or finite differences for discrete actions.
Trains induced commands by imitation, using double backpropagation to align local field geometry with expert actions.
Uses demonstration timing to calibrate progress values and enable execution-time progress monitoring.
Demonstrates improved performance over behavioral cloning in simulated and real robot manipulation.

papers.title: Progress Predicts Policy

papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.
authors: Wenbo Zhu, Paul Yi-Chia Chen, Yuanhan Li, Zishen Wan, Christopher Torng
bullets: JEPA world-model planning is slow because sampling-based MPC repeatedly runs predictor inference at large scale.
The method groups action sequences around shared reference roots, manufacturing latent similarity and hardware-exploitable differential sparsity.
A tightly coupled accelerator uses this sparsity and planner-exposed structure for efficient scheduling.
Across three JEPA world models, it achieves 1.28–1.80× speedup and 38–52% lower energy than a dense accelerator.
Compared with prior bit-sparse hardware at the same area, it achieves 1.22–1.58× speedup and 16–36% lower energy.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Planner and accelerator design for efficient planning. papers.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
papers.tldr: A planner–hardware co-design accelerates JEPA-style world-model MPC by deliberately creating differential bit-level sparsity among candidate action sequences.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.
authors: Yanchao Li, Jiaqing Xie, Ben Gao, Yusu Zhang, Beilun Wang, Yanbo Wang, Xiaohua Xu, Zhongyu Huang, Tianfan Fu, Nanqing Dong
bullets: Existing pruning methods typically use one fixed token budget for every question, even though pruning harms only some answers.
PRUDENT first answers with roughly half the token budget, then reallocates saved tokens to questions where a small full-image VLM disagrees with the pruned answer.
Across 18 benchmarks, it outperforms eight pruning methods at the same average visual-token budget, with larger gains under tighter budgets.
The disagreement signal identifies most pruning failures and also improves strong existing pruning methods and multiple VLM families.
The approach focuses extra computation on uncertain answers rather than improving token ranking alone.

papers.title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents
papers.tldr: PRUDENT improves visual-token pruning by using a small full-image VLM to detect likely pruning errors and selectively re-answer those questions with more visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.
authors: Yican Zhao, Bolin Yang, Ruizhe Wang, Haiyang Guo, Fuji Yang, Bingo Wing-Kuen Ling, Zelin Zang
bullets: Latent distance-to-goal objectives can create local minima, especially near walls, corners, and dead ends.
EKR penalizes candidate plans near a novelty-gated memory of visited latents using a top-k Gaussian kernel.
Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR improves reported average success while using the same planning budget.
It reduces stuck episodes and revisits, often steering plans away from visited states even at higher base cost.
The method transfers without tuning to DINO-WM with CEM and improves performance on Wall, PointMaze, and Push-T tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free episodic memory repulsion improves latent world-model planning; directly relevant to world models and embodied memory.
papers.title: Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
papers.tldr: Training-free episodic kernel repulsion helps latent-world-model planners escape revisited dead ends and improve goal-reaching success without changing the model or planner.

papers.abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.
authors: Yifan Chang, Jian Yang, Jiangnan Shao, Xiaofeng Wang, Zhaoxin Fan, Renjing Xu, Ming Lu, Xingang Wang, Zheng Zhu

Recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system before constructing constrained Blender scenes.
Uses programmatic consistency checks to guide agent refinement and produces editable scenes plus frame-aligned blockout videos.
Reports 27.5–41.1-point overall gains over corresponding vanilla baselines; one configuration reaches 73.2 while reducing reconstruction time by 53%.
Provides MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs, with planned public release.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Chang Sun, Yijun Tian, Zhenwei Tang, Yuchen Deng, Yifan Simon Liu, Chenxu Wang, Wei Wang
bullets: Targets hallucinations caused when irrelevant or misleading audio, video, or text cues distort another modality’s prediction.
Uses Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration when unimodal branches disagree, selecting task-relevant evidence and alternative answers.
Uses Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery when branches agree, checking layer-wise evidence consistency and strength to detect false consensus.
Evaluated on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across hallucination mitigation and audio-visual reasoning tasks.
Reports up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding and 7.7% average improvement over the best baseline, as stated in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.
authors: Arusa Kanwal, Pablo Valle, Paola Roggero, Miren Illarramendi, Shaukat Ali, Aitor Arrieta
bullets: Addresses the limited use of recorded VLA trajectories for assessing future executions and guiding policy repair.
Adapts spectrum-based fault localization by treating workspace voxels as analyzable elements.
Builds voxel suspiciousness maps from binary tool-center-point coverage and success/failure outcomes.
Evaluated 34 techniques across four VLA models and 96,000 simulated Pick-Up trajectories.
Achieved a macro ROC-AUC of 0.704 and outperformed eight action- and trajectory-based baselines; performance depended on voxel granularity and training-set size.

papers.tldr: VoxelSBFL uses voxel-level trajectory coverage and execution outcomes to predict failures in unseen VLA robot executions without accessing model internals.

papers.abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.
authors: Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Jinze Liu, Ziting Qin, Qianshan Wei, Jihuai Zhu, Yipeng Yu, Baohua Dong, Hangcheng Zhu, Ruohui Huang
bullets: OPD’s apparent resistance to backdoors is challenged because teacher probability distributions can still transmit malicious behavior.
Unlike offline distillation, propagation is rare at low poisoning ratios but rapidly approaches full attack success beyond a critical threshold.
The mechanism is continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass from the teacher, rather than explicit malicious target responses.
Experiments across multiple model families and datasets, supported by theoretical analysis, identify this overlooked security risk.
A trigger design is proposed that enables propagation with zero explicit trigger injection.

papers.abstract: Learning-based methods now let humanoids run robustly, and they have begun to compete in athletic events. Yet few reports describe a complete autonomous humanoid running system in an actual race, where the robot must follow a lane at a new venue, pace itself within hardware limits, and finish without intervention. We report such a system deployed on the Unitree G1, a commercially available general-purpose humanoid, in the 100 m, 400 m, and 1500 m events of the World Humanoid Robot Games 2026. The system integrates vision-based lane perception, path tracking, and a running policy trained by reinforcement learning with a human motion prior. To address the challenges of humanoid running, we stabilize head-camera images against body motion and use IMU-assisted leg odometry to bridge flight phases. To manage motor heating, we penalize hip-pitch torque during training, add heat-dissipation plates, and apply temperature-based speed limiting with event-specific pacing. The robot placed 13th of 74 in the 100 m, 10th of 44 in the 400 m first round before falling in the semifinal, and seventh of 35 in the 1500 m. In this deployment, thermal margin set the pace in every event, and the semifinal fall followed a lane-detection error.

Managed overheating through torque penalties, heat-dissipation hardware, and temperature-based event pacing.
Placed 13th/74 in the 100 m, 10th/44 in the 400 m first round, and 7th/35 in the 1500 m; a semifinal fall followed a lane-detection error.

papers.abstract: Occlusions and limited sensor range make ego-only 3D perception insufficient for safe driving. Collaborative perception addresses this by enabling connected vehicles to share complementary observations, yet it remains constrained by tight vehicular communication budgets. While spatial selection is more flexible than fixed-rate feature compression, existing selectors remain largely sender-driven and waste scarce bandwidth on ego-visible targets. Furthermore, applying convolutions after masking spreads isolated tokens into their neighborhoods, silently violating low-bandwidth constraints. To address this, we propose Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bandwidth-adaptive framework centered on bilateral demand-supply consensus. Instead of unilateral token selection, the ego vehicle formulates a content-aware demand prior while each collaborator evaluates its local supply. This single-round consensus allocates the token budget to critical ego-missed evidence rather than ego-visible redundancy, without transmitting dense maps. To guarantee exact budget compliance, an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline refines features prior to discrete token selection, preventing receptive-field leakage. A lightweight deformable sampler then aggregates these sparse messages with learned local offsets, compensating for the spatial context lost to token selection and mitigating inter-agent pose drift. Evaluated at a stringent 64KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the best AP@0.7 on the simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset. These results demonstrate that combining bilateral consensus with budget-exact transmission is key to efficient low-bandwidth collaborative perception.
authors: Linshan Yan
bullets: Addresses occlusions and limited sensor range that make ego-only perception unsafe.
Uses bilateral demand–supply consensus: the ego proposes content-aware needs, while collaborators assess available evidence.
Refines features before discrete masking to prevent convolutional receptive-field leakage and guarantee budget-exact transmission.
Applies lightweight deformable sampling to recover local context and reduce effects of token sparsity and pose drift.
At 64KiB, achieves the best AP@0.7 across simulated OPV2V/V2XSet and real-world DAIR-V2X evaluations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.
authors: Lixuan He, Tianzhe Chu, Shulin Tian, Shikang Zheng, Feng Chen, Yi Ma
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between sequence-level rewards and sparse visual evidence in multimodal reasoning.
Infers a latent reward landing field from cross-modal representations and local predictive uncertainty.
Reweights token-level updates toward positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing, while preserving total rollout credit.
Requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural changes.
Improves Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.
authors: Siqi Lai, Haitao Li, Hao Liu
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational cost of repeatedly invoking LLM-based System-2 reasoning.

As the harness improves, fewer System-2 interventions are needed, amortizing reasoning costs over time.

papers.abstract: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://towzeur.github.io/RCR/.
authors: Nicolas Larue
bullets: Neural-collapse classifiers can separate samples within their task while routing them to the wrong task block globally, causing high Task-IL but low Class-IL accuracy.
The paper formalizes route accuracy from the global class argmax to distinguish within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability.
Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR) combines standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, neural-collapse-shrunk class representatives.
Across three datasets and two replay-buffer budgets, RCR achieves the best Class-IL FAA in five of six settings and reduces forgetting in all six.
Reported gains reach up to +6.75 FAA over the reference and preserve Task-IL performance, with larger improvements in difficult routing regimes.

papers.abstract: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.
authors: Zhaofeng Sun, Lanxiang Hu, Yu-Yang Qian, Jiaqi Leng, Yuanbo Yang, Chi Zhang, Youyou Lu, Peng Zhao, Hao Zhang

The method preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution with O(Rd) extra hidden-state storage.
At eight loops, it reduces perplexity and improves downstream accuracy over both vanilla PLTs and non-looped baselines.
Overhead is 0.3% in decoding time versus vanilla PLTs, with the same logical KV-cache footprint.

papers.abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.
authors: Pengfeng Song, Yunkai Zhuang, Liye Shi
bullets: Addresses limited context space when relevant facts are scattered across sources and surrounded by distractors.
Learns to select both the next source and the amount of text to read, linking fine-grained passages to original sources.
Uses contrastive training and a reranker that scores each candidate’s added evidence relative to an anchor passage.
A selector assembles evidence under a 400-token budget; evaluated on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue with a frozen 2B answer model.
Improves F1 over query expansion while reducing memory input by 23.1–26.9%; all eight tested small answer models improve over query expansion and MMR on HotpotQA.
