papers.selection_reason: Proposes a learned multigranular memory retrieval method for small language model agents, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: LMMR helps small language-model agents answer multi-hop questions by retrieving complementary evidence at multiple granularities within a strict token budget.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.
authors: Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang, Jinqiao Wang
bullets: Fixed or single-level geometric fusion cannot meet the differing representation needs of tasks such as distance estimation and route planning.
GeoFus uses a gating network conditioned on text, visual semantics, and geometry to combine shallow, intermediate, and deep features across LLM decoder layers.
Negative-entropy regularization helps prevent gate collapse during adaptive fusion.
Gate visualizations suggest that the framework adjusts geometric granularity according to task requirements.
SpatialMind achieves competitive spatial-benchmark performance, including a 72.3 score on VSI-Bench.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the SpatialMind architecture. Our framework adopts a decoupled fusion design and introduces GeoFus for taskadaptive integration of multi-level geometric features with visual tokens. By jointly conditioning on textual, visual, and geometric contexts, GeoFus dynamically adjusts the contributions of geometric representations at different LLM injection layers according to task requirements.

Each row reports the average gating distribution over 50 randomly sampled examples from the corresponding VSI-Bench subtask. The upper five rows correspond to low-level perception tasks, while the lower three rows correspond to high-level reasoning tasks.

Figure 3: Effects of Multi-Level Geometric Features. Shallow features contribute more to low-level tasks, while deep features are more important for high-level tasks, demonstrating hierarchical specialization and cross-level complementarity.

Figure 9: Task-Dependent Geometric Response Visualization on VSI-Bench. The low-level absolute-distance task emphasizes finegrained local geometry, whereas the high-level route-planning task produces broader responses over global scene structures.

SpatialMind produces predictions consistent with or closer to the ground truth, whereas the baseline exhibits substantial metric and directional errors.

papers.tldr: SpatialMind improves 3D spatial reasoning in multimodal LLMs by dynamically selecting the geometric feature granularity suited to each task.

papers.abstract: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting. Sign spottings already locate words in time at corpus scale, but training subtitle alignment jointly on subtitle and word spans remains underexplored. We present SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator that maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval. It is first trained jointly on subtitle spans and word spans from sign spottings, then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples. On the subtitle test set of the British Broadcasting Corporation-Oxford British Sign Language (BOBSL) corpus, the refined model reaches 66.68 F1@0.50 (F1 with a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of one half), the best among compared systems without external sign-video resources. This overlap-reward refinement outperforms cross-entropy continuation from the same jointly trained model. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment in a pair of our generators matched in code, labels and maximum update budget. The advantage remains after both models of the pair are refined with overlap rewards. For word queries, the refined model follows the queried word, not a fixed position in the video: when the word's sign lies away from the video centre, it is far more accurate than predictions that use position alone. Together, these findings support one shared span generator refined with overlap rewards, aligning subtitles and producing word spans for human review.
authors: Jongbhin Woo, Youngjoon Jang, Joon Son Chung
bullets: Targets two granularities: subtitle spans for alignment and word spans for sign spotting.
Uses a prompt-conditioned visual-language generator to predict start/end frames for sentence or word queries.
Trains jointly on subtitle and sign-spotting word spans, retaining word examples during refinement.
Achieves 66.68 F1@0.50 on the BOBSL subtitle test set, best among compared systems without external sign-video resources.
Word-query predictions follow the queried sign rather than relying on fixed video position; scope is evaluated on BOBSL and matched comparison systems.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.
authors: Mehul Arora, Dhruv Agarwal, Ambuj Agrawal
bullets: A 250M-parameter VLA addresses large performance drops under paraphrased instructions and the difficulty of distinguishing language errors from execution failures.
A text encoder produces shared interpretable step codes; a visual planner translates them into action codes for a language-independent actor.
It reaches 91.4% success on LIBERO-Goal and 81.1% across 4,092 unseen LIBERO-Para paraphrases, with 17 ms control-step latency.
It completes 48.8% of free-form two-step tasks without two-step demonstrations, indicating scope beyond the primary benchmark setting.
Stage analysis shows 91% success when instructions are correctly encoded versus 27.2% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main remaining failure source.

figures.caption: Figure 2. CoBoVLA separates understanding from acting through two discrete codes. (a) At test time, stage 1 maps the instruction to a learned step code; the canonical instruction and two paraphrases receive the same code. The frames show the first-level code being executed in a successful LIBERO-Para episode. (b) Step codes come from a meaning codebook trained on paraphrase pairs: the codes of each paraphrase must predict those of the other. papers.selection_reason: VLA model for robot manipulation with decoupled language, planning, and control directly fits embodied AI, vision-language-action, and robot learning.
papers.title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation

papers.abstract: As real-robot data collection scales, collection-system design shapes both operator efficiency and the behaviors learned by robot policies. Workspace limitations, control-interface friction, and latency can introduce pauses, detours, and corrective motions into otherwise successful demonstrations. We investigate these effects across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ policies. The embodiment study shows that positional reachability overstates orientation-aware task coverage and that modest shoulder motion can substantially expand the effective workspace. Teleoperation experiments show that parallelizing body-part control reduces task completion time by 43-53%, while compliant control improves success and reduces peak contact forces on constrained and contact-rich tasks. Policy-learning experiments show that demonstrations must capture the visual information underlying action choices: active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%. Calibration experiments reveal that mixed-calibration training data remain usable in our tested configurations when an inference-aligned subset is retained, whereas inference-time miscalibration causes all 30 trials to fail. Policies also retain approximately 90% of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing how inefficient operator motions persist in learned behavior. Together, these findings connect collection-system design to demonstration quality and downstream policy execution. They motivate evaluating effective workspace, control efficiency, observation completeness, calibration alignment, and motion quality before scaling collection, and addressing system-induced compensations at their source.
authors: World Manipulation Team, Che Tsang Calvin, Xingyu Chen, Bowen Jiang, Naixiang Gao, Xiongfeng Cai, Enlin Gu, Ruiying Li, Peize Li, Mianrui Zhu, Haomiao Zhang, Xin He, Minhui Yu, Jun Zhao, Zihao Zhu, Yang Chen, Jingmei Jin, Keru Zhou, Chen Wang, Chang Zhou, Zhiwen Hou, Di Yang, Wenjun Sun, Fan Yang, Liyan Zhang, Yi Lu, Haojun Ma, Jun Zhu, Pengxin Zha, Zhaosheng Wang, Xin Zhao, Xindong He, Chiming Liu, Jianheng Song, Jiayao Ma, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren, Qian Wang, Wei Shan, Yang Yang, Li Liu, Wenhao Wang

Parallel body-part control reduces task completion time by 43–53%, while compliant control improves success and lowers peak contact forces on constrained tasks.
Active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%, highlighting the importance of capturing visual information behind actions.
Inference-time miscalibration caused all 30 tested trials to fail, while mixed-calibration training remained usable when an inference-aligned subset was retained.
Policies preserved approximately 90% of extra path length from detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing that inefficient operator motions can be learned.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes real-robot data collection quality and its effect on downstream policy learning.
papers.title: Hidden Variables Behind Real-Robot Data Quality: Lessons from Hundreds of Thousands of Hours

papers.abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.
authors: Muhammad Zain Khawaja, Zaynab El Mawas, Ryota Yamada, Gabriela Cordova, Arseni Lysak, Intisar Chowdhury, Bharat Jayaprakash, Apostolos Georgiadis, Shri Harsha Adapala, Jatin Gautam, Christoph Bank, Alejandra Solarte Uscategui, Atanasko Boris Mitrev, Hassan Ali Ansari, Nishad Sahu
bullets: Targets real-time end-to-end autonomy across advanced driver assistance and robotaxi research.
Uses a temporal bird’s-eye-view architecture with multi-camera perception, HD-map data, route conditioning, temporal fusion, and a recurrent trajectory planner.
The v1.0 release includes checkpoints, training/evaluation code, and an experiment-visualization dashboard.
On KITScenes validation, it reports 0.745 m ADE and 2.020 m FDE over a three-second horizon.
Includes preliminary real-vehicle research, but remains an early release with open-loop evaluation and no validated closed-loop autonomy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The working group’s planned three-band architecture. The reactive model at 10 Hz (violet band) is AutoE2E, the subject of this paper, already implemented and evaluated here. The world-action model at 1 Hz and the reasoning model at 1 Hz (grey bands) are planned interfaces, not yet implemented or trained; no result in this paper depends on them. The world-action band’s objective is explicitly non-linguistic: a JEPA-style future-feature reconstruction loss in the camera’s own embedding space, not a language-model reasoning trace – the design choice the paper’s title refers to.

Figure 10: The DataModelConsole dashboard: the six-camera mosaic, a speed/acceleration/yaw timeline scrubber, the bird’s-eye-view panel (ground truth vs. prediction), and the navigation map, alongside the sidebar’s dataset, experiment, run, and occupancy browsers.

Figure 9: Checkpoint lineage (top) and the two evaluation protocols (bottom). Protocol A is checkpoint-internal validation that runs the model; Protocol B is replay of the released deterministic control overlays. The two are never mixed in a single ranking table. Val and Test are different scene populations.

Figure 2: The evaluated map- and route-conditioned AutoE2E configuration. At each of eight times, six 512×512 camera views are processed: the current time plus seven history times. A 1024×1024 front view is added only at the current time. A frozen ResNet-50 + FPN and six-layer single-frame BEVFormer V2 encoder are applied independently per time, followed by T8 convolutional fusion across the eight BEVs; a navigation pathway encodes the 14-channel map and the 2-channel route separately, gated summation, deformable navigation fusion, 6.4 s of ego-motion history, a GRU control planner, and unicycle integration. All reported counts are parameter counts measured by instantiating the implementation (79,906,522 total; 1,448,582 trainable). Dashed boxes denote branches present in the checkpoint but disabled.

Figure 8: Parameter allocation. (a) The frozen camera-BEV pathway is 97.98% of all parameters. (b) Among the 1.45 M trainable parameters, the GRU planner is 57.7%, deformable navigation fusion 24.2%, and the map/route encoders plus route gate 16.9%.

Figure 6: Internal structure of the separate navigation encoding and the deformable navigation fusion. Left: map encoder Emap (0.167 M) and route encoder Eroute (0.078 M), the per-channel gate, and the addition. Right: deformable cross-attention that uses each cell of Bimg as a query and samples 8 points on Bnav (8 heads, 256 channels, 0.350 M). The output projection and the final FFN linear layer are zero-initialized, so the fusion is exactly the identity at the start of training.

Figure 3: Temporal contract. The camera branch uses 8 frames at 0.5 s intervals (3.5 s), the ego-motion history uses 64 steps at 10 Hz (6.4 s), and the output is 64 steps at 10 Hz (6.4 s). Under the KITScenes benchmark protocol, only 40 history steps (4.0 s, the remainder zero-padded) and 50 future steps (5.0 s) are real data, so the effective horizon coverage of external replay is 50/64 = 78.125%.

Figure 14: Qualitative examples from KITScenes. The top row shows the model-input front tile of each sample (center crop); the bottom row shows the logged trajectory (obsidian, 5 s) and the replayed trajectories of the fine-tuned and baseline checkpoints on the sample’s own map and route raster. The 5 s FDE is annotated in each panel.

Figure 4: The 14 map channels and 2 route channels for one KITScenes validation sample. papers.abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.
authors: Kangjie Huang, Yucheng Xin, Xinchun Wang, Dong Liu, Yan Fan, Shuming Liu
bullets: AuditEmbodied independently varies holding reference and wait duration while keeping recovery executors frozen.
A 960-execution factorial compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from matched post-wait physical states.
At a 1 s wait, completion rankings reverse between registered holding and position-only holding.
The main performance gap arises during grasp formation: small target residuals at observation precede large tracking errors.
Gradual position reanchoring substantially improves CAD recovery after long waits, including faster and more frequent completion.

papers.abstract: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.
authors: Akul Santhosh, Chaitra Sathe, Aastha Jhunjhunwala
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting robot failures at scale and broad coverage.
Fine-tunes a world model on successful and failed executions, then transfers failure-associated donor segments into compatible host trajectories.
Generates continuous rollouts with optional spatial offsets, followed by event annotation and visual-quality filtering.
Evaluated in two task and robot configurations, with visual failure detection as a downstream application.
In a preliminary comparison, adding generated data improved average precision from 0.41 to 0.51 and detected 33/36 versus 28/36 failure intervals.

Generated videos are labeled according to their observed events, with a cleanup filter for unreliable examples. Each retained example includes the video, its associated motion sequence, and temporal event labels.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingLin00/ContraSense.
authors: Ling Lin, Heng Su, Xiangzeng Liu, Yang Bai, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen
bullets: Existing vision-language benchmarks may reward statistical co-occurrences because their examples usually match human expectations.
ContraSense uses carefully curated counter-intuitive image–text pairs that require reasoning from visual evidence.
Evaluations cover diverse open- and closed-source multimodal large language models.
The strongest closed-source model reaches about 60% accuracy, versus 96.04% for humans.
The benchmark highlights the need for more visually grounded multimodal reasoning and is publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: We propose a new benchmark called ContraSense, which is both creative and imaginative. The benchmark consists of 4,698 carefully crafted and manually calibrated high-resolution (1024 × 1024 pixels) text QA pairs. Each image contains at least one counterintuitive scenario designed to assess whether visual-language models can provide accurate responses based on the image content itself without relying on common-sense prior knowledge from the training data. This benchmark provides a unique and powerful tool for studying the robustness and real-world visual understanding capabilities of VLMs.
Fig. 6: The figure shows the performance trends of mainstream multimodal models at different resolutions.
TABLE VI: Model performance was evaluated on the ContraSense dataset for different types of questions.
TABLE V: The comparison between ContraSense with other LVLM benchmarks.

papers.title: Can Vision-Language Models Truly Understand Images? A Benchmark Beyond Commonsense Bias
papers.tldr: ContraSense shows that current multimodal language models often rely on commonsense and dataset biases rather than faithfully understanding image content.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.
authors: Tao Zhang, Yi Zhong, Jinhao Ruan, Yipeng Gao, Linfeng Zhong, Youming Yang, Yuan Wang
bullets: Addresses inference-induced stalls caused by blocking action-chunk generation.
Uses an action-conditioned predictor to forecast next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state.
Precomputes a speculative KV cache and action chunk with a frozen VLA, then accepts or repairs them based on predicted–real differences and task conditions.
On LIBERO, reports 2.67× and 1.27× query speedups over synchronous π0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT baselines while maintaining competitive success rates.
Under target-motion perturbations, retains baseline-comparable success with 1.52×–1.93× query speedup.

(a)–(b) separate exposed prediction from forward computation with the real inputs. (c) LIBERO-Spatial task success and SR-VLA repair rate under target displacement, where 0 cm denotes no motion.
Fig. 4. Selective KV repair schematic. (a) predict-real error and task relevance on image patches. (b) Visual KV replacement.

papers.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
papers.tldr: SR-VLA reduces VLA control stalls by speculatively precomputing actions from predicted inputs and selectively repairing the KV cache when reality differs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.
authors: Seng Pei Liew, Teppei Suzuki, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Analyzes the trade-offs between early fusion, which mixes modalities from the start, and late fusion, which adapts a pre-trained language model.
Separates learning trajectories by data type from modality competition-induced distribution shifts.
Predicts validation losses across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes.
Finds that early fusion better preserves text performance, while late fusion favors vision performance under a fixed data budget.
The trade-off increasingly favors early fusion as model size grows, with experiments supporting the law’s predictive accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Scaling laws extended to varying model sizes (N). (a) While caption loss decreases monotonically with scale , (b) the gap between different data mixtures (L(R1)−L(R2)) shrinks for captions but remains constant for text. (c) The amplitude B0 of the shift term follows a power-law decay with model size for captions but is size-independent for text.

Figure 9: Comparison of the exponential and fraction formulations for modeling the mixture ratio (R) dependency of the text loss shift term. The fraction form kR/(kR + 1 − R) better tracks both the mixed (R < 1) and unmixed (R = 1) training regimes.

Figure 4: Mixture Ratio Dependency. (a,b) Text and interleaved validation loss curves for interleaved fusion varying the mixture ratio R. (c,d) Fitted shift amplitude as a function of R using the proposed fraction form for caption fusion, showing good fits at step 4,000 and robust validations at step 64,000.

Figure 2: Base decomposition and cross-modal exchange rates. The insets illustrate the shift term ∆L growing and saturating over CPT steps independent of Dpt. (c) Caption validation loss curves with respect to total training steps across various fusion points Dpt. (d) When plotted against CPT steps, caption loss curves collapse onto each other, indicating that text tokens play dimunitive role in caption loss.

Figure 6: (left) MME benchmark accuracies over training for from-scratch multimodal (caption) pre-training of 1b VLM. We compare our rewriting strategy (with and without image prefix), with naive scoring with continuation formats (letter, letter + option, option words). Our strategy maintains a positive visual grounding gap (scores with image prefix higher than without) and steady learning progression, while naive formats collapse to chance or produce erratic scores due to prior biases. More results in Appendix E. (right) Illustration of the rewriting strategy used for downstream evaluation of base VLMs. Multiple-choice questions are converted into statements conditioned on the image prefix to enable log-likelihood ranking and avoid answer-prior collapse.

Figure 1: Schematic of early versus late fusion in our fusion timing experiment and their scaledependent performance trade-off. (a) Late fusion begins with text-only pre-training before switching to dense multimodal continued pre-training (high mixture ratio R), inducing a large distribution shift that favors vision loss at the cost of text degradation. In contrast, early fusion distributes multimodal data across all steps (lowest R), avoiding distribution shift to protect text capability at the expense of visual performance. (b) Across model size, the text-loss penalty paid by late fusion is essentially independent of model size (γtxt ≈ 0), while its vision-loss advantage shrinks: ∝ N−0.5, so the trade-off tilts increasingly toward early fusion as models scale (see also Tab. 3). Combined with the observation that vision loss reduction does not translate to vision benchmark gains (see Sec. 6.2), early fusion becomes the preferred recipe at scale.

Figure 14: DocVQA evaluation results via continuation perplexity per byte of the reference answers, with and without the image, for 1B model trained from with interleaved data only (left) and early fusion with caption (right). We see that only early fusion with caption produces scores that improve with training and positive visual grounding gap. Training with interleaved data even has negative visual grounding gap, raising questions about the effectiveness of interleaved data in multimodal pre-training.

Figure 13: Extrapolation of the scaling law to early fusion regimes (Dpt = 0). The top panels map the predicted versus observed loss trajectories, while the bottom panels display the corresponding residuals to demonstrate accurate predictions even for early fusion.

Figure 7: Caption validation loss dynamics across training stages. The two panels on the left show that text pre-training provides negligible benefit to caption loss. The two panels on the right show that the loss gap across varying mixture ratios (R) remains almost constant when measured by effective caption tokens (R× CPT steps) rather than raw CPT steps.

Figure 8: The validation loss gap between mixed runs (R < 1) and the multimodal-only run (R = 1). The gap shrinks when compared at equal CPT steps (left) but remains nearly constant when aligned by effective caption tokens (R× CPT steps) (right).
Figure 11: Validation loss trajectories for both fitted runs and held-out configurations (extrapolated fusion points and CPT horizons) across interleaved, caption, and text modalities.

Figure 10: Fitted shift amplitude as a function of the multimodal mixture ratio (R) using exponential and fraction forms. The single fraction form unifiedly captures the concave curvature for interleaved/caption losses and the convex curvature for text loss using a single parameter km.

papers.abstract: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same identity, yet the answer depends on the target granularity. Two records may match at the base level but not at the variant level: they share an underlying design while differing in attributes such as color or size. Final matching accuracy does not separately characterize the capabilities involved. To study this problem, we use e-commerce as a challenging real-world domain. We introduce PURE, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching covering four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment. The benchmark comprises 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks, derived from real-world matching pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%. Understanding receives the highest mean score and Judgment the lowest, with weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment. Modality ablations show that models benefit from multimodal evidence but can incorrectly identify conflicts between matching records. In direct matching, most models recognize matching pairs more reliably than non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. PURE therefore reveals what aggregate matching accuracy hides: not only whether models judge a pair correctly, but where they struggle to interpret evidence and apply matching criteria.
authors: Hengyu You, Xintong Wang, Jin Cao, Liang Ding
bullets: Introduces a real-world e-commerce benchmark with 1,457 expert-verified multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks.
Evaluates four capabilities: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment.
Across 10 recent MLLMs, scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%; Understanding is strongest, while Judgment is weakest.
Models struggle with visual difference localization and variant-level matching rules, despite benefiting from multimodal evidence.
Models are generally better at identifying base-level matches but show the opposite pattern for variant-level matching; some also misidentify conflicts between matching records.

papers.title: PURE: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multi-Granularity Multimodal Identity Matching

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $\Theta(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}\alpha\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.
authors: Juyoung Park, Heejun Lee
bullets: Targets the storage and serving overhead of FP16 adapters in QLoRA-style fine-tuning.
Introduces NormScale and LearnThresh, using learned layer scales and straight-through estimation for binary adapters.
Theory shows bounded norms, near-isotropic full-rank updates, and an explicit generalization bound unavailable for standard FP16 LoRA.
On Qwen2.5, BQ-LoRA improves benchmark averages over QLoRA by 0.8–3.5 points across model scales; results on LLaMA-2 are competitive but not uniformly best.
BQ-SGMV enables up to 15.6× more adapters in A100 HBM; training memory matches QLoRA and step time increases by under 4%.

papers.abstract: A visual question answering (VQA) model can pass every image-only and question-only test yet fail when the same changes occur together. Standard robustness reports average over conditions and therefore cannot say which accepted requests remain vulnerable. We introduce M3-Test, a coverage audit that aligns each clean input with its single-modality variants and a complete 5x5 family, 4x4 strength joint library, so that any reduced test suite can be replayed on the same requests. Across 2.6 million responses from four vision-language models, joint failures affect 26-29% of the Qwen questions that pass all 40 single-modality tests, although fewer than 0.6% of their joint records fail. Passing the 25 maximum-strength corners does not close this gap: 11-14% of the accepted questions still fail elsewhere in the library. Re-executing the archived failures reproduces about 90% of them, against a 0.3-0.6% flip rate among matched passing controls, and re-checking the most fragile failure records supports 80-89% of them. On the evidence examined, neither execution noise nor grading error can fully account for the gap. The same aligned grids make previous evaluations reusable. On held-out images, a risk order learned from other models discovers about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 additional queries, compared with 65-68% for maximum-first and 53-57% for pairwise covering arrays. M3-Test thus turns a passing robustness suite into a request-level account of what remains untested, supporting acceptance, regression review and test allocation.
authors: Enhui Wan, Xiaowan Wang
bullets: VQA models can pass all image-only and question-only tests yet fail when both modalities are perturbed together.

Across four vision-language models, 26–29% of Qwen questions passing 40 single-modality tests still had joint failures; maximum-strength corners missed 11–14%.
Archived failures were reproduced at about 90%, while matched passing controls flipped only 0.3–0.6%, suggesting noise and grading errors do not explain the gap.
A cross-model risk order found about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 extra queries, outperforming maximum-first and pairwise covering-array strategies.

papers.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.
authors: Weitao An, Chenghao Xu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Addresses the growing storage costs and limited knowledge evolution of observation- and embedding-based navigation memories.
Uses a two-timescale memory that stores sparse experience atoms and continually consolidates repeated observations, transitions, and task feedback.
Distills category co-occurrences and feedback into structural knowledge without predefined object–room relations.
Combines direct goal evidence with learned structural knowledge to guide search on the current traversability map.
Demonstrates experience reuse, improved path efficiency, compact persistent memory, and real-robot transfer across multiple navigation settings.

papers.abstract: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines. Codes link: https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/InertialWorld
authors: Yuan Gao, Fan Xu, Yu Guo, Yuxu Lu, Zhengru Fang, Hao Wu, Xiaomeng Huang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and unstable dynamics caused by repeatedly reconstructing each video frame.
Uses Inertial Memory with a dense Eulerian grid and persistent Lagrangian carriers tied to canonical coordinates.

Performs competitively with strong video world-model baselines across robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation.
The abstract establishes broad evaluation but does not specify numerical gains or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.
authors: Vedant Jhaveri, Arashpreet Singh Mor, Satyam Kumar, Alex Tsun, Qing Lan, Shaunak Mishra, Sriram Vasudevan

Scores compact codebook candidates while streaming the full-vocabulary normalizer to preserve the model’s valid-token scores.
Shared-context attention reuses prompt key/value blocks while keeping beam-specific decode tails.
Implemented in SGLang; the combined system achieves up to 5.57× throughput over CLP and 2.63× over BF16 FlashRec at beam width 200 on one workload.

papers.abstract: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.
authors: Xiaoqian Zhang, Zhihao Zhang
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra generation cost in text-based communication between multimodal language models.
Provider models observe complementary video frames and transfer projected, aligned visual KV states to a carrier model via gated residual updates.
The injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while adding provider and communication-module computation.
Experiments on MLVU and Video-MME report modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower latency than the evaluated text-based baseline.
More provider-side frame coverage helps selected tasks, but some categories are unchanged or worse; computation budgets remain an open consideration.

papers.title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments

papers.abstract: Human data can support robot policy pretraining, but gains attributed to a data recipe may also reflect subset size, training variability, or downstream adaptation. In an HPT implementation on a 20-task MetaWorld suite with three training blocks, a constrained random 5,000-recording subset matches most of the task-informed subset's gain over the 40,000-recording pool at 20,000 updates (3.69 of 4.29 percentage points), leaving equal-size selection differences of 0.60 points at 5,000 recordings and 0.45 points at 1,250 recordings, with wide paired intervals. Across 12 comparisons, task orderings repeat across seeds for several contrasts, but a fixed predictor built from the other two seeds trails the mean or difficulty reference in at least one held-out fold for every comparison. Neither mechanism probe shows its predicted positive interaction: task-slot mismatch yields an interaction of $-0.0347$ points after adaptation, and in a six-task observation experiment the observation-by-pretraining interaction changes sign between seeds ($-18.29$ and $+1.04$ points) while full-state pretraining gains are positive in both ($+6.37$ and $+2.31$ points). This retrospective study shows how equal-size and capacity controls, seed-level reporting, and targeted interventions change the interpretation of apparent transfer gains.
authors: Jiachen Li, Shihao Li, Soovadeep Bakshi, Longteng Fan, Dongmei Chen, Long Chen, Zhuo Xu
bullets: A constrained random 5,000-recording subset captures most of the task-informed subset’s gain over the 40,000-recording pool.
Equal-size selection differences are small and have wide paired intervals, limiting confidence in selection-specific benefits.
Task orderings recur across some seeds, but cross-seed predictors fail to consistently outperform mean or difficulty references.
Two proposed mechanisms receive no consistent support: task-slot mismatch has a near-zero negative interaction, while observation effects change sign across seeds.
The study emphasizes equal-size and capacity controls, seed-level reporting, and targeted interventions when interpreting transfer gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1. One transfer pipeline, three questions. Human recordings pretrain the HPT trunk under data recipes from three separate protocol families; only the trunk transfers to robot adaptation on 20 Meta-World tasks, and every model is evaluated on 144 initial states per task across three training seeds. The analyses then ask whether a recipe beats a matched control, whether its task-level effects repeat across seeds, and whether targeted interventions support the proposed mechanism.

Figure 4. The six observation-probe tasks. papers.abstract: Diffusion-based end-to-end autonomous driving models have shown strong potential in generating multimodal planning trajectories. However, their performance still depends heavily on trajectory initialization, mode evaluation, and supervision quality. Weakly constrained noisy initialization may introduce infeasible proposals and increase the burden of denoising. Moreover, selecting the optimal mode remains challenging when candidate trajectories are geometrically similar but differ in safety, interaction risk, and progress. To address these issues, we propose FIRE-Drive, a feasibility-informed risk evaluation framework for end-to-end autonomous driving. FIRE-Drive improves diffusion-based planning through dynamic feasible anchor initialization, candidate-specific bird's-eye-view risk evidence, and compact high-quality candidate supervision with lightweight refinement. This design aligns the initial support, risk-aware scoring, and multimodal supervision of trajectory modes under a unified planning objective. It enables the diffusion decoder to focus on refining plausible trajectories while the scorer distinguishes modes using local risk evidence. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 show that FIRE-Drive achieves a Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 with a ResNet34 backbone. Additional closed-loop evaluation on 220 Bench2Drive routes yields a Driving Score of 71.43 and a Success Rate of 42.73%. Component ablations and a scorer comparison under matched candidate inputs support the contributions of feasible initialization, auxiliary supervision, and risk-informed selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/Latte00/FIRE-drive.
authors: Qifeng Xie, Kai-Yuan Feng, Wenkang Wan, Yue Wu, Maoguo Gong, Kai Sheng
bullets: Addresses infeasible noisy proposals, difficult mode selection, and weak supervision in diffusion planning.

Adds lightweight refinement and compact high-quality supervision to align multimodal planning.
Reports a NAVSIM v1 Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 and closed-loop results on 220 Bench2Drive routes, with ablations supporting its components.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.
authors: Selin Yildirim, Ali Zeyrek, Deming Chen
bullets: Speculative decoding performance varies substantially with GPU, concurrency, output length, draft length, and precision.
An analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and reduce the search space.
Calibration measurements guide a Jev-based predictor that selects high-throughput configurations on held-out GPUs.
Across four NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, full calibration achieved 2.01× AR throughput and 1.36× standard SD throughput; the predictor achieved 1.30× over SD.
The predictor retained 97.36% of full-calibration SpecSearch throughput while avoiding deployment-GPU calibration.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies fill their context with the demonstrations whose frames look most like the current observation under frozen DINOv2 embeddings. We ask whether visual similarity selects the demonstrations that make the policy succeed. For a frozen retrieval-augmented VLA (RICL on $\pi_0$-FAST, LIBERO), we make the demonstration pool swappable at run time and score each demonstration's utility by regressing the closed-loop success of 60 fixed-size pools on their membership. On initial states disjoint from those used for scoring, pools of the five highest-utility demonstrations succeed on 66.4% of 760 paired episodes across 19 tasks, pools of the five most similar on 55.7%, and random pools on 55.5%. Utility beats similarity by 10.8 points ($p=3.2\times10^{-6}$; positive on 15 of 18 untied tasks), including on 12 tasks the policy was never primed on, and similarity-selected pools do no better than random ($+0.1$ points). Within a task, a pool's visual similarity to the test scenes tracks its success at Spearman 0.10; across tasks, similarity separates tasks whose scenes differ and falls to chance when two tasks share a scene. The gain comes from on-task closed-loop evidence: best-of-ten direct search over pools recovers two-thirds of it with 100 rollouts. Against the shipped 20-demonstration pool, utility-curated pools of five lead by 7.0 points over 560 paired episodes from two evaluation runs ($p=0.006$), and utility-ordered retrieval inside the full pool leads by 4.5 points ($p=0.055$).
authors: Jiachen Li, Zhigen Zhao, Shihao Li, Dongmei Chen, Long Chen, Zhuo Xu
bullets: Utility-ranked pools of five achieved 66.4% success versus 55.7% for the five most visually similar and 55.5% for random pools across 760 paired episodes and 19 tasks.

Visual similarity was weakly related to within-task success and no better than chance when different tasks shared the same scene.
Directly searching for high-utility pools recovered two-thirds of the gain using 100 rollouts.

Utility-curated five-demonstration pools improved over the shipped 20-demonstration pool by 7.0 points; utility ordering within the full pool improved it by 4.5 points, with weaker statistical evidence.

papers.abstract: Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze $13\times13$, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on $9\times9$ and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.
authors: Xianyao Li, Ruitong Tian, Rui Min, Fang Xu, Jing Du
bullets: Addresses how physical agents can use visual or tactile information after it is no longer observable.

papers.abstract: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.
authors: Kaixin Li, Meng Luo, Yanlin Li, Yuchen Tian, Xiang Liu, Xiangru Jian, Yan Yang, Zhiheng Xi, Yang Zhang, Ziyang Luo, Mingfei Cheng, Hongzhan Lin

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

papers.abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl
authors: Abdullah Waqar Malik, Hamza Tariq, Adeel Akhtar
bullets: TFL controllers can become undefined at singularities such as zero speed or zero thrust, making their safe region of attraction important.
The constrained region of attraction is characterized as the largest forward-invariant subset of the admissible state set.
The method decomposes the Zubov value function into an analytic quadratic cost-to-go and a learned safety value function using fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels.
An interval branch-and-bound inner layer is formally verified, while a learned outer layer is evaluated on samples.
Coverage averaged 72.0%, 83.4%, and 19.1% for two unicycle tasks and a planar quadrotor, respectively; competing baselines reached at most 11.3%, 4.0%, and 0.0%.

papers.abstract: Accurate seasonal precipitation forecasts help societies prepare for drought, flooding, and crop failure months in advance. While data-driven methods have made rapid progress in weather and subseasonal forecasting, operational seasonal precipitation prediction still relies on numerical ensemble systems. These systems are computationally expensive and exhibit biases and drift that increase with lead time, motivating more efficient data-driven alternatives. Yet this transition faces three linked challenges: comparing data-driven forecasts with operational ones requires (1) a global benchmark that does not exist, scoring them requires (2) metrics that capture operational priorities beyond anomaly correlation (ACC) and RMSE, and training them must (3) rely on a single, short observational record. To address the first two challenges, we introduce \BenchName, the first such benchmark, covering monthly precipitation forecasts 1--5 months ahead. It pairs global $1^\circ$ satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, includes seven operational centers, and provides 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models for training. Beyond standard scores, we introduce two operationally motivated metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position. To address the third challenge, we develop \MODEL, which learns from simulations what the record lacks and transfers it to Earth through three modules: SimForced aligns the climate background, SimMemory transfers a history encoder pretrained on simulations, and SimAnalog supplements Earth labels with simulated analog outcomes. Extensive experiments show that \MODEL{} improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0\%, 3.6\%, 2.9\%, and 0.3\% over the strongest operational or data-driven model, opening a path from simulated worlds to Earth system prediction.
authors: Qiuyan Sun, Mengxuan Chen, Haoyuan Liang, Guowen Li, Zhen Huang, Jianhao Lin, Juepeng Zheng, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Addresses the lack of a global benchmark, operationally relevant metrics, and sufficient observational history for seasonal precipitation forecasting.
Covers monthly global precipitation forecasts at 1° resolution, includes seven operational centers, and provides simulated training data from 52 climate models.
Introduces metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position alongside standard ACC and RMSE-style evaluation.
MODEL uses simulated-data alignment, pretrained history representations, and simulated analog outcomes to transfer knowledge to Earth observations.
Experiments report improvements in ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position over the strongest baseline; the approach is evaluated within the benchmark’s global seasonal-forecasting scope.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.
authors: Yijun Sun, Xudong Liao, Zhuobin Huang, Kai Chen, Nikita Lazarev, Zhizhen Zhong
bullets: Problem: GPU HBM capacity limits serving concurrency because hot KV buffers and fully resident K-index caches consume substantial memory, even with scale-up memory pools.
Method: Dynamically selected KV entries use TMA-based retrieval fused with attention in a tile-level pipeline, while predictable K-index pages use GPU-initiated DMA prefetching.
Contribution: A sparse-attention offloading system implemented atop SGLang for scale-up memory expansion.

Results: On emulated scale-up memory, it achieves up to 4.98× and 4.52× higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, and up to 1.34× over naive same-platform integration across 16K–1M contexts.
Scope: Evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool.

papers.abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.
authors: Peng Yu, Xiaoyu Wen, Zhida He, Ziyuan Zhou, Han Qi, Shao Zhang, Qiaosheng Zhang, Ying Wen, Chaochao Lu
bullets: Addresses attacker strategy collapse and defender adversarial forgetting in evolving adversarial training.
Models attack diversity across risk categories and attack styles rather than relying on textual novelty.
Uses normalized marginal coverage gain to provide a bounded exploration signal for attackers.
Maintains a Bayesian adversarial replay pool with time-decayed Beta–Bernoulli posteriors and Thompson sampling.
Abstract reports improved out-of-distribution robustness, preserved general capabilities, and broader attack-strategy coverage across several benchmark types.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of DACE. Two phases: Phase 1 (Warm-up) SFTs the attacker on strategyconditioned CoT data to produce ⟨think, strategy, answer⟩ outputs. Phase 2 (Co-Evolution) alternates attacker-first: (i) attacker RL with normalized marginal coverage gain over the attack strategy space, and (ii) defender RL on a mixed batch Dtrain = Dnew ∪Dreplay of fresh and replayed attacks. The unified archive tracks both strategy frequencies (for the coverage reward) and per-entry Beta–Bernoulli threat posteriors (refreshed by per-round time decay and Thompson sampling).

papers.abstract: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.
authors: Ting-Hsuan Chen, Siheng Zhao, Han Jiang, Qi Pan, Louison Lu, Jiaheng Luo, Henghui Bao, Yiyu Chen, Quan Nguyen, Yue Wang
bullets: Addresses coordinated whole-body interaction, long-horizon planning, and synchronization in multi-humanoid collaboration.

Uses a vision-language planner and speech-based leader-follower mechanism for high-level coordination.
Introduces HH-Bench with 12 tasks spanning teams of 2–10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams.
Evaluations and real-world experiments show robust collaboration and consistent improvement over baseline methods.
