papers.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) foundation models provide transferable representations for diverse perception tasks in all-weather Earth observation. However, their development often relies on costly large-scale SAR pretraining, raising the question of whether such extensive domain-specific pretraining is necessary. We find that modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) already provide visual encoders that can outperform dedicated SAR foundation models as downstream initializations. This motivates a new paradigm: reuse general visual capabilities and devote domain training to brief specialization. We therefore introduce SARVIA, an adaptive post-pretraining method that specializes modern MLLMs using self-supervised visual questions with computable answers. These questions are constructed from unlabeled observations through general image tasks that capture spatial relations and SAR-specific tasks that exploit native measurements and SAR--optical correspondence. A shared answer-prediction objective jointly trains low-rank adapters across visual and language components, with loss-driven task sampling. We then export the adapted visual encoder as a standalone backbone. With 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models on all six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks. Compared with dedicated SAR pretraining, SARVIA reduces domain-training costs by orders of magnitude while improving visual transfer across architectures and scales. This new paradigm shifts the emphasis from repeated, costly pretraining to a reusable specialization process that can benefit from advances in open MLLMs. Dataset and code: https://github.com/zcablii/SARVIA.
authors: Yuxuan Li, Zichen Tian, Qianru Sun
bullets: Motivation: Large-scale SAR-specific pretraining is costly, and modern MLLM visual encoders can provide strong downstream initializations.
Method: Adapt MLLMs with self-supervised visual questions derived from unlabeled imagery, combining general spatial tasks with SAR-specific measurements and SAR–optical correspondence.
Optimization: Jointly train low-rank adapters across visual and language components using a shared answer-prediction objective and loss-driven task sampling.
Result: Using 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models across six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks.
Scope: The adapted visual encoder is exported as a standalone backbone, emphasizing reusable specialization rather than repeated SAR pretraining.

papers.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking has enabled humanoid dancing, athletic motions, and teleoperation, providing a foundation for capability demonstrations and manipulation data collection. However, existing tracking policies lack awareness of nearby humans and proactive avoidance capabilities, while motion substitution and local constraint-based corrections may compromise reference motion integrity and tracking continuity. We propose ALERT, a general lightweight pipeline for extending motion tracking to shared human-robot environments. Through lightweight adaptation, it integrates human perception and proactive avoidance into pretrained tracking policies, balancing avoidance demands with reference motion tracking while preserving existing motion capabilities. Simulation and real-world experiments across tracking backbones demonstrate reliable collision-free execution through localized human avoidance, preserving whole-body coordination and enabling rapid recovery of reference tracking, while retaining the ability of pretrained policies to track unseen motions.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.
authors: Hejia Zhang, Zhongming Yu, Yimin Ding, Wei-Ting Chen, Hengjia Yu, Wentao Ni, Yijun Liu, Cong Xu, Xin Chen, Matrix Yao, Fan Zhao, Jishen Zhao
bullets: Problem: Separate worker contexts can prevent the lead agent from accessing all evidence needed to identify factual conflicts.
Method: Introduces a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler using controlled conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks.
Delegation raised retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7%, but lowered conflict detection from 16.2% to 13.2% across three models.
Workers reported both claims in only 35.2% of retrieved conflict pairs; detection was better when one worker saw both claims than when claims were split across workers.
Scope: Results concern the evaluated models and Harvey LAB document-review setting.

papers.abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

Shorter prompts may trigger more agent steps, offsetting token savings.
Concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes, distorting cost comparisons; evaluation should account for token prices and subsequent behavior.

papers.abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.
authors: Himanshu Mishra
bullets: Scoring final-answer tokens saturates because answers are already stated in the chain of thought, causing major accuracy losses versus scoring reasoning tokens.
Causal importance is not reliably localized to individual neurons; stable attribution emerges only for groups of roughly 100 neurons.
Reasoning-specific importance cannot be cleanly separated from generic importance and performs worse when used for protection.
Perplexity can mask pruning damage, so accuracy is the preferred evaluation metric.
The study recommends scoring reasoning tokens, attributing importance at coarse granularity, and evaluating with accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Pruning reasoning language models and importance attribution directly fits efficient AI model compression.
papers.title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
papers.tldr: Attribution-guided pruning for reasoning language models is highly sensitive to how importance is measured, making naive pruning decisions unreliable.

papers.abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.
authors: Rapha\"el S\'egas, Bal\'azs Opra, L\'eo Ghafari, Thomas Stewart
bullets: A 13-node lumped RC thermal model predicts all 12 motor temperatures across robots, gaits, payloads, and speeds with mean RMSE below 1°C.
The policy minimizes predicted long-term motor-temperature asymptotes based on gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds.
This bypasses slow thermal dynamics: asymptotes respond within one gait cycle, enabling reinforcement-learning credit assignment without temperature input.
On a Unitree Go2 carrying 5 kg at 1 m/s, runtime increased from 19 to 174 minutes, while distance increased from 1.1 to 10.0 km.
On an unloaded circuit with stairs and ramps, the policy completed 47 laps versus 25 for the baseline, retaining 22°C of thermal margin.

papers.abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.
authors: Fengyuan Liu, Jay Gala, Siva Reddy, Dzmitry Bahdanau
bullets: MoE expert parallelism is bottlenecked by synchronous inter-device communication, especially as compute outpaces network bandwidth.
EchoMoE uses an earlier-layer hidden state as a reference and transmits only compressed differences, with periodic reference refreshes.
The method can retrofit pretrained MoE models with roughly 8,500× fewer training tokens than full pretraining and little computational overhead.
It reduces inter-node communication by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while keeping average benchmark performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks.
The approach supports quantized communication without measurable quality loss and provides integrations for pretrained models and vLLM.

papers.tldr: EchoMoE accelerates distributed MoE inference by communicating compressed changes to hidden states instead of full activations.

papers.abstract: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. Supplements are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/joint-id/home

papers.abstract: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from images is important for applications such as gaming and augmented reality. Feedforward methods make avatar reconstruction accessible by reducing inference time to a few seconds, but recent approaches rely heavily on scaling model capacity, training data, and computation. We ask whether such scaling is necessary. To this end, we introduce ARG-Avatar, an efficient feedforward framework with only 68M trainable parameters that achieves SOTA reconstruction quality. Our key insight is that 3D animation and rendering already provide strong geometric correspondences that existing methods largely attempt to learn from data. In light of this, we design the Foreground Avatar Coordinate RoPE attention (FACRoPE) and Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR) pipeline to guide avatar tokens to attend to their corresponding patches. Experiments across multiple datasets show that ARG-Avatar consistently outperforms prior methods when using two or more input images. Compared with LHM++, ARG-Avatar uses approximately 9$\times$ fewer trainable parameters, 4.8$\times$ fewer training sequences, and 14$\times$ less training compute, while running 6$\times$ faster and achieving a 2.7 dB PSNR improvement on the out-of-distribution NeuMan benchmark.
authors: Jianjin Xu, Soham Dasgupta, Fernando De la Torre

Outperforms prior methods across multiple datasets with two or more input images.
Compared with LHM++, uses about 9× fewer parameters, 4.8× fewer training sequences, and 14× less compute; it runs 6× faster and improves NeuMan PSNR by 2.7 dB.

papers.abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets memory-bound attention caused by repeatedly reading growing historical KV caches.
Builds shared read plans from seed queries using exact priority and recovery tiers, while recomputing attention with fresh queries and current-block KV.
Protects potentially useful history from permanent eviction and amortizes sparse-support construction without modifying the backbone or decoder.
On DreamReasoner-8B, it preserves comparable task performance and reports up to 5.53× attention speedup at 128K context.
Across eight settings and three models, it decodes faster than tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

papers.abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.
authors: Ege Kaya (University of British Columbia)
bullets: The study examines whether 4-bit safety shifts are caused by quantization generally or by a particular weight perturbation.
Across three 3–4B chat models, Qwen2.5-3B produced more harmful continuations in one test, while Llama-3.2-3B complied less often on held-out jailbreaks.
Matched shuffled and Gaussian perturbations averaged near zero, whereas scaling the real quantization error changed behaviour approximately linearly.
Llama-3.2-3B already complied 5.8 percentage points less often at half the real error, despite nearly unchanged likelihood.
The findings suggest each quantized build should be evaluated against its original model; results were obtained in this pre-registered study using paired tests, blind human labels, and an 8-bit null.

papers.abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.
authors: Soham Dan
bullets: Rendered scenes isolate five 3-D relations, with the image cue correct for half of the statements and wrong for the other half.
At low reasoning effort, three frontier models show shortcut gaps of +18 to +37 percentage points, or +7 to +29 when confounded relations are excluded.
When given ground coordinates and relation definitions, the models reach 99–100% accuracy, locating the main failure in image-to-layout reasoning.
Top-down scene maps usually preserve depth order but compress depth; GPT-5.5 largely copies the image, while Opus 5.5 and Gemini partially undo the compression.
The models also lose accuracy on photographs when reliable 2-D cues conflict with the true relation; pixel measurements with camera depths reduce the gap for objects fitting through openings.

papers.abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.
authors: Jingyu Liu, Zongze Li, Zach Xu, Zhanhui Zhou, Tahseen Rabbani, Dawn Song, Ce Zhang
bullets: BRIDGE uses chained observation notes, hybrid BM25–cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering with one LLM call per ingestion or query.
It matches prior state of the art on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and outperforms the best matched-reader baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7–6.3 points.
BRIDGE operates at roughly 5–7K reader-prompt tokens per query, suggesting many advanced memory primitives may not justify their cost on standard benchmarks.
Five adversarial probes show no architecture wins universally: atomic-fact extraction favors rule application, while block summaries favor pattern induction.
Retrieval benchmarks miss failures in how agents use memories: fact extractors lose demonstrated patterns, while block summaries may retrieve rules without prompting action.

papers.title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
papers.tldr: A minimal RAG memory can match complex memory systems on recall benchmarks, but agentic memory should be judged by what retrieved information enables agents to do.

papers.abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.
authors: Daehee Lee, Dongsu Lee, Sanghyun Ahn, Minjong Yoo, Honguk Woo
bullets: Targets reconfigurability: assembling new behaviors from existing skills under sparse task and procedure specifications.
Represents skills through multiple task-agnostic procedure views and stores their induced transitions in a knowledge base.
Resolves task-specific compositional queries over stored relations to bind executable skill sequences.
On an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, reports 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms task inference per episode.
Real-robot studies show adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

papers.abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.
authors: Guochen Zhou, Yijun Yang, Qiqi Duan, Qing Su, Weiming Ou, Li Shen, Shihao Ji, Yuhui Shi, Zhisong Zhang
bullets: Offline-to-online distribution shifts make it difficult to choose a fixed optimism–pessimism balance.
Optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, while pessimistic policies perform better on familiar online tasks.
The method formulates the trade-off as a bi-objective problem and constructs a Pareto policy pool with MOSAIC.
A hierarchical contextual bandit selects the most suitable policy during online fine-tuning.
HiP3 achieves the strongest aggregate performance across same and novel tasks, including under stronger distribution shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3). In the offline stage (gray box), our MOSAIC algorithm generates a diverse pool of Pareto policies exhibiting varying optimism-pessimism trade-offs via multi-objective optimization with reference vectors and neighborhood search. In the online stage (blue box), a contextual bandit (LinUCB [33]) selects a candidate policy conditioned on the current state from the top-K subset; the selected policy is then fine-tuned via a Dyna-style method [15].

Figure 1: (a) Pareto policy pool discovered by HiP3, containing policies with different optimism-pessimism trade-offs. (b) On the novel online task (details in Appendix C.1), optimistic P1 achieves the highest return. (c) On the same online task, pessimistic P4 achieves the highest return. Together, these results motivate preserving multiple trade-off policies offline and deferring the choice among them to online adaptation, rather than committing to a single trade-off in advance.

papers.abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.
authors: Zhekai Wang, Luqing Luo, Wenhao Yao, Junjie Lu, Huanan Zhu, Feifei Gao, Yuhua Jiang
bullets: Targets border misses, occlusion errors, and temporal jitter in egocentric 3D hand pose estimation.

Accepts refinements only when they improve all ten benchmark metrics without significant regression.
Reduces MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC, while roughly halving jitter.
Provides Lite, Medium, and Heavy accuracy-speed variants; code, evaluators, harnesses, and weights are public.

papers.abstract: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.
authors: Kailin Wang, Haoxiang Jie, Yaoyuan Yan, Zhiyou Heng, Zhaosong Li
bullets: EgoHandWAM predicts future wrist/fingertip trajectories and visual features from current images and recent hand states.

Future-feature supervision leaves trajectory accuracy nearly unchanged.
Recorded hand history improves visual-feature prediction; shuffling histories removes the gain, indicating session-specific temporal information.
Observed future displacements and tracking-validity masks help in a four-task probe, while predicted trajectories and human examples do not consistently improve RoboTwin success.

papers.abstract: HandUMI captures robot-free bimanual demonstrations with a hand-worn parallel-jaw interface. Swappable fingertips match the robot's installed gripper; Quest/PICO controllers track hands and encoders measure aperture. Robot-agnostic recordings are retargeted by inverse kinematics to seven simulated bimanual arms (median position error $\leq 1.2$ mm; $\leq 4.7$% of episodes rejected). On bimanual towel folding, 562 robot-free demonstrations train policies on real PiPER arms: ACT succeeds in 12/20 attempts and fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ in 7/20; ACT on the first 101 and base $\pi_{0.5}$ each succeed in 0/20. Hardware and software are open source (Apache-2.0), and a pair costs USD 557 with Quest 3S, excluding the optional ZED Mini and host computer. Project website: https://murobotics.ai/research/handumi.

papers.abstract: Short-video platforms are now a common way for the public to follow unfolding events. Their rapid, visually persuasive format also makes fake news easier to spread. Unlike text-image posts, short-video news interleaves multiple modalities and changing scenes, making it difficult to identify which frames verify a claim. Existing detectors either pool sampled frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity. Both overlook that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim, whereas less dominant context may challenge it. We present CEVA (Complementary Evidence Verification Approach), to our knowledge the first short-video fake news detection framework to explicitly organize frames by their evidential roles before multimodal fusion. Its Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames, and cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization operates on the reorganized evidence. On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among the compared methods. Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors. Together, these results establish pre-fusion evidence organization as an effective and transferable component of short-video fake news detection.
authors: Wenshen Yang, Junfeng Hao, Jing Li, Decheng Liu, Yangkunfei, Shuyu Jiang, Haizhou Wang
bullets: Short videos combine changing visual scenes and multiple modalities, making relevant verification frames difficult to identify.
CEVA’s DBCR module separates explicitly aligned frames from potentially complementary context frames.
Bidirectional contrastive regularization is applied during cross-modal fusion of the reorganized evidence.
CEVA achieves the best overall results among compared methods on FakeSV and FakeTT.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.
authors: Changxuan Fan, Zhongwei Xie, Boyi Zhang, Shaoli Hu, Chang Xu, Xiyu Ren, Yufei Li, Qiao Xiao, Huihao Jing, Kawai Chung, Wenbin Hu, Hongyu Luo, Lingyun Xie, Yisen Gao, Chunyang Li, Haoyu Huang, Wuganjing Song, Yuxuan Liu, Chiu Yeung Tang, Fangneng Zhan, Xi Yang

Agents must act from camera images alone while the environment continues running, without ground-truth object positions.
The adaptive system completes 28 tasks with gpt-6.1-sol and 27 with opus-5.5; four other models complete at most 3.
Adaptive, single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized systems achieve similar task counts but trade off speed and token use.
No evaluated model or control system is simultaneously fast, inexpensive, and reliable; retries are common and tasks can take hours.

papers.abstract: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.
authors: Joel Sadler, Daniel Graham, Melanie Worley
bullets: Addresses the need for accessible, automated monitoring of fruit-fly lifecycle transitions that are often recorded manually.
Uses a single-board Linux computer, day/night camera, deterministic image capture every ten minutes, and a cloud-based coding agent operating through the device.
The agent helps configure capture, repair software errors, monitor experiments, and notify researchers when recording stops.
A 26-day pilot produced about 3,580 frames; capture continued during 11 days of agent logout, while a 51-hour outage informed the layered system design.
Pupariation curves were generated through a researcher-in-the-loop workflow; accuracy validation and real-time computer vision remain future work.

(3) After eclosion, the adult flies that emerge can be imaged and analyzed with computer vision for assisted phenotyping, shown here with a segmentation model measuring a wing.

papers.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).
authors: Hang Zhang, Qijian Tian, Yuan Xie, Xuhong Wang, Xin Tan
bullets: Motivation: LEGO generation must ensure physical support and prevent bricks from being blocked during construction.
Method: A versioned construction SDK compiles decisions from semantic subparts to individual bricks into canonical building operations.
Verification: A Meta-Reviewer replays the generated model and construction process, diagnoses failures, and routes bounded repairs.
Contribution: The system produces models and instructions suitable for both human builders and robot assembly.
Results: Experiments report better performance than recent agentic systems and demonstrate downstream robot-manipulation utility.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Liang Ma, Manoj Rao
bullets: Quantization generally makes models effectively “warmer” and increases their sensitivity to sampling temperature.
TempQuant learns decoding settings without labeled answers to align quantized next-token probabilities with those of the full-precision model.
It supports global settings per requested temperature and token-level adaptive temperature/top-p settings.
On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, global TempQuant improved MATH accuracy from 34% to 51% under the compared recommended configuration.
The method is most useful when quantization causes substantial degradation, while also improving behavioral similarity under lighter degradation.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) is essential for detecting objects beyond the categories seen during training. Establishing vision-language associations is crucial for recognizing unseen categories, while integrating complementary visual features across levels supports detection at different scales. However, existing methods often provide insufficient textual guidance for object regions, rely on limited cross-modal alignment strategies, and underuse complementary features across levels, limiting their ability to detect unseen categories and objects of varying scales. To address these limitations, we propose a Text-Guided Modality Correction Network (TMCNet) that incorporates textual guidance into region feature extraction, cross-modal alignment, and multi-scale decoding to strengthen region-category semantic correspondence and promote complementary feature fusion across levels. First, a text-guided modality encoder incorporates textual semantics into queries to guide regional feature aggregation, reducing semantic ambiguity in object representations. Second, a cross-modal alignment module strengthens the correspondence between region representations and category semantics through interactions between visual and textual features. Finally, a progressive text correction decoder combines a top-down pathway with lateral connections to progressively fuse text-guided deep semantic features with shallow visual features at the corresponding scales, preserving both semantic information and spatial detail for objects of different sizes. Experiments on two public datasets, COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD, demonstrate that TMCNet achieves strong performance in open-vocabulary object detection using simple text queries as guidance. Extending TMCNet to open-vocabulary segmentation also yields performance gains, demonstrating its cross-task applicability and extensibility.
authors: Yu Quan, Dong Zhang, Ping Gong, Peng Huang, JinHui Tang
bullets: Targets weak textual guidance, limited vision-language alignment, and underused multi-scale features in OVD.
Uses a text-guided modality encoder to incorporate category semantics into regional feature aggregation.

papers.abstract: Segmenting small parts on high-resolution 3D scans, such as nails on hand scans and teeth on intraoral scans, poses three challenges: 1) each part covers a tiny fraction of the scan, 2) its boundary is only a subtle change of height and curvature, and 3) it faces its own direction. Existing methods fall into two groups, and both fall short. The first group processes the whole scan at once and sees each part too coarsely. Point and mesh networks must shrink the scan to fit in memory, so a small part keeps only a few of its points. Multi-view methods render images of the whole object, so each part fills only a few pixels and a tilted part is seen from the side. The second group first finds each part and then segments it up close. But these methods find the parts with knowledge about one kind of part, for example the shape of the dental arch for teeth. Such knowledge does not carry over to other kinds of parts. We find that accuracy is limited by how a part is seen, from which direction and at what scale, not by how many points land on it. We therefore present FrameSeg3D. It first predicts a local frame for every part, its center and the direction it faces, from a low-resolution view of the whole scan. It then segments the part in views around its frame normal at the scanner's resolution, so covering the whole scan no longer costs resolution. Because every part arrives centered, facing the camera, and at a fixed scale, one segmentation network can serve different kinds of parts and learn from few labeled masks. We test FrameSeg3D on two kinds of parts, nails and teeth. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on hand scans (mean Dice 0.970 on nails) and on the Teeth3DS+ test fold (per-tooth IoU 96.5), with the most accurate tooth boundaries (boundary IoU 70.5).
authors: Xinwen Zhang, Tongyan Wang, Huawei Lin
bullets: Small parts are difficult to segment because they occupy few points or pixels, have subtle boundaries, and face different directions.
The method predicts a center and facing direction for each part from a low-resolution whole-scan view.
It then creates normalized, high-resolution views around each local frame for segmentation, avoiding whole-scan resolution loss.
A shared segmentation network can handle different part types and learn from few labeled masks.
On nails and teeth, it reports mean Dice 0.970, per-tooth IoU 96.5, and boundary IoU 70.5.

papers.abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Builds concept- or role-specific expert paths from frequently used experts and biases router logits toward those paths during generation.
Format-path steering changes the form of generated text, while concept-path steering shifts next-token probabilities with limited impact on text.
Concept paths identified in another language can still produce a concept-related probability shift.
Partial-generation experiments suggest formats become self-reinforcing once initiated; concept effects are strongest for religion and money and in middle layers.
Variation across concepts is examined through embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

papers.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

papers.abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
authors: Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan
bullets: Addresses stale long-term memories and delayed feedback when memory validity is hidden.
Maintains Local and Global Advisors, using comparisons with a no-memory answer as evidence.
A Meta Governor defaults to local updates and switches to global sharing only after positive pooled utility accumulates.
Provides a finite-time switching guarantee under delayed feedback.
Outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2–7.3 points across reported disagreement episodes and held-out settings; removing modules lowers accuracy by 2–7 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RegimeCouncil. (1) At step t, a query arrives for key kt; whether the stored record is valid is hidden from the prompt, and the router chooses between injecting memory (at=1) and using the no-memory anchor (at=0). (2) The Global Advisor pools recent paired outcomes across all keys, whereas the Local Advisor reads only the latest revealed outcome on key kt. (3) The Meta Governor compares what each advisor would have scored over recent revealed episodes, follows Local by default, and switches to Global only when At > 0. (4) After a delay of at most τ steps, the episode’s paired outcome arrives and updates both advisors and the governor.

Figure 1: Three regimes of influence scale, i.e., the propagation scope of delayed feedback: (1) a single fact when drift is isolated; (2) a store-wide use-threshold after a cluster of corrections; and (3) a cold-start prior from pooled outcomes when the queried fact has no local history.

Without the Meta Governor (§3.5) the row falls below either advisor alone in all four settings (on Schedule A, 6.8 points on Qwen and 6.5 on GPT-4o; 21.8 and 17.2 disagreement-slice points). papers.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Xiaojin Fu, Tao Zhong, Linqi Song
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed memory-update operators and schedules in evolving LLM-agent memory.
Uses a policy conditioned on memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate Abstract, Refine, Bridge, or Reframe operators.
Trains the policy with bi-level fitness: transformation-level retrieval gains regularized by memory complexity, and strategy-level historical efficacy, prediction accuracy, and diversity.
Evaluated under one-pass online plus frozen-transfer settings on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB).
Reports improvements over MemP and MemRL, with the largest ALFWorld gains; ablations support the importance of both fitness levels and the operator library.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EvoDisco. A frozen language model interacts with a one-pass task stream, retrieves a subgraph, and writes new memories after each episode. A strategy policy reads the memory-graph state and selects one of four operators—ABSTRACT, REFINE, BRIDGE, and REFRAME—which the operator executor applies to the graph. Immediate utility scores each edit by the change in retrieval quality regularized by graph complexity. Every N events, strategic efficacy combines operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity, and updates the policy. Evolution runs only before the cutoff; afterward the agent continues to write memories. Held-out evaluation freezes the accumulated memory.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.
authors: Thorben Prein, Elton Pan, Rafael G\'omez-Bombarelli, Santiago Miret
bullets: Motivation: Experiments provide coupled molecular and spectral measurements, but conventional models often use only one conditioning direction.
Method: Randomly masks modalities and trains a transformer on multiple denoising tasks across 3D structures, UV, IR, and Raman spectra.
Contribution: A single model supports flexible any-to-any generation and arbitrary subsets of available measurements.
Result: On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, with reported gains over spectra-to-structure and specialist structure-to-spectra baselines.
Scope: The approach also supports molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references; ablations show benefits over structure-only training across model sizes.

papers.abstract: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).
authors: Qingyuan Tang (Shanghai Jiaotong University), He Zhu (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Shixuan Sun (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Anbang Wu (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Jingwen Leng (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Minyi Guo (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Yu Feng (Shanghai Jiaotong University)
bullets: Addresses the high cost of evaluating deformation networks for every Gaussian at every frame in 4DGS.
Uses a frozen pretrained backbone, local temporal prediction, and a lightweight router to select exact updates within an offline-calibrated scene budget.
Selection considers prediction reliability and rendering contribution; selected Gaussians are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead.
Drift-triggered full-deformation frames periodically rebuild prediction history and limit accumulated error.
Across four 4DGS algorithms, achieves up to 6.74× speedup on Jetson AGX Orin and 8.15× on Orin NX, with at most a 0.16 dB average PSNR drop.

The merged state is rendered and stored in history. (3) Adaptive refresh uses drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild history, with partial precomputation after target timestamps are fixed.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.
authors: Boyu Han, Qianqian Xu, Shilong Bao, Zhiyong Yang, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses the conflict between contrastive discrimination and generative reconstruction in visual encoders for MLLMs.
Recasts reconstruction as a ranking problem that scores matched outputs above mismatched ones.
Introduces AUCGR for AUC-based ranking and pAUCGR for focusing on reliable mismatched comparisons to reduce supervision bias.
The objectives are plug-and-play and require no architectural changes.
Experiments report improved discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation, supported by theoretical generalization analysis.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. An overview of our method. (a) A generic comparison principle for generative reconstruction. (b) AUC-oriented instantiations, including AUCGR and pAUCGR. (c) Reconstruction learning pipeline. Our method serves as a plug-and-play optimization module that replaces the original optimization strategy in existing reconstruction learning methods, thereby yielding balanced enhanced visual representations.

Fig. 10. Ablation study on different generative model structures. We evaluate our method with Stable Diffusion v1.5, Stable Diffusion v2.1, and Rectified Flow as the generative reconstruction backbone. All experiments use OpenAI CLIP ViT-L@224 as the visual backbone. The results show that our framework is not tied to a specific generative architecture and consistently improves both P-Ability and D-Ability.

Fig. 1. Motivation of our method. (a) Reconstructive learning improves P-Ability by preserving a sparser representation space. (b) Contrastive learning improves D-Ability by organizing representations into compact semantic clusters. (c) The naive method searches for a balanced representation through heuristic weight tuning between contrastive learning and reconstructive learning, but the proper weights are difficult to determine. (d) The target balanced representation, which is directly optimized by our method without heuristic weight tuning.

Fig. 2. Training results of linearly combining contrastive learning and reconstructive learning (Naive Method) on the OpenAI CLIP ViT-L@224 backbone, which verify that the naive method indeed falls into the Tragic Triad regime.

Fig. 19. Computational costs under different batch sizes. Training time and GPU memory are measured for our method on DIVA with OpenAI CLIP ViT-L@224. The pairwise objective constructs a B ×B score matrix, so its per-batch computation and intermediate storage scale as O(B2). We use B = 16 in all experiments because it provides a favorable balance between performance and resource consumption.
Fig. 16. Expanded qualitative results on the MLLM benchmarks. Ours denotes the model that replaces the original CLIP vision encoder with the pAUCGR-enhanced CLIP encoder.

Fig. 9. Ablation comparison with naive linear weighting and gradient-balancing methods. We evaluate the trade-off between P-Ability and D-Ability on two generative reconstruction baselines, DIVA and GenHancer, across OpenAI CLIP ViT-L@224 (O-1), MetaCLIP ViT-L@224 (M1), and SigLIP ViT-SO@224 (S-1). Here, D-Ability is measured by ACC on zero-shot clustering benchmarks, while +N, +P, +C, and +G denote +Naive, +PCGrad, +CAGrad, and +GradNorm, respectively. Compared with both naive linear weighting and gradient-balancing methods, AUCGR and pAUCGR achieve a better balance between the two abilities.

Fig. 12. Expanded qualitative results of AUCGR on the MMVP-VLM benchmark. The predictions from the original CLIP and the AUCGRenhanced CLIP are indicated by red and green arrows, respectively. AUCGR helps the model capture fine-grained visual details that are missed by the original CLIP.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.
authors: Zewen Huang, Xiangwen Zhuge, Yingkun Hu, Zheng Yang, Qiang Ma
bullets: Targets underutilized cloud-GPU decoding and the limited concurrency of edge FPGAs.
Assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding based on accelerator capacity, queue load, prompt length, and network state.
Reduces offloading overhead using pipelined layer transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV-cache compression.
On a V100–Alveo U280 prototype, achieves up to 4.11× request goodput and 61.1% lower mean latency than cloud-only vLLM at 500 Mbps.
Benefits are strongest for communication-intensive workloads and include lower per-request energy, with performance dependent on network conditions.

papers.abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Ying Wu, Chen Jiang, Randy Freeman
bullets: Addresses the limitation of binary safety constraints in safety-critical navigation.
Estimates kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal risks for objects and people.

Demonstrated in a simulated restaurant scene; broader real-world performance is not established in the abstract.
