papers.abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.
authors: R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy
bullets: Addresses the limitation of pairwise latent-action learning, which may miss how physical transitions evolve over time.
Uses a shared inverse dynamics model for compact latent actions and a recurrent latent world model for multi-step JEPA feature prediction.
Transfers the learned representation to a vision-language model through latent distillation and recurrent future-feature prediction, then adapts it with action flow matching.
At deployment, removes the auxiliary latent-action and world-model branches so the VLM directly predicts robot actions.
Achieves 97.9% on LIBERO, 70.0% on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations, and ranks second on both LARY metrics among compared methods.

papers.abstract: When applied to two-dimensional features such as images, Mamba-based methods either flatten the feature map into 1D sequences and fuse multiple scans, which breaks spatial adjacency and multiplies computation, or recurse directly on the 2D grid but rescale the recurrence with a fixed input-independent factor and aggregate only the predecessors on a single anti-diagonal, leaving the discrete step unconstrained by 2D stability theory. We propose \textbf{FM-Mamba}, a native 2D selective state space model built on the general Fornasini--Marchesini (FM) model. Its coupled recurrence evolves along both spatial axes; cross-axis coupling induces a discrete diagonal-predecessor term $\tilde A_0$, and two independent input-dependent step sizes $\Delta_1(i,j)$, $\Delta_2(i,j)$ govern propagation along the two axes, so that the coefficients adapt per position and per direction. A normalized ratio $r_k=a_{0,k}/(a_{1,k}a_{2,k})$ yields a closed-form piecewise bound on the two step sizes; when a configuration falls outside the stable interval the steps are projected onto this bound, and the criterion is re-verified per position after training, which suppresses systematic local amplification without global damping. The recurrence is executed by a dual-diagonal wavefront scan: each update gathers information from two anti-diagonals, and the input enters the current state through a single projection, so that neither training nor inference flattens the feature map. Code is available at https://github.com/BitSsm/FM-Mamba-Runtime
authors: Shengyuan Hu, Yiyong Sun, Weihang Shan, Yongzhe Chang
bullets: Addresses inefficiency and spatial-adjacency loss from flattening 2D features, as well as stability limitations in prior recursive 2D Mamba methods.
Uses the Fornasini–Marchesini model with coupled recurrences along both spatial axes and a diagonal-predecessor interaction.
Employs two input-dependent step sizes per position and direction, constrained by a closed-form stability bound and projected when unstable.
Implements a dual-diagonal wavefront scan without flattening during training or inference.

papers.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
authors: Hyunjong Ok, Jaeho Lee
bullets: Three frontier LLMs were given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox to generate weights or design architectures.
On mainly multiple-choice tasks, LLM-designed sparse tables reached up to 54.4% test accuracy.
One designed model outperformed the best released Transformer written by the same LLM while using about 1,800× fewer parameters.
The table structure makes facts interpretable and locally editable: each row corresponds to an answer and errors identify rows to revise.
The proposed associative-memory model was up to 17× faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer; pretrained LLMs remained more accurate.

papers.abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.
authors: Jiang Xiaobo, Dinghong Lai
bullets: LAS identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as key sources of generation difficulty and performance variation.
DSADiff combines these factors into a unified generation-difficulty representation.
The representation guides both feature modeling and training-strategy optimization across samples with different structures and difficulty levels.
Across three CSP benchmarks, including Carbon-24, DSADiff improves Match Rate and RMSE, with up to a 9% Match Rate gain.
The method reports new state-of-the-art performance and offers a framework for analyzing and reducing bias in complex materials spaces.

papers.abstract: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.
authors: Zhixu Du, Kuo Yang, Jingwei Sun, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: Inference quality varies substantially with how a fixed computation budget is allocated along the denoising trajectory.
BATMoS routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser.
A magnitude-based temporal rule reuses guidance in low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh evaluations elsewhere, controlled by one integer budget parameter.
On CogVideoX-2B across all 16 VBench dimensions, it achieves the best score among eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full guidance with 20% fewer branch evaluations.
Combined with feature reuse, it reduces effective branch evaluations from 80 to 62 with a 0.11-point score decrease.

papers.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.
authors: Muhammed Fatih Bal{\i}n
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of independently rounded INT4/FP4 values and the large tables or restricted decoders of prior trellis codes.
Decodes 1–6-bit formats by multiplying a state by two coefficients, using product top bits to index a compact 64-byte table.
Comes within 0.07 bits of the information-theoretic ideal at 4 bits and matches a random-permutation trellis code with a table thousands of times larger.
Achieves the lowest reported KL divergence across tested bit widths for Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP codebooks, by up to 27%.
Runs at native FP4/FP8 throughput on AWS Trainium 4 with negligible systolic-array area; scope is tensor quantization without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: World models have shown great potential in serving as a simulator for robot manipulation. However, existing models are either fit to a single environment or lack ability to simulate long-horizon contact-rich events. We present DreamFAR, a world model whose dynamics model is trained from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, with no internet-video pretraining. We present an architecture and learning recipe designed for training on robot-native data. DreamFAR is significantly smaller than the high-performance video generation models, yet shows better understanding of contact and causality, and runs 10 FPS on a commercial GPU. Experimentally, DreamFAR significantly outperforms existing models in predicting the long-horizon future. We further demonstrate various applications where DreamFAR can be used, including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training. Project page: https://www.yimingdou.com/DreamFAR/
authors: Yiming Dou, Botao He, Antonio Loquercio, Andrew Owens, Jitendra Malik, Sumedh Anand Sontakke, Ruoshi Liu
bullets: Addresses the limited environment scope and poor long-horizon contact simulation of existing world models.
Trains from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, without internet-video pretraining.
Introduces an architecture and learning recipe tailored to robot-native data.
Runs at 10 FPS on a commercial GPU while outperforming existing models on long-horizon future prediction.
Supports applications including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Contact-based memory keeps placed objects persistent. Three models with the same architecture but different memory selection. We show one frame from a rollout of each model. Without memory the bin is empty, sparse time-strided memory hallucinates its contents, and contact-based memory matches the real observation.

Figure 2: Overview of DreamFAR: (a) Each view is encoded as per-position latents projected onto the unit sphere and decoded by a flow decoder. (b) When the robot makes or breaks contact with an object, we insert the corresponding keyframe into contact memory, which are index by end effector pose. (c) We use a transformer that has a number of design decisions that make it well suited to streaming and long-horizon generation.

Figure 5: Metric Drift on ABC over one minute. We evaluate the video prediction performance of DreamFAR and the existing baseline models on standard video quality metrics, including PSNR, LPIPS and FID. We run 60-s rollout (600 frames) on 1,000 held-out episodes and average the results into 10-s bins. DreamFAR degrades the slowest on all three metrics and significantly outperforms all baseline models, indicating the stability of its long-horizon prediction.

Figure 4: Visual comparison against baselines on a long-horizon prediction. We run 60-s rollout on an episode of “write a sentence on a whiteboard” task, and qualitatively compare DreamFAR against the existing baseline models. IWS collapses within seconds, WEAVER hallucinates texture drastically in the wrist view, Cosmos-Predict 2.5 drifts and over-sharpens texture, while DreamFAR manages to keep the scene layout and the manipulated objects consistent over the whole minute, and it even predicts the writings on the whiteboard that is visually similar to the GT.

Figure 6: Policy evaluation inside DreamFAR against the real robot. We run policy evaluation on both the real robot and inside the DreamFAR. (a) shows the task progress over time for one episode of the “t-shirt folding” task, on the real robot (×) and inside DreamFAR (◦). (b) summarizes the mean progress per policy and task. The simulator is generally optimistic in absolute progress but preserves the ranking on two of three tasks.

Figure 3: Rollouts on diverse interactions. DreamFAR predicts accurate dynamics across diverse interactions, including compositional assembly (Lego), tool and container use (bags, bread, plates) and deformable objects (skirt).

Figure 7: Co-training with demonstrations collected inside DreamFAR. DreamFAR enables real-time teleoperation without a real robot, and we collect 75 demonstrations of the “place bags of chips into a basket” task in both real and simulated environments. The π0 policy finetuned on the combination of both nearly doubles the real-only performance.

Metrics against the real video are averaged over the two wrist views. DINO is the cosine similarity of DINOv2 features (Oquab et al., 2023). Contact-based memory achieves the best performance on every metric.

papers.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
authors: Ziv Kfir, Ido Kfir
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra derivation between stored conversations and assistant queries.
Restores cached sessions and appends the question, while retaining raw text as the authoritative fallback.
Defines budget-based retention, append-only reads, bounded aggregation, and a cost model for storage and querying.
Estimates substantially higher cache storage than text, with costs varying by model architecture and retention scenario.
Introduces logical QA evaluation via session prefill plus a separate real-cache replay test for numerical equivalence and runtime cost.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Published system-level comparisons under two different benchmarks and source evaluation protocols: (a) LongMemEval’s 97-question subset with 3–6-session histories [1, Fig. 4a]; (b) LoCoMo J scores from Mem0’s vendor-authored evaluation [2]. Full-history reading scores highest among the selected systems shown in each panel, not across all evidence. Zep’s separate vendor-reported LongMemEval-S comparison favours its retrieval system over a full-context baseline averaging about 115K tokens and is not plotted here (§3.2, §8.1). These comparisons do not isolate a memory mechanism, and scores depend on evaluation labels and judges (§9.1). L1–L4 are our descriptive memory modes; KV-LTM has no measured accuracy bar (§8). Costs are modelled separately (§7).

Figure 2: KV-LTM write flow (once per session): canonical per-session prefill creates the stored state at session end; session text, metadata with integrity digests, and native reader state are retained under the §4.8 storage and latency policy, which may evict or invalidate state — the text is always kept. Boxes denote logical steps or stored objects, not software components.

MLA values assume compressed-latent storage. Kimi-Linear shows only its MLA-layer component (bMLA = 8,064 B/token); its per-session recurrent state is symbolic and not drawn. The plotted per-token spread is ∼40× (the hybrid’s bMLA part at the low end); among the non-hybrid configs the spread is ≈10.5× (31,104 → 327,680).

Figure 3: KV-LTM read flow (per question): each retained session’s text is verified against its stored digest first — a known-good copy is recovered and re-verified on failure, and an unrecoverable session counts as unavailable (out of coverage), never as evidence. Valid state is read from a request-local working copy; when policy allows, invalid or evicted state is rebuilt from the verified text (§4.3), otherwise the session is counted as not cached and delegated to the §4.8 text fallback, outside the depicted cache-read path. Per-session outputs supply bounded evidence to the aggregator (§4.6); optional hybrid, verifier/reranker and joint-evidence lanes (§4.5, §4.7) complement the reference read. Boxes denote logical steps or stored objects, not software components.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes persistent per-session KV caches as long-term memory for LLM assistants, directly addressing LLM memory and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
papers.tldr: KV-LTM proposes storing each conversation session’s raw text and model KV cache to preserve long-term memory while accelerating future question answering without recomputation.

papers.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

papers.abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.
authors: Hsiang-Hung Lee
bullets: Zero-shot image-level detection is strong on MVTec AD but weaker on MVTec AD 2.
The decision head’s routing attention provides poor pixel localization, and hiding image tokens does not change detection.
Backbone attention can indicate defects, but localization depends on question wording and textual context and may fall below chance.
Anomaly location can be recovered through region-specific questions, head retraining, or backbone probing, though none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.
A larger Clef model also produces no useful localization map in its decision head.
papers.selection_reason: Case study of a Qwen-based multimodal decision model and its anomaly localization is relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
papers.tldr: Clef-flash detects industrial image anomalies but its decision head generally does not reliably localize them.

papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.
authors: Yijin Zeng
bullets: Addresses the underuse of CLIP’s semantic text structure in existing few-shot methods.
Projects estimated image prototypes into the text-embedding subspace to reduce the image–text modality gap.
Represents prototypes with a small number of text-embedding coefficients instead of estimating them in the full image space.
Computes coefficients using a Bayesian posterior mean with a prior centered on the original text-embedding coordinates.
Experiments on 12 image-classification benchmarks show significant improvements over existing training-free methods.

papers.abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.
authors: Maor Farid
bullets: Introduces a Three-Clock Dictionary connecting 15 nonlinear-dynamics concepts to transformer layers, training steps, and generated tokens, labeling links as proved, measured, or conjectured.
Develops reduced-order analogies for softmax, gradient descent, loss spikes, attention synchronization, and repetition loops.
Finds that repetition-loop escape in GPT-2 and Pythia follows an Arrhenius-like law, with barriers tied to logit gaps and affected by generation length, temperature, and model size.
Reports that coherent text occurs within a narrow temperature range; training increases layer expansiveness, and a small transformer operates near a multimode stability boundary.
Controllers derived from escape analysis remove repetition loops but do not outperform the best fixed temperature; twelve open problems remain.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Four physical systems and their language-model twins. In each row the mechanical system (left) and the language model (right) look nothing alike, yet they share the term of the governing equation (middle) that produces the behavior; Section 4 derives each correspondence. (a) A mass M on a spring with linear stiffness k1 and cubic stiffness k3, friction coefficient ζ, harmonic forcing of amplitude A and frequency Ω, and white noise ξ of intensity D; with k1 < 0 the potential 1 2k1q 2 + 1 4k3q 4 has two wells. (b) An overdamped particle in a potential well under thermal noise of intensity D, whose escape rate over the barrier ∆U is given by Kramers’ formula equation 6. (c) Metronomes on a board that can roll, which synchronize through the small motion of the board; their phases follow the Kuramoto model equation 4. (d) A well whose depth grows with the time the particle has spent in it and then saturates.

Figure 1: The three clocks of a transformer language model. Clock 1 (blue) iterates the residual update over layers for a fixed input and fixed weights. Clock 2 (green) iterates the optimizer over the weights; it hands its current weights to the model. Clock 3 (orange) iterates sampling: each new token is appended to the context and the whole stack runs again. One tick of clock 3 contains a full run of clock 1, and clock 2 changes the map that both of them iterate. Typical behavior studied on each clock is listed next to it; Table 1 maps it onto dynamical-systems concepts.

Figure 8: Generation as a dynamical system: the same four pictures for a mechanical oscillator and for a language model. Left: the forced double-well Duffing oscillator q̈+0.25q̇−q+q3 = 0.1 cos(1.2τ)+ √ 0.5D ξ(τ), sampled once per time unit, at noise intensities D = 0 (periodic orbit in one well), 0.125 (noisy orbits with hops between the wells) and 2.88 (noise-dominated). Right: GPT-2 continuing one prompt for 576 tokens at T = 0.3 (a loop of period 19), 0.9 (coherent text) and 1.6 (incoherent text); the state is the final hidden state of each token, scaled to unit norm and standardized per feature, after a transient of 64 tokens. (a) Time history of the first coordinate (q, or the first principal coordinate of the hidden state). (b) Its power spectrum (Welch), with the spectral entropy Hs. (c) Phase portrait: (q, q̇), or the first two principal coordinates. (d) Recurrence plot of the full state at a fixed recurrence rate of 5%, with the determinism DET.

Figure 5: Depth as a dynamical system: synchronization of oscillators and clustering of tokens. (a) Kuramoto model equation 4 with n = 60, J = 1.5 and ωi ∼ N (0, 0.32): phases at τ = 0, 3 and 30 (outer to inner ring). (b) Its order parameter ρ = |n−1 ∑ j e iψj |. (c) The attention dynamics on the circle with β = 1 and 60 tokens: the same order parameter, now over layers. (d) GPT-2, measured: order parameter of the residual stream entering each block, ρℓ = ∥n−1 ∑ i x ℓ i/∥xℓi∥∥, for 20 prompts (mean ± one standard deviation). With random weights the tokens synchronize over depth as the idealized model predicts (ρ from 0.19 to 0.80). The trained model starts from aligned embeddings (ρ = 0.81) and stays between 0.76 and 0.87 over the twelve blocks.

Figure 6: Noise-driven escape in a mechanical system and in a language model, on the same axes. (a) An overdamped particle, dq = −U ′(q) dτ + √ 2DdW, in the double well U(q) = (q2 − 1)2/4 with barrier ∆U = 1/4: inverse mean first-passage time from q = −1 to q = +1 (400 particles per noise level) against 1/D, with Kramers’ rate ( √ 2/2π) e−∆U/D. The fitted slope gives ∆U = 0.23. (b) Twelve repetition loops of GPT-2 from Experiment 3: exact probability of leaving the loop during one cycle, computed from the stored logits, against 1/T . At low temperature each curve is a straight line whose slope is the logit gap of the loop, as Proposition 1 predicts (ratio of slope to gap 1.05 to 1.12).

Figure 3: Training as a dynamical system: period two at the edge of stability. (a, b) Gradient descent on the double well L(u) = (u2 − 1)2/4, whose minimum has curvature λ = 2, with ηλ = 2.10 and 2.54: the last 40 iterates lie on a period-2 and a period-4 orbit. (d, e) Their power spectra, with peaks at frequencies 1/2 and 1/4. (c) The one-block transformer of Experiment 2 trained by full-batch gradient descent at η = 0.137, at the edge of stability: training loss over the last 40 steps after removing a slow polynomial trend, in units of 10−5. The loss alternates from step to step. (f) Spectrum of the detrended loss over the last 400 steps: the same peak at 1/2, on top of a low-frequency band from the slow modulation of the oscillation (Section 5.2).

Figure 4: Basins of attraction in a mechanical system and in training. (a, b) Forced double-well Duffing oscillator q̈ + 0.25q̇ − q + q3 = A cos(1.2τ): the attractor reached from each initial condition after 40 forcing periods (blue: right well; orange: left well; gray: motion that keeps visiting both wells). At A = 0.1 the basins are separated by a smooth boundary; at A = 0.25 the boundary is fractal and a region of cross-well motion appears. (c) A one-hidden-layer tanh network (width 16) trained by full-batch gradient descent for 500 steps on eight random points, with separate step sizes for the two layers, following Sohl-Dickstein (2024): blue runs train (darker: lower mean loss), orange runs diverge (lighter: later divergence). (d) Zoom into the box in (c).

Figure 9: The reduced-order model of loop escape against the full computation. (a) Smallest logit gap of each cycle (dots) along three GPT-2 loops of at least 15 cycles, with the saturating fit of equation 14 (lines). (b) Locking temperature for a horizon of 16 cycles after a burn-in of two cycles, from the reduced model (three numbers per loop read from the greedy run, one attempt number ν per model) against the full computation from all logits, one point per loop. (c) Median locking temperature against the horizon for both models, full (filled) and reduced (open).

Figure 7: Escape over time. (a) Position of an overdamped particle in the double well U(q) = (q2 − 1)2/4 under noise of intensity D = 0.06: long rests near q = ±1 separated by quick hops. (b) GPT-2 continuing one prompt with plain temperature sampling at T = 0.55: at each generated token, the period of the repetition loop the text is in, where a stretch counts as a loop when it repeats at least three times (zero outside a loop). The text enters two loops, stays in each for more than a hundred tokens and leaves both.

Qwen3-0.6B on GSM8K test problems with plain temperature sampling, with thinking (18 problems, 1024-token budget) and without (20 problems, two samples each, 640 tokens). papers.selection_reason: Analyzes LLM training and generation through nonlinear dynamics; relevant to LLM architecture and behavior.
papers.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
papers.tldr: This paper frames language models through nonlinear dynamics across three timescales—depth, training, and generation—and validates several resulting explanations experimentally.

papers.abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.
authors: Hyojung Han
bullets: Packed INT2/INT3 kernels execute natively, but all tested INT2 configurations degenerate during generation.
Module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive, with Korean and reasoning tasks showing different sensitivity patterns.
The final recipe uses 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head.
On the untouched FINAL-81 set, it uses 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory, retains 0.904 Korean teacher-correct accuracy, and reaches a 0.939 TPOT ratio versus BF16.
It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by 1.4 percentage points, though the roles of activation precision and INT8 allocation are not isolated.

papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization for efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.tldr: A deployment-constrained mixed-precision recipe for Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 passes memory, Korean-quality, and latency gates, outperforming NVFP4 W4A4 while revealing major risks in ultra-low-bit quantization and candidate selection.

papers.abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.
authors: Eliza Berman, Rohan Subramanian, Shreya Jha, Lohit Jagarapu, Romain Lopez, Rajesh Ranganath
bullets: Introduces a dataset of PDE solvers represented as code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories.
Uses controlled corruptions and lexical code perturbations to test cross-representation consistency and physical-invalidity detection.
Across eight open-weight models, conflicting evidence causes systematic preferences for certain representations.
Execution improves judgments of physical validity, but some agents identify correctness without finding the underlying causal defect.
Lexical changes in code can affect interpretations of unchanged representations, revealing fragile reconciliation across modalities.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.
authors: Timo Oksanen
bullets: Addresses adapting automatic tractor guidance when the machine or steering actuator changes, without gradient descent or an optimiser.
GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable edited a 253-parameter controller using natural-language guidance and limited simulated feedback.
With simulated feedback, both models repaired a controller trained for another tractor and created a working controller from zero weights; evolution strategy found none from zero.
The generated controllers were sparse and classically cascaded, and all operated the real tractor without intervention with errors comparable in order to pure pursuit.
Gradient descent achieved higher accuracy but required substantially more simulation; unsupported or limited cases include Fable’s occasional success without simulation.

papers.selection_reason: LLMs directly write neural-network weights for a real tractor steering controller, a novel embodied navigation and control contribution.
papers.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
papers.tldr: Large language models can directly write neural-network weights to create or adapt tractor-steering controllers that work in simulation and on a real tractor.

papers.abstract: Mamba models deployed on streaming data, such as limit order book updates, run far past the sequence lengths they were trained on. A guarantee on how much a small change of input can move the hidden state therefore has to hold at every length. The closest existing bound we know of measures the change of the timescale additively, and it grows linearly with the sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. In this paper, we measure the change on a log scale instead. The key observation is that the decay factor of each step then moves by at most a fixed fraction of that step's input weight, so the per-step errors cannot pile up. Using this, we prove that two runs of a selective-scan cell from a common start stay within a bound that holds at every length, shrinks to zero with the size of the change and needs no lower bound on the timescale. We give a construction showing that, for small changes, this bound is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible, and we extend it to the update used in Mamba's released code when the timescale is bounded above. We then evaluate block-level bounds built from the theorem on two small models trained on one day of order book data. With a bounded timescale, a bound built on the existing analysis is tighter than ours for at most the first 8 steps. With Mamba's softplus timescale, whose certified lower bound is as small as $10^{-21}$, it is looser at every length. Our bounds hold for every input to a block, but they remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks find.
authors: Jack Humphries, Daniel Midgley
bullets: Existing additive-timescale bounds can grow linearly with sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero.
Measuring timescale changes logarithmically prevents per-step errors from accumulating and yields a bound valid at every sequence length.
The bound vanishes with the input perturbation and is within about a factor of 2 of optimal for small changes.
The analysis extends to Mamba’s released update when the timescale is bounded above.

On two small order-book models, the new bounds outperform existing analysis beyond 8 steps or at all lengths with softplus timescales, but remain over five orders of magnitude above gradient-attack changes.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical perturbation bounds for selective state space models used in LLMs; relevant to long-context and streaming language models.
papers.title: A Log-Timescale Perturbation Bound for Selective State Space Models at Every Sequence Length
papers.tldr: A log-timescale analysis gives selective state space models a sequence-length-independent perturbation bound without requiring a positive lower bound on the timescale, though the resulting block-level bounds are still very loose in practice.

papers.abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin
bullets: The commitment–verdict gap measures expected remaining change in answer quality and the benefit of stopping immediately.
Accuracy-versus-budget declines are driven mainly by which chains continue running, not by answers deteriorating within those chains.
On MATH-500, continuing from an already-correct commitment lost 3.6 percentage points on average for one evaluated model, with losses concentrated in a few problems.
Across six models on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench, chains still reasoning generally maintained or improved their answers despite declining aggregate accuracy curves.
An oracle stopping rule provided limited gains: up to 1.8 points for the 1.5B model and 2.5 points for the 7B model.

papers.selection_reason: Framework for stopping rules and harmful overthinking in reasoning models; informs efficient inference.
papers.title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
papers.tldr: Final correctness alone cannot detect harmful overthinking; comparing a model’s current commitment with its eventual verdict reveals when continuing reasoning reduces accuracy.

papers.abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.
authors: Jugal Gajjar, Kamalasankari Subramaniakuppusamy
bullets: The study tests whether answers depend on the regions models cite in their reasoning chains.
It blacks out cited boxes and compares answer flips with same-sized control boxes elsewhere in the frames; the difference is the cite gap.
On CLEVRER, the cite gap was 0.089, with cited-box masking flipping 2.2× as many correct answers as controls.
On NExT-QA, the cite gap was 0.003 and cited-box masking caused only 1.1× as many flips; cited entities remained visible across most frames.
Grounding checks alone miss this distinction: citations can be verifiable and relevant without being causally necessary for the answer.

papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual intervention test for grounded reasoning chains in video-language models, directly relevant to video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
papers.tldr: A citation can be correctly grounded yet irrelevant to a model’s answer, so grounded reasoning should be tested by removing what the chain names—not just where it points.

papers.abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.
authors: Javad Amirian, Armin Kiani, Lo\"ic Schaeffer, Tim Sprecher, Mohamed Taha, Karthik Yadati
bullets: Addresses the limited environmental and object diversity of imitation-learning data and the scarcity of skilled work in existing egocentric video.
Contains 10,124 hours of 1080p head-mounted video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial data from 12,227 contributors.
Covers 15,548 environments, 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types, and 35 action families; 83% of footage is workplace-based.
Provides 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0.
Measures dataset diversity and discusses collection, curation, privacy, data formats, and properties linked to policy performance; benchmarks are deferred to later releases.

papers.selection_reason: Large-scale egocentric video dataset of skilled work for robot learning.
papers.title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
papers.tldr: HubEgo-100K v1.0 is a large, diverse dataset of real-world egocentric skilled-work videos with synchronized IMU data, designed to support more generalizable robot learning.

papers.abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
authors: Samuel Sch\"onherr, G\"unther Waxenegger-Wilfing, Sascha Ranftl
bullets: Standard PINNs enforce initial and terminal states with weighted penalties, making training sensitive to loss-weight choices.
The method embeds boundary conditions directly into the trajectory representation through a simple transformation.
This converts constrained, multi-objective training into unconstrained single-objective thrust minimization over admissible trajectories.
Numerical experiments show improved convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
The approach leverages the low-dimensional boundary structure of trajectory optimization problems.

papers.selection_reason: Neural trajectory optimization with exact boundary conditions; transferable to learned planning and navigation.
papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for spacecraft trajectory optimization with exact boundary conditions
papers.tldr: A physics-informed neural-network approach reparameterizes spacecraft trajectories so boundary conditions are satisfied exactly, improving optimization stability and accuracy.

papers.abstract: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves $O(\log^2 T)$ expected regret over $T$ interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.
authors: Luca Vignola, Melanie Zeilinger, Bruce D. Lee
bullets: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system.

With positive definite input penalties, certainty-equivalence polylogarithmic regret requires restrictive identifiability of all unknown parameters under optimal feedback; singular penalties relax this requirement.
A certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves O(log^2 T) expected regret whenever controller identifiability holds.
An Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound is established for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails.

For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker condition than knowing the full input matrix and applicable to underactuated systems such as a cart-pole.

papers.selection_reason: Online LQR with polylogarithmic regret, relevant to robot control.
papers.title: Polylogarithmic Regret via Certainty Equivalence in Degenerate LQR
papers.tldr: For degenerate LQR with singular input penalties, a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short exploration phase achieves O(log^2 T) expected regret under controller identifiability, and this identifiability condition is weaker than in positive-definite-penalty settings.

papers.abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.
authors: Jameson Sandler, Shane Bergsma, Mostafa Elhoushi, Bin Claire Zhang, Gavia Gray, Joel Hestness, Nolan Dey, Ferdinando Fioretto
bullets: Existing feature encoders can distort target features, forget rejected proposals, and overlook important target hidden states.
DNeo introduces Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA) with working memory for previously rejected proposals.
It further uses 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target-layer selection.
The resulting system reports 1.3× faster generation than DFlash-2 with unchanged drafter footprint and generation quality.

papers.tldr: DNeo improves speculative-diffusion decoding by giving parallel draft models richer, memory-aware target-feature encoding, achieving 1.3× faster generation than DFlash-2 without reducing quality.

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
authors: Katharina Winter, William Engel, Zain A. Alishammat, Fabian B. Flohr
bullets: Addresses the challenge of running autoregressive language generation alongside real-time onboard driving planning.
Uses lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception, spatially structured tokens, and frame-wise scheduling to interleave planning with asynchronous language generation.
Supports trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, navigation instructions, driving explanations, and scene question answering.
Reports 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM, 57.6% nuScenes-QA accuracy, 32.7 ms standalone planning latency, and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline.
Evaluations include public benchmarks, proprietary recordings, and open-loop operation on a research vehicle; the abstract notes both strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

papers.abstract: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.
authors: Tianyi Zhang, Feiying Chen
bullets: The study tests whether models trained to predict every token can answer two-hop questions with unseen intermediate entities.
Standard, looped, and DiscoLoop transformers answer almost none of these questions on a synthetic corpus.
Baton passes the intermediate entity to a second loop as a token embedding; two answer-only variants achieve near-perfect performance.
With next-token training, Baton accuracy initially improves but later declines.
Gradient analysis shows that removing training-set-dependent terms raises peak accuracy but does not prevent the decline, which occurs during the second hop.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
authors: Xin Guo, Qiang Zhang, Xiang Zhou, Arushi Rai, Siyu Lin, Yifan Wu, Xiang Shen, Lei Huang, Qunshu Zhang, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: Repeated profile-text prefills dominate ranking inference because profiles appear after varying prompt prefixes, preventing effective prefix caching.
Lightweight LoRA writers, trained by self-distillation, generate reusable profile KV caches during profile updates.
A KV scheduler overlaps host-to-GPU cache transfers with computation for the next batch.
On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill across memory updates.
Under saturated load, throughput improves 4.0–4.5× for scoring and 1.4–1.9× for profile updates.

papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/
authors: John Hua Yao. Qi Wu, Yihuai Gao, Chelsea Finn, Zipeng Fu
bullets: Collects natural, near-human-speed demonstrations through kinesthetic teaching on a backdrivable bimanual platform.
Uses test-time action smoothing for smoother high-speed policy execution.
Applies masking to align visual data during demonstration collection and deployment.
With 50 demonstrations per task, achieves over 80% success on tasks including ball catching, clothing folding, battery insertion, and table bussing.
Demonstrates performance close to human speed across these bimanual tasks.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.
authors: Wenhe Zhang, Boxing Chen
bullets: Exact-attention analysis shows the main issue is selector mis-ranking of relevant blocks, not exhausting the fixed budget.
A teacher-forced calibration probe identifies heads that attend to the needle but lose it when mean-pooled key summaries dilute its decisive token.
For InfLLM-V2 and NOSA-8B, the same three blind heads explain much of the multi-key retrieval loss; similar patterns appear in several other sparse-attention methods.
Repairing flagged heads with full attention or a 4-bit scorer preserves the shipped budget and recovers most of the loss without training.
Reported gains include MiniCPM4.1-8B improving from 54.1% to 97.5% at 64K, while selective full attention retains 84–89% of sparse attention’s TTFT savings; MoBA shows many more blind heads.

papers.title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: A small number of blind attention heads cause most sparse-attention retrieval failures, and selectively repairing them largely restores full-attention accuracy at much of sparse serving’s speed benefit.

papers.abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.
authors: Yanghong Liu, Yang Chen, Kailang Xu, Bang Du, Feiyang Yang, Jiawei Xia, Zhengtao Yao, Yubiao Zhang, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Ruihai Wu, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses costly robot demonstration collection and the embodiment gap between humans and bimanual dexterous robots.
Uses human-object interactions to select task-relevant robot grasps from geometry-based candidates.
Combines object trajectories with relative bimanual wrist trajectories to preserve task structure and coordinated motion.
Adaptively weights object- versus wrist-level guidance according to confidence in video-derived object motion, then refines behavior under robot constraints in simulation.
Evaluates simulation data generation and downstream vision-based diffusion-policy learning on pouring, sweeping, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate-cleaning tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of PriDex. Given a human manipulation video, PriDex reconstructs object motion, relative bimanual wrist motion, interaction regions, and time-varying object-motion confidence, and uses the recovered contact cues to initialize robot-specific grasps. The PPO policy then refines these priors in simulation: reliable object motion provides task-level guidance, while lower-confidence segments allow greater residual adaptation and increased wristmotion guidance. Successful full-episode rollouts under perturbed initial conditions are retained as robot demonstrations and distilled into a vision-based Diffusion Policy for real-robot deployment.

papers.title: From Human Videos to Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Data: Confidence-Guided RL Refinement of Video Priors
