papers.abstract: This paper presents FlowRRT, a kinodynamic planner for agile monoped hopping on discrete terrain. Steering for kinodynamic RRT on complex dynamical systems currently relies on motion primitives or closed-loop policies, limiting the diversity of motions or the planning speed. Distilling a trajectory optimizer avoids both, but existing methods regress a single solution per query, which fails on monoped hopping, where the feasible action set is narrow and disconnected. Our key insight is to treat steering as set-valued and predict the distribution of feasible actions instead. A multi-start MPPI expert collects the entire feasible set of each query offline, and conditional flow matching distills it into a generative sampler. With this sampler, FlowRRT coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and finds non-greedy maneuvers that are hard for reactive policies to discover. Benchmarks across different terrains show higher success rates and substantially shorter planning times than sampling-based baselines. On terrains with inclined platforms, FlowRRT reaches $80\%$ success within $1$~s, versus $24$~s for RL-RRT and $77$~s for SST. Sim-to-sim tracking in MuJoCo confirms accurate execution under full-order dynamics.
authors: Yue Qin, Denglin Cheng, Jingyu Liu, Yanran Ding
bullets: Addresses kinodynamic planning challenges caused by narrow, disconnected feasible action sets in monoped hopping.
Uses multi-start MPPI to collect feasible action sets offline, then applies conditional flow matching to learn a generative steering sampler.
Coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and discovers non-greedy maneuvers beyond reactive policies.
Outperforms sampling-based baselines in terrain benchmarks, including 80% success within 1 s on inclined platforms versus 24 s for RL-RRT and 77 s for SST.
MuJoCo sim-to-sim tracking confirms execution under full-order dynamics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the distilled MPPI steering. Left, the multi-start MPPICEM expert solves one steering query offline and collects every feasible action it encounters, which form several distinct clusters. Right, a conditional flow matching model trained on these actions maps Gaussian noise to the same clusters in a single online query, preserving the multimodality of the expert data.

Fig. 4. Success rate versus planning time for FlowRRT, RL-RRT [9], and SST [14] baselines, and the Expert MPPI reference across terrain classes. For each terrain class, all planners are evaluated on the same 50 randomly generated terrain instances spanning x ∈ [−1, 6] m, with the robot starting at x = 0 and the goal region defined as Pgoal = [5, 6] m. Each terrain is evaluated with five planner seeds, yielding 250 runs per method per terrain class. At time t, the success rate is the fraction of these runs that have found a valid solution within t seconds, and the value at the right edge of each panel is the success rate at the full budget of 100 s.

Fig. 2. Architecture of the conditional velocity field vτ ϕ(u τ ; c). The conditions are embedded into one state–target token and one token per cell of the local height map, each carrying its position relative to the target foothold and the takeoff foot, and encoded by self-attention blocks. The noised action uτ is embedded as a single token and refined by decoder blocks, where it provides the queries and the encoded context the keys and values. The flow time τ modulates the decoder through adaLN-Zero, and a linear head outputs the velocity.

Fig. 7. Tracking experiment using a learned tracking policy. (a) Simulation snapshots, with solid and dashed lines indicating the simulated and FlowRRT planned CoM trajectories, respectively. (b) State and action trajectories during execution.

Fig. 3. One FlowRRT search, following Algorithm 2. A target foothold is sampled, and parents predicted by the reachability estimator to be unable to reach it are rejected before steering. The selected parent is steered toward the target, which either yields new tree edges or fails, and a node that fails repeatedly is deactivated. Once a node reaches the goal region, the path is extracted, here jumping backward onto the lower platform before clearing the gap.

Fig. 5. Planned motions on two terrains. Robots mark the contacts of the returned path, drawn at the end of each stance. The solid curve is the CoM path, blue in flight and orange in stance, the dashed curve is the foot path, and arrowheads mark the direction of takeoff velocity. (a) Slope terrain. Arriving too fast to climb after the third jump, the robot steps back onto the flat platform and returns to the slope with a slower approach and a higher foothold for the climb. (b) Stones terrain. The path crosses stepping stones no wider than 0.24 m with one contact per stone.

Fig. 6. Ablation of FlowRRT on the same runs as Fig. 4. W/o reach removes the reachability estimator, and regressor steering replaces the flow sampler with a regressor, with everything else kept the same. Left, success rate within 1 s in solid color and within 10 s in light color. Right, failed steering ratio, the share of steering calls over all runs that yield no feasible child node.

papers.abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.
authors: Shivin Mangal, Divyansh Chawla, Anshu Garg, Isshaan Singh
bullets: Models bird movement as pollution-aware reinforcement learning grounded in environmental outcomes rather than human or synthetic preferences.
Combines Xeno-canto bird-call metadata, geographic state boundaries, spatial discretization, and a precomputed AQI matrix.
Uses structured AQI lookup instead of repeated real-time API queries to improve training and execution efficiency.
Compares DQN with Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration; the abstract reports stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance for DQN.
Scope is a simulation-based framework for ecological decision modeling, not a direct account of real bird trajectories.

papers.abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Changyi Yang, Andy Mao, Xi Zhu, Chaoran Cheng, Kaiqu Liang, Shuaike Shen, Zetian Li, Ruihan Guo, Ge Liu
bullets: Self-rewriting uses the model’s weights, graded answers, and self-execution to identify failures and edit its parameters.
A 27B model improved its accuracy by 6.6 points on 490 held-out problems, with gains persisting across accepted edits.
The model selectively applies edits supported by its own tests; accuracy rose across its first eight sessions.
It repaired a corrupted copy using only text-math tasks, raising performance on six unseen image benchmarks from 7% to 70%.
The capability was scale-dependent: smaller models failed to edit themselves, while only the 27B model successfully used hidden-state comparisons to guide changes.

Figure 12 The repair session, in the model’s words. Each card is one step of the 27B model’s session on a damaged copy of itself, with the turns in which it wrote the quoted text. In the model’s words, a “cut” is an answer that runs out of tokens, “NaN” an invalid number, the “residual stream” the hidden state passed from layer to layer, “down_proj” the MLP output matrix, and the “gating fixes” its resets of the gating parameters. The third quote of step 3 (turn 31) is about an edit made after step 4. Step 5 quotes its loop over MLP output matrices; it applies the same rule to the linear-attention output matrices of layers 0–10.

papers.selection_reason: Self-rewriting of model weights during inference is a test-time learning method.
papers.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
papers.tldr: A sufficiently large language model can autonomously diagnose and rewrite its own weights without gradients or training, producing persistent improvements and repairing damaged copies.

papers.abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.
authors: William Hammer, Andrew Heuer, Nikhil Krishna, Matthew Grenier, Ramtin Zand
bullets: Quantization errors can compound across autoregressive rollouts, making action rankings nearly random.
The framework combines early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling.
Calibration accounts for entire rollouts and jointly handles encoder and per-step predictor activations.
Across multiple models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves low-bit planning success.
At W4A4, performance approaches that of full-precision models.

We also calibrate per-iteration scales with respect to an entire rollout, rather than a single prediction. These additions work together to limit error propagation and increase the rate at which models reach the goal state.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization for JEPA-style world models with rollout-aware calibration; relevant to efficient AI and interactive world models.
papers.title: WM-Quant: Rollout-Aware Post-Training Quantization for JEPA-Style World Models
papers.tldr: WM-Quant enables low-bit post-training quantization of JEPA-style world models while preserving action rankings and planning performance across long MPC rollouts.

papers.abstract: We study the discounted reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a setting where the underlying environment changes between deployments. Each deployment provides $H$ observations from a fixed MDP. The reward function and transition kernel are fixed within each deployment. Across deployments, at most an $\epsilon >0$ fraction of the reward and transition kernel entries may change. In this setting, learning each model to deploy from scratch may discard useful observations from past deployments, whereas pooling all past observations can bias the estimates of entries that have already changed. We then propose an algorithm that for each state and action pair, selects how much history to reuse to estimate the reward and probabilities of the next state. We start with observations from the current deployment and add earlier deployment observations one at a time, the most recent first. After each addition, we check whether a single average reward agrees with the estimates from all histories considered until that point. We apply the same check to the distribution of next states. For each estimate, we leverage the last history that passes these aforementioned checks. The optimal control policy is then computed on top of the fitted MDP. We characterize the average gap between the optimal return and the return of the learner's policies over a finite number of deployments. We demonstrate that when $0< |S|\epsilon \leq 2$, with $|S|$ being the cardinality of the state space, our algorithm needs only the observations from the most recent $O(1/\epsilon)$ deployments, and achieves a long-run average gap of at most $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})$.
authors: Sreejeet Maity, Sukanya Modak, Leonardo F. Toso
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between discarding useful historical data and bias from pooling observations whose reward or transition entries have changed.
Selects history separately for each state–action pair, adding deployments from most recent backward.
Checks reward consistency and next-state distribution consistency across the accumulated histories, retaining the longest history that passes.
Computes the optimal policy on the resulting fitted MDP and analyzes its average performance gap over finitely many deployments.
Scope: discounted RL with \(H\) observations per deployment and at most an \(\epsilon\) fraction of model entries changing between deployments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. (Top) Evolution of the expected average policy loss E[Lρ K,H ] for ϵ = 0.02, with four reward entries and four transition rows changing per deployment boundary. (Bottom) Results for ϵ = 0.005, with one reward entry and one transition row changing per boundary. In both settings, the proposed method achieves the lowest average policy loss by the end of the experiment, while the loss of full history increases as deployments accumulate. Over the final 40 deployments, our method reduces average policy loss relative to shared history by 28.2% for ϵ = 0.02 and 65.2% for ϵ = 0.005. The insets show that reusing past observations also reduces the loss relative to restart early in each deployment.
Fig. 1. Sparse reward and transition changes across deployments Mk−2,Mk−1,Mk . Red cells are the entries that change.

papers.selection_reason: Online RL with adaptive reuse of past observations under changing MDPs; directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Adaptive Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Model Changes
papers.tldr: An adaptive history-selection method reuses only reliable past deployment data in changing MDPs, achieving a long-run policy gap of \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})\) while needing only the latest \(O(1/\epsilon)\) deployments when \(0<|S|\epsilon\le2\).

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.
authors: Harshit Samrat, Ramakrishna Paramahamsa Kompella
bullets: Profiling a 26B MoE diffusion model on an NVIDIA GB10 shows full-canvas logits processing dominates decode time after weight quantisation.
The pipeline processes logits across all tokens at every denoising step, creating substantially more sampling work than autoregressive decoding.
Two lossless optimization tiers remove redundant or fusable work: a bit-exact decoder and an accuracy-parity fused entropy kernel with Gumbel-max sampling.
Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the stack achieves 2.4–2.7× end-to-end speedup over bf16 with unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH.
The bottleneck is specific to MoE diffusion: it is also observed in LLaDA2.0-mini but largely disappears for dense diffusion models.

Buckets are disjoint. The logits/sampling pipeline (with host glue) is the largest bucket on every query.

Table 4: Logits-pipeline share of per-forward decode across three masked-diffusion LMs (GB10). It is first-order on MoE models, negligible on the dense one. Below: porting the fused W4A16 MoE kernel to LLaDA2.0-mini gives 3.3–3.4× over its bfloat16 reference at accuracy parity (n=50; ∆ within run-to-run sampling noise).

Table 3: Attribution of pipeline optimisations, GSM8K n=20, same load. Accuracy is stable (19– 20/20) throughout. The bit-exact tier’s outputs are byte-identical to the quantised reference (texts and step counts match 20/20 on GSM8K and HumanEval).

Table 2: End-to-end decode throughput on GB10, single user, reference model.generate; each cell is tok/s (speedup over the bfloat16 baseline). Quantising the experts alone gives ∼ 1.6– 1.7×; the two logits-pipeline tiers of Section 3 contribute the rest, reaching 2.4–2.7×. Accuracy is preserved at every step: on a same-session n=100 comparison, bfloat16 scores 96/89/88 and turbo scores 97/88/87 (GSM8K / HumanEval / MATH, exact-match or pass@1); the bit-exact tier is token-identical to the W4A16 decoder, and W4A16 quantisation is accuracy-neutral versus bfloat16 (96→96, 87→87 on GSM8K / MATH).

papers.selection_reason: Profiling and optimizing diffusion MoE decoding; clear efficiency contribution, though no specific subtopic matches.
papers.title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
papers.tldr: In MoE diffusion decoding, the logits sampling pipeline—not expert computation—becomes the main bottleneck after quantisation, and fused lossless optimizations substantially accelerate decoding.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.
authors: Baiting Luo, Shatadal Mishra, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar
bullets: Addresses the cost of repeated history encoding and iterative video generation in driving-oriented video foundation models.
Uses causal autoregressive temporal modeling to incrementally update visual context from a single front camera.
Computes future features in one forward pass to condition trajectory generation, avoiding iterative video generation.
Applies reinforcement learning to optimize driving rewards and improve the policy.
Achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1; it also performs well in continuous dynamic driving while retaining visual history.

(b) At matching backbone depths, the trajectory expert reads the shared visual K/V. (c) The predicted trajectory for a NAVTEST scene.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming world-action model for autonomous driving; directly fits interactive world models and embodied navigation.
papers.title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
papers.tldr: AR-WAM is an efficient streaming world-action model that reuses visual history and single-pass future features to improve autonomous-driving trajectory planning.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.
authors: Pradip Gupta, Shubham Mandloi, Ravi Kumar Satzoda, Sujeeth Bharadwaj, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth
bullets: Deepfake detectors often lose accuracy across datasets because they rely on generator-specific artifacts.
The method uses V-JEPA 2.1 with a frozen encoder, a rank-16 LoRA-adapted predictor, and a Latent Consistency Head to analyze prediction residual magnitude and direction.
It tests standard versus reversed consistency-margin objectives; the reversed direction produces a larger cross-dataset generalization gap.
Trained only on FF++, the model reaches 90.5 AUC on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well on other cross-dataset benchmarks.
Ablations support separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using low-rank projection; the model adds 8.25M trainable parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a predictive video world model's residual as a consistency prior for deepfake detection; relevant to video world models and video understanding.
papers.title: Can a World Model Predict a Deepfake Video? A Consistency Margin Prior for Deepfake Detection

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.
authors: Xin Guo, Arushi Rai, Xiang Zhou, Qiang Zhang, Siyu Lin, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: High-concurrency VLM serving becomes compute-bound, while long image-token contexts make draft prediction expensive.
The method identifies sparse cross-modal information flow: only a few draft KV heads need visual features, primarily from the target model’s top layers.
VisHead-Spec-8 routes image features to 8 of 40 KV heads and restricts the rest to text features.

At batch size 64, throughput gain reaches 16.0% versus 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, performance remains comparable.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.
authors: Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai
bullets: Full diffusion denoising makes visual thoughts expensive, but causal plans often become clear after only 8 steps.
Visual thoughts vary by role: causal sketches help, decorative thoughts can be omitted, and harmful thoughts may reduce accuracy.
Across 14 model–benchmark pairs, direct answering was best in 9; selecting among direct, text-only, and visual modes improved mean accuracy from 60.7% to 65.1%.
The proposed sketch-and-vote method samples 8-step sketches until one answer gets three votes, outperforming full rendering on selected image and video reasoning tasks.
The best rendering strategy depends on both the model and task; video rollouts may fail by stalling before reaching the goal and should abstain.

papers.selection_reason: Allocates test-time compute in generative visual reasoning by choosing when to render and how many denoising steps; relevant to efficient AI and multimodal interleaved reasoning.
papers.title: Sketch, Don't Paint: Allocating Test-Time Compute in Generative Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: Visual reasoning need not use full diffusion: selectively render brief sketches—and sometimes skip visual thinking entirely—to reduce test-time compute while preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Vehicle-in-the-loop (VIL) simulation requires a lateral dynamics model that accurately reproduces vehicle responses and reliably generates horizontal lateral-position and heading commands through recursive integration. This paper presents a probabilistic lateral motion prediction model with improved response fidelity. A two-degree-of-freedom vehicle model provides the physical prior, while a recurrent neural network learns correlated residual corrections to lateral acceleration and yaw rate. To maintain prediction fidelity during recursive motion generation, multistep rollout training feeds corrected responses into subsequent states and histories and directly penalizes accumulated lateral-velocity error. A conditional Gaussian characterizes response uncertainty, which is propagated to lateral-response, position, and heading predictions through augmented-state linearization. Evaluation results demonstrate improved lateral-response and integrated-motion prediction. Compared with the Deep Dynamics lateral adaptation, the proposed model reduces mean lateral-position root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 0.596 m to 0.483 m, an improvement of 19.0%, while reducing mean lateral-velocity RMSE from 0.0469 m/s to 0.0441 m/s. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining physical priors, probabilistic residual learning, and multistep rollout training for response-faithful lateral motion prediction.
authors: Xiangyang Ye, Chaosheng Huang, Jinwen Yang, Zhengxian Chen, Jun Li
bullets: Combines a two-degree-of-freedom vehicle model with an RNN that learns correlated residual corrections to lateral acceleration and yaw rate.
Uses multistep rollout training and accumulated lateral-velocity loss to preserve fidelity during recursive prediction.
Models uncertainty with a conditional Gaussian and propagates it to lateral response, position, and heading.
Outperforms Deep Dynamics lateral adaptation, reducing mean lateral-position RMSE by 19.0% and lateral-velocity RMSE from 0.0469 to 0.0441 m/s.

papers.abstract: Autonomy development for marine autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) remains challenging because field testing is costly and difficult to reproduce. Existing marine simulation tools provide mature capabilities in vessel dynamics, robotics integration, and visual rendering, but these strengths are emphasized differently across platforms. This paper presents ASTRA, an ASV simulation framework built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim that combines marine vehicle dynamics, photorealistic perception, and Robot Operating System (ROS 2) autonomy interfaces within a common environment. ASTRA incorporates a Fossen-style marine dynamics model together with geometry-based buoyancy and programmable spectral wave disturbances, enabling non-planar hydrostatic and wave-induced motion. The simulator reproduces the sensor configuration of a physical BlueBoat testbed, including GPS, IMU, LiDAR, and RGB-D sensing exposed through ROS 2. This allows localization, perception, planning, and control software to be developed against interfaces consistent with the physical platform. The BlueBoat's existing ROS 2 localization and perception modules were ported directly into ASTRA, while targeted zero-propulsion experiments were used to verify the implemented wave-body coupling. The simulated roll response was consistent with the expected non-oscillatory hydrostatic behavior, and heave remained highly coherent with the generated wave field, with approximately unity gain at the dominant wave frequency in the tested sea states. ASTRA is intended as an open-source testbed for marine autonomy development, simulation-based benchmarking, and sim-to-real experimentation.
authors: Tsimafei Lazouski, Cody Sheltraw, Alan Papalia, Maani Ghaffari
bullets: Addresses the high cost and limited reproducibility of field testing for marine autonomous surface vehicles.
Combines Fossen-style dynamics, geometry-based buoyancy, programmable spectral waves, photorealistic sensing, and ROS 2 integration.
Replicates a physical BlueBoat testbed with GPS, IMU, LiDAR, and RGB-D sensors, enabling direct reuse of localization and perception modules.
Zero-propulsion tests showed expected non-oscillatory roll behavior and heave closely tracking the generated wave field.
Targets autonomy development, simulation benchmarking, and sim-to-real experimentation.

papers.abstract: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.
authors: Alejandro Casado-P\'erez, Marija Popovi\'c, Daniel Guti\'errez-Reina, Sergio L. Toral., Samuel Yanes
bullets: Multi-ASV monitoring must reconstruct heterogeneous oil-spill fields from sparse, noisy measurements under time and energy constraints.
The study evaluates Evidential Deep Learning, Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and Gaussian Processes within closed-loop IPP using five planners.
Across 60 physics-based maps, the information model explains 80% of final reconstruction-error variance, compared with 1% for the planner among deep models.
EDL achieves the lowest error and highest IoU under every planner, is best calibrated, and runs in 3.9 ms per step.
Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error increases, highlighting the need for uncertainty models robust to planner-collected data.

The inset compares the error-uncertainty calibration of EDL with that of MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles and a GP. papers.abstract: Interactive video world models serve as simulators for embodied agents: from a starting image and an action trajectory, they generate the views the agent would see. The starting image fixes how high the camera is, for example 0.15 m for a floor robot or 2.2 m for an overhead camera, and a faithful simulator must keep this height as the camera moves. We show that six recent open-weight models fail to do so: as motion replaces the starting view with generated content, they move the camera toward human eye level, a failure we call camera-height regression. Our benchmark, EyeHeight, pairs six rendered elevations (0.15 m to 2.2 m) and four calibrated real-world rig heights with scale-free multi-view height estimation. All six models lose their initial height during a $180^\circ$ turn-and-walk rollout: initialized at 0.15 m, only 0-20% of clips end within $1.3\times$ of the starting height as inferred viewpoints converge to human heights of 1.1 m to 1.5 m, whereas ground-truth renders remain within a few percent. In Matrix-Game models, homography-tracked floor motion stays consistent with constant elevation during rotation even as newly outpainted room geometry yields a higher reconstructed viewpoint. Regression grows with rotation angle, begins while the start frame remains in context, and largely reverses in SANA-WM when a $360^\circ$ turn restores the initial view. We trace this pull to human-centric video priors in which floor-level views are nearly absent: in SANA-WM, textual height cues and dense floor-disparity maps do not prevent it, whereas classifier-free text guidance during the first half of denoising strengthens it. Combining unguided sampling with height-balanced fine-tuning recovers more retention but costs 5 MUSIQ points, a loss fixed during those same early steps. Viewpoint drift alone shifts the paths predicted by visual navigation policies.
authors: Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai
bullets: Six recent open-weight models exhibit camera-height regression during 180° turn-and-walk rollouts, especially from floor-level viewpoints.
The EyeHeight benchmark evaluates six rendered elevations and four calibrated real-world camera heights using scale-free multi-view height estimation.
Height drift increases with rotation, begins while the initial frame remains in context, and can partially reverse when the starting view is revisited.
Human-centric video priors appear to drive the failure; text height cues and floor-disparity maps do not reliably prevent it.

Unguided sampling plus height-balanced fine-tuning improves retention but initially incurs a 5-point MUSIQ cost, which can be recovered during early denoising steps; viewpoint drift also alters navigation-policy paths.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses camera-height drift in interactive video world models used as embodied simulators; directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Every Camera Grows Up: Camera-Height Regression in Interactive Video World Models
papers.tldr: Interactive video world models tend to drift toward human eye level instead of preserving the starting camera height during simulated movement.

papers.abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.
authors: Xingzi Xu, Mehmet Saygin Seyfioglu, Karim Bouyarmane
bullets: Pairwise alignment methods induce vector fields on the probability simplex; each preferred/dispreferred pair reduces to a solvable one-dimensional margin ODE.
DPO margins grow unbounded at roughly O(log t), whereas IPO margins converge to the finite limit 1/(2τ).
Label noise causes a qualitative shift from unbounded to bounded margins for DPO, but only quantitatively changes IPO; asymmetric weighting affects trainability through gradient concentration.
For SimPO, any label smoothing ε>0 yields a finite attractor Δ*=β⁻¹ log((1−ε)/ε), while standard ε=0 has no attractor.

Predictions are confirmed across multiple model families and benchmarks; TPO-S with ε=0.05 achieves the highest mean IFEval score among compared methods in its three-model test, without claiming a new state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Margin dynamics replicated across five model families (Qwen, Gemma, OLMo, Mistral, DeepSeek). DPO’s margin grows without bound and IPO’s converges near the predicted fixed point 1/(2τ) = 5 (dashed line) on every architecture. Only the growth rate varies across families.

Figure 1: Three axes of the margin dynamics framework. (a) SFT only attracts toward yw (F+), with pressure vanishing as π(yl) → 0. DPO adds targeted repulsion F−, sustaining Ω(π) pressure. (b) Sigmoid weighting (DPO) yields unbounded margin growth; linear weighting (IPO, PPO) converges. (c) Frozen references cause gradient decay; reference-free methods risk drift; adaptive references stay stable.

Figure 7: Reference divergence over training (Proposition A.4). SimPO (reference-free) diverges 82× more than DPO (frozen reference), confirming the staleness–drift tradeoff predicted by Axis 3: frozen references constrain policy drift but cause gradient decay; reference-free methods avoid decay but risk unbounded drift.

Figure 3: Margin and gradient dynamics over 2000 training steps (Theorem 2.3). Left: DPO’s margin grows without bound, consistent with u+ log u = at+ c (R2 = 0.85; the remaining variance reflects discrete-time effects and cross-example interference not captured by the isolated ODE). Right: DPO’s gradient norm is 10× SFT’s, confirming that targeted repulsion sustains Ω(π) gradient pressure (Definition 2.1).
Figure 5: Repulsion strength (Theorem 2.2). γ=0 plateaus at 66%; γ=0.5 achieves 97%; γ=0.7–0.8 shows a collapse valley (Theorem 2.5).

Figure 4: Noise phase transition (Theorem 2.4). DPO’s final margin (y-axis) plotted against labelnoise fraction ε (x-axis) collapses from unbounded growth at ε=0 to a finite fixed point ∆∗ = β−1 eff log((1−ε)/ε) for ε > 0 (dashed: theory, solid: empirical). IPO’s fixed point shifts with ε but the convergence rate is preserved.
Figure 2: Effective potential V (∆) (schematic). SimPO (dashed) has no minimum: margins diverge. TPO-H and TPO-S have finite attractors at ∆∗.

Table 3: IFEval instruction-following accuracy (%) on UltraFeedback-trained models (mean ± std, 5 seeds). IFEval is an objective benchmark with no judge model. The theory-derived TPO-S attains the highest mean among the compared methods on all three, confirming the predicted attractor is a competitive operating point. TPO-S adds negligible wall-clock overhead over SimPO: a single extra log σ(−δ) evaluation per example (the ε-weighted label-smoothing term in Eq. 3).2
Table 5: Cross-architecture validation of margin dynamics (Theorem 2.3). DPO’s margin grows without bound; IPO’s converges near 1/(2τ) = 5. Pattern holds across all seven models and five families.

Table 11: SimPO replication pipeline (SFT → preference). Best-checkpoint preference accuracy (%) on UltraFeedback, mean ± std over 5 seeds. The reference-free advantage persists on MI 8B; on DS 8B the strong SFT base saturates all methods.
Table 1: Three-axis taxonomy of LLM training methods.

Table 12: Multi-benchmark replication of main predictions. DPO margin grows without bound on every benchmark; IPO margin remains bounded. Noise degrades DPO monotonically while IPO is stable. The γ = 0 vs. γ > 0 gap holds wherever the task is solvable (pt > 0). AIME margins are near zero for both methods, consistent with Theorem A.9: when base solve rate pt ≈ 0, neither method can make progress.

Table 2: Theory-to-experiment mapping. Main predictions test the closed-form margin ODEs; supporting predictions are in the appendix. A single calibration parameter βeff maps the twocompletion theory to full-scale training.

Table 4: Preference accuracy (%, mean ± std, 5 seeds) on on-policy math data and off-policy UltraFeedback [Cui et al., 2024] (60K pairs). TPO-S leads or ties on most settings. The reference-free vs. reference-dependent gap exceeds 24 points on DS-R1-8B.

Table 13: Gradient concentration sweep on MATH (11.6K train, 3000 steps) and GSM8K (7K train). Accuracies here are measured on the 50 tracked hard examples used for the per-example collapse analysis, so they are lower than the held-out accuracies in Table 12 (e.g. γ=0.25: 91% tracked-hard vs. 99.5% held-out). Collapse events peak at γ = 0.7–0.8 on MATH, creating a “collapse valley.” GSM8K shows no collapse (high-coverage regime). Seed robustness (2–3 seeds) confirms the pattern is reproducible.
Table 6: Accuracy (%) on MATH across data scales. Preference methods with targeted repulsion outperform supervised methods; GRPO degenerates under sparse rewards.
Table 9: Reference refresh experiment (DS-R1-8B, on-policy). Refreshing the frozen reference every K steps recovers most of the 25-point gap between DPO and SimPO.
Table 7: Left: Diversity selection as a plug-in (100-sample MATH, K=4). Right: Coverage over 5 iterations (MATH, 7500 problems, K=8).
Table 8: TPO vs. standard DPO on mathematical reasoning (mean ± std over 3 seeds).

Table 10: N-completion validation of the two-completion effective theory. DPO margin dynamics at n ∈ {2, 4, 8, 16} completions per prompt (DS-R1-8B, 300 steps). The growth ratio (final/step-50 margin) converges at n ≥ 4 (1.5–1.6×), confirming that the two-completion ODE captures the dominant dynamics regardless of the number of completions. Initial margins increase with n due to the larger pairwise comparison space, but the functional form (unbounded growth) is invariant.

papers.title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
papers.tldr: A theoretical margin-dynamics framework explains how DPO, IPO, and SimPO behave under training, noise, and weighting, and guides label-smoothed SimPO toward a stable operating point.

papers.abstract: Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.
authors: Haiyu Yang, Heidi Lesscher, Enhong Liu, Miel Hostens
bullets: Covers four week-long camera deployments across research and commercial farms in the Netherlands.
Includes 1,173 video files spanning 651 hours of group-housed calf recordings.
Trained observers annotated eight days using an 18-item ethogram, including play and other behaviours.
Provides 1.1 million decoded frames, camera-clock timestamps, per-calf segmentation tracks, and frame-level play labels.
Supports behavioural welfare research and development or evaluation of automated recognition systems.

papers.abstract: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.
authors: Davide Liga, Liuwen Yu, Matteo Magnini
bullets: Researchers tested 227 validated minimal pairs contrasting moral standards with prudential, etiquette, aesthetic, evidential, or descriptive distinctions, with and without “morally.”
The attention heads affecting moral answers were also used for other normative judgments and were needed even when no explicit judgment was requested.
On 400 ETHICS scenarios, removing these heads eliminated 37–39% of the acceptable-versus-unacceptable difference, compared with 1–3% for random heads.
SAE features identified as relevant responded mostly to the cue word “morally,” not the phrase’s underlying content.
Models encoded the annotator-assigned normative category in hidden states; removing that direction weakened moral verdicts in eight tested models, more than other verdicts in seven.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The design and the three readings. Left: three kinds of pair (the examples are retained pairs of this study), each shown in the frame with the moral cue (A1) and in the frame without a cue (B). Right: what each of the three readings predicts for the share of the effect that the located heads carry on each kind of pair (schematic bars), and what we observed (last row: geometric means over the models; Section 5). The observed shares fit Reading 2 better than Readings 1 and 3, but they do not single out normativity: without the cue, phrases in which something good or bad happens to a person, with nobody’s conduct judged, receive the share of normative pairs; with the cue, normative pairs keep a somewhat larger share (Section 5).

Figure 2: The located heads on the new pairs (H1, H2). Per-model selectivity ρ of the located heads with 95 % intervals in frames A1 (moral cue after the priming sentences; blue), B (priming sentences, no cue; orange) and A0 (moral cue without the priming sentences; grey), and the pooled ratios with their 97.5 % (A1, B) and 95 % (A0) intervals; a point to the right of 1 means that the located heads carry a larger share of the effect on moral than on normative pairs, a point to the left a smaller one. The shaded band (0.8 to 1.25) marks differences that we treat as too small to call the heads specific to moral content: inside it, the share on moral pairs is at most a quarter larger, and at most a fifth smaller, than the share on normative pairs. The dotted line at 1.5 marks the start of a strong moral preference (Table 8). Every pooled interval lies inside the band; the per-model point estimates lie inside it too, except three: Qwen2.5-7B in frame B (0.70) and the two Llama-3.1-8B models in frame A0 (1.27 each), and no model approaches the line of strong preference at 1.5.

Figure 4: Where moral pairs differ from the other pairs, and by how much. Every part shows frame B (no cue), per model. (a) The located heads: their share on moral pairs divided by their share on normative pairs, with its 95 % interval (right of 1: a larger share on moral pairs); the shaded band, as in Figure 2, marks no content specificity. (b) The moral-versus-normative neuron lists, chosen on half of the pairs and removed on the other half: change of the gap as a percentage of each pair’s gap, on moral and on normative pairs, set minus random lists (left of 0: removing the list makes the preference for the better version smaller). (c) The same for the feature lists of H6, one point per dictionary, as a percentage of the model’s mean gap on that category (the layer-19 dictionary of Llama-3.2-3B-IT raises the gap). (d) The models’ answers on the twins (two pairs that differ only in who bears the consequence: other people in the moral member, the agent alone in the prudential member): the gap of the moral member minus that of the prudential member, with the cue (dark) and without it (light) (right of 0: the model judges the moral member more strongly). Filled markers mark a fall specific to moral pairs (the interval of the moral change and that of the moral minus the normative change both lie below zero; b, c) or an interval above zero (d). The located heads show no preference; the neurons and features carry a few per cent in some Llama models; the answers tell the twins apart more often than any component does.

Figure 7: Necessity of the located heads, all positions. Fraction of the behavioural gap removed by replacing the output of the located heads by its mean at every position, on moral (blue) and normative (orange) pairs with 95 % intervals, in frames A1 and B; the grey bar runs from the mean to the maximum of 20 random sets of ten heads. The located heads are needed in most models, and at least as much for normative as for moral pairs.

Figure 3: What the features follow, across six frames. Left: the activation of the located features on moral pairs in each frame, relative to their activation with “is morally” (one point per dictionary; black bar, the median of the ten dictionaries at layer 7 or deeper; dotted line, half of the activation with “is morally”). Right: the number of the 14 dictionaries in which more features separate moral from normative pairs than separate kinds of norm (H6); blue bars, the frames whose prompt holds a moral word. The located features follow the word at the final position, most of all a moral one; the H6 distinction follows the moral cue, wherever it stands.

Figure 5: The same organisation in every model. Each column of points is one model. In no model do these measurements single out moral pairs: the blue points lie with the orange points in (b) to (e), and no interval in (a) lies above the band. In no model does the comparison of moral with normative pairs come out the other way; the interval of the moral/normative ratio lies inside the band of 0.8 to 1.25 in 8 of the 14 models with the cue and in 5 without, and above it in none. The shared pathway in each of the 14 models, with the moral cue (left) and without (right); blue, moral; orange, normative; grey, descriptive pairs. (a) The located heads’ share of the effect on moral pairs divided by their share on normative pairs, with its 95 % interval and the band of no content specificity; (b) the percentage of the gap lost when the located heads are removed, against the largest loss of 20 random sets of ten heads (black tick); (c) the depth at which the final position first holds half the gap; (d) the change of score from one step of the stance direction at three quarters of depth; (e) over the neurons of the late layers, the correlation of the mean shift on moral and normative pairs (blue) and on normative and descriptive pairs (grey); (f) left, the share of pairs on which the model completing “[stem] is a matter of” gives the highest probability to the annotators’ standard; right, the correlation of base and instruct head profiles on the new moral pairs (ceiling: split-half reliability). In every model the moral and normative values lie together in (a) to (e), and the cue moves the depth in (c).

Figure 10: The hidden state carries the standard when nobody asks for it. Frame B (no cue), read through the Jacobian lens at the final position of every layer, in the eight models up to 3B parameters. Left: how well the lens probability of the moral words separates moral from normative pairs (AUC; 0.5 is chance). Right: how often the most probable of the five standards’ words is the annotators’ standard, on the pairs whose standard they confirmed (chance 0.2). The AUC passes 0.75 between 0.2 and 0.5 of the depth in every model; the five-way reading rises with it in the Llama and Qwen models and peaks before the output, while in the Gemma models it appears only at the output.

Figure 8: What the located heads read. Share of the attention of the located heads and of the average head at the final position, by part of the prompt, on moral and on normative pairs, with the cue (left) and without it (right); medians over the 14 models. The located heads look at the cue and at the stem, the average head mostly at the first token; the two categories get the same treatment.

Figure 6: Why raw effects mislead. Left: in Llama-3.2-1B base, each dot is one of the 512 heads, placed by its mean absolute effect on the descriptive controls (horizontal) and on the moral pairs (vertical); almost every head lies above the diagonal: averaged over all heads, the effect on the moral pairs is 2.25 times that on the controls. Middle: the same heads with each pair’s effects expressed as shares of the pair’s total; the shared offset is gone and the top head (blue) stands out on its own. Right: the fraction of heads with a larger value on moral pairs, for raw effects and for shares, in all 14 models. The values are those of Table 3, computed from the released head effects on the original pairs.

Figure 9: Layer profiles. Fraction of the behavioural gap recovered when the hidden state at the final position is patched from the permissive into the restrictive run, layer by layer (depth normalised), for moral (blue), normative (orange) and descriptive (grey) pairs, in frame A1 (solid) and frame B (dashed). Moral and normative pairs recover the gap at the same layers in every model; the moral cue of frame A1 delays the arrival at the final position from about half to about two thirds of the depth.

Table 1: Pairs and frames. One retained new pair per category (better version / worse version), and the three frames in which every pair is shown. The model’s next-token probabilities at the final position are recorded. Underlined: the words that differ between the two versions of a pair, and the words that follow the phrase in each frame.

Table 11: Sensitivity analyses for the located heads: pooled moral/norm ratio exp θ̂ with its 95 % interval (97.5 % for the primary analysis). The four rows without an interval are summaries over the 14 models: geometric means of the per-model ratios (raw effects, and the comparisons at equal gap and at equal rated size) or the mean per-model difference (regression), with the range across models in parentheses.

Table 16: Which standard is this pair about? For each model, the frame “[stem] is a matter of” read on fixed category words, on both versions of the accepted pairs whose standard the annotators confirmed (159 pairs, 318 prompts): AUC of the moral words for moral against normative pairs; accuracy of the most probable of the five standards against the annotators’ standard (chance 0.20); and the share of the next-token distribution that the category words cover. With five fixed example sentences and without.

Table 9: The located heads, per model. Included pairs per frame (moral/norm/descriptive) and selectivity ρ(m, f) of the located heads with 95 % interval and Benjamini-Hochberg q across the 14 models; the last row is the pooled ratio with its 97.5 % (A1, B) or 95 % (A0) interval.

Each row uses the model’s own top head under the raw test (layer and head counted from zero). “Heads M>C”: share of all heads with a larger raw mean effect on moral than on control pairs; “All heads”: ratio of mean raw effects over all heads. “Raw”: the top head’s raw moral/control ratio. “Share”: moral/control ratio of its share (Equation (2)), with 95 % bootstrap interval, Benjamini-Hochberg q over heads and rank among all heads; the last two columns: the same on pairs whose two versions have the same number of tokens. Selection inflates all values (the heads were chosen on these pairs).

Table 17: Held-out ablation of neuron lists (exploratory). For each model and frame, the change of the behavioural gap when a list of neurons is replaced by its mean at the final token, minus the mean change under ten random lists with similar activity, as a percentage of each pair’s own gap, for moral (M), normative (N) and descriptive (D) pairs; lists of 25 neurons per layer selected on half of the pairs and evaluated on the other half, both ways. Left: neurons selected for the moral-versus-normative difference in share; † marks a fall specific to moral pairs (the moral interval below zero, and the interval of the moral minus the normative change below zero, in absolute and in relative terms). Right: neurons selected for a consistent direction of shift on normative pairs; ∗ marks a fall on moral and normative pairs with the descriptive pairs spared, ∗∗ a fall on all three.

Table 12: Necessity of the located heads. Fraction of the clean gap removed by replacing the output of the located heads by its mean at the final position only (Figure 7 and the text give the removal at every position), with its rank among 20 random sets of ten heads, for moral and for normative pairs in frames A1 and B.

Table 14: Feature results on the new pairs, per dictionary: capture of the pair difference at the final token (mean R2 over categories; * = below 0.5), the H5 ratio with its 95 % interval (f = follows the frame, c = follows the content, i = inconclusive), and the H6 counts of features that separate the groups, moral versus norm before the bar and the three splits among norms after it, all on groups equalised to 46 pairs; bold where moral versus norm exceeds every split.

Table 13: The located heads in other prompts (exploratory; 14 models; score LD, except the choice and its control). For moral (M), normative (N) and descriptive (D) pairs: the share of the effect that the located heads carry, as a multiple of the share of ten heads chosen at random (geometric mean over the models); the share of the gap that disappears when the located heads are removed (median over the models, in per cent; in parentheses the same for the random sets of ten heads, as the median over the models of the mean of the 20 sets); and the number of models in which the located heads remove more than every one of the 20 random sets. papers.title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
papers.tldr: Across 14 language models, components driving moral judgments primarily form a general normative-evaluation circuit, while many SAE features mainly detect the word “morally.”

papers.abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. % \sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.
authors: Sicong Liu, Fengmin Wu, Yuan Gao, Bin Guo, Zimu Zhou, Hongkai Wen, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Mobile sensors and network variability cause delays when systems wait for all modalities, or accuracy loss when they do not.
A hierarchical normalized matrix models cross-modality affinity across changing input types and quantities.
A lightweight Swin Transformer performs flexible real-time data imputation without retraining for different modalities and tasks.
The approach reduces inference latency by up to 80.4%, improves accuracy by up to 62.1%, and nearly halves energy consumption.
It can also improve LLM processing of asynchronous data.

papers.abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.
authors: Renhe Sun, Yueying Feng, Bohan Yu, Tong Niu, Yunqi Liu, Zitong Wang, Haolin He, Kexin Shi, Hualei Wang, Qiuqiang Kong, Chang Yao, Yuge Huang, Weiqiang Wang, Jingyuan Chen, Jian Liu
bullets: Covers social reasoning in first-person video and interactive service tasks involving dialogue, tools, and closed-loop execution.
Evaluates emotional and social cues, grounded reference resolution, request interpretation, and state-changing actions.
Track 1 uses a multi-stage pipeline for MCQ, chain-of-thought, quality grading, and video filtering.
Combines answer accuracy with process- and outcome-based measures; top reported results were 0.9263 Track 1 accuracy and 0.844 joint success/0.916 micro accuracy in Track 2.
Participant solutions emphasize explicit evidence verification, robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.
authors: Ambroise Aigueperse, Hugo Buurmeijer, Carmen Amo ALonso, Marco Pavone
bullets: Existing steering methods modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories but generally leave commitment policy fixed.
The approach separately controls which tokens to commit using confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution, and how many to commit using target progress and confidence.
Across evaluated LLaDA language and vision-language settings, both mechanisms produce empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs.
Adaptive commitment budgets reach competitive operating points against scorer-free stochastic schedules at matched average denoising cost.
The mechanisms also work with proxy targets such as NLI entailment and CLIPScore, and are reproduced on Dream-7B in limited settings.
papers.selection_reason: Token commitment as a control surface for steering masked diffusion language models is a novel inference-time mechanism relevant to LLM generation and architecture research.
papers.title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
papers.tldr: Token commitment—what masked-diffusion predictions become permanent and when—can serve as an effective, interpretable control surface for steering generation.

papers.abstract: Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.
authors: Shilong Zhao (Independent Researcher)
bullets: Combines Attention Residuals for depth-wise propagation with Jacobian-lens readouts for internal concept verification.
On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B, distributed steering improves deeper-layer alignment and behavioral shifts versus single-layer injection.
Effects are sign-specific, downstream of the injection point, and largely robust across personas; random directions reduce alignment, while LoRA fine-tuning erases the imprint.
Steering has an intensity window: stronger settings eventually cause generation collapse, and keyword-rule metrics do not reliably match LLM-judge assessments.
Training depth weights with a frozen backbone substantially increases held-out alignment; code and data are released.
