papers.abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.
authors: Eric Zou
bullets: Tests Hoel’s overfitted-brain hypothesis: dream-like distortion may prevent overfitting to recent experiences.
An LLM agent rewrote text memory nightly after simulated conversations, with controlled detail or random-text corruption and memory limits.
Across 30 runs, corruption did not improve transfer of earlier learning to new tasks.
Replacing details in 40% of turns reduced recall from 76% to 60%; the agent answered corrupted-detail questions correctly 40% of the time versus 75% without corruption.
Random text had little consistent effect because the model recognized and excluded it as corrupted; future tests may need a learner less able to detect corruption.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method. Each simulated day adds about 130,000 tokens of conversation. The left panel fits a flexible curve to only these points, and the curve passes through every point and swings between them. papers.tldr: Corrupting an LLM agent’s nightly memory replay did not improve learning and often caused it to store false details as facts.

papers.abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.
authors: Mario Prignano, Gabriele Cirillo, Alessio Morosini, Luca Cerovaz, Alessandro Bartolocci, Emanuele Rodol\`a, Giulio Starace, Francesco Pappone
bullets: Trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a mathematics-focused corpus.
Supports context lengths up to 131k tokens and uses a jointly designed architecture and training recipe for efficient reasoning.
Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR.
Scores 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, according to the report.
Released under Apache 2.0 with model checkpoints and an optimized serving implementation.

papers.abstract: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.
authors: Su Dong, Jiayan Lin, Yujia Liu, Zijin Hong, Qinggang Zhang, Feiran Huang, Xiao Huang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity detection for interactive text-to-SQL under limited dialogue budgets.
Generates contrastive SQL interpretations from query terms and complementary probes, then compares canonical SQL components.
Prioritizes recurring SQL differences as user-facing clarification targets and tracks unresolved dialogue state.
Improves normalized Reward by 4.40–8.97 points and critical-ambiguity coverage to 82.75%–85.14% on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full.
Clarification signals also improve two fixed text-to-SQL systems by up to 13.97 Reward points.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.
authors: Changjiang Jiang, Jiang Zhou, Xinbin Yuan, Fan Zhang, Tao Feng, Zhuohan Xie

papers.abstract: In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4-6.4 times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20-1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.

papers.abstract: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.
authors: Jeonghwan Cho
Minsu Kim
Junyoung Hong
Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Rendered mask supervision can leave occluded or low-contribution Gaussians poorly learned despite accurate 2D masks.
VODA uses local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervise every Gaussian in selected depth clusters.
The authors introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and Removal Depth Error (RDE) to measure volumetric completeness.
Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA improves Removal-3D segmentation while maintaining or improving LERF and ScanNet performance.
Analysis indicates that VODA recovers low-contribution Gaussians more effectively than gradient reweighting or spatial propagation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of VODA. The depth-aware rasterizer groups per-pixel contributors using adjacent depth gaps and selects the cluster with the largest total rendering contribution. Alphaweighted pixel features are aggregated into detached Gaussian-level targets. A direct feature loss supervises every Gaussian in the selected cluster, including low-contribution Gaussians, without contribution-weighted gradient delivery. The baseline feature-rendering loss remains active.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

papers.abstract: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present Déjà-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from Déjà View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

papers.abstract: Existing Large Vision-Language Model benchmarks primarily evaluate visual understanding in general everyday scenarios, leaving historical consistency with a specified era and country largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose AnachroBench, a controlled discriminative benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in visual scenes. It contains 1,600 image pairs from eight countries spanning the late 19th to the early 20th century, each pairing an original historical image with an anachronistic version containing a seamlessly inserted modern object. AnachroBench evaluates three aspects: Inserted Object Perception, which tests whether models detect the inserted modern object; Era-Country Consistency, which assesses whether the scene is consistent with the specified era and country; and Conditional Era-Country Consistency, which measures consistency judgments only when the inserted object is correctly perceived. A false consistency judgment occurs when a model perceives the modern object but still judges the scene as historically consistent. Overall, AnachroBench reveals a gap between inserted object perception and era-country consistency judgments, providing a targeted evaluation of this behavior.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.
authors: Zhen Xu

papers.abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams

papers.abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.
authors: Matthias Jammot
Pembe Gizem Özdil
bullets: Fixed-gain PD control cannot simultaneously optimize motion and contact-force tracking across swing and contact phases.
A reinforcement-learning policy predicts per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements during training.
The policy uses inertia-scaled impedance priors, enabling control across subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric inputs.
Across 129 participants and six activities, it improves kinematic and force fidelity over fixed-gain PD, torque-based, muscle-actuated, and existing imitation controllers.
The learned impedance representation transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot, and generalizes to withheld activities.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it also stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that gain most by storing the order fall behind.

bullets: Addresses a key failure mode of OPSD-trained skills: memorized step order can override what the model actually sees.
Stores pairwise step-order counts outside the VLM and uses them only when one or both queried frames are unavailable.
When both relevant steps are visible, the agent answers from the frames; otherwise, it consults the external prior.
Requires no training beyond standard on-policy self-distillation.

papers.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer others' beliefs, goals, and intentions, is a cornerstone of social intelligence. Multimodal ToM requires inferring an agent's mental state from evidence that is available to that agent, rather than from the complete episode observed by the solver. Existing LLM-based and Bayesian model-based approaches reconstruct global event traces, yet they do not explicitly distinguish objective events from agent-admissible evidence during hypothesis evaluation. Consequently, agent-inaccessible events or semantically misaligned actions and utterances may influence the inferred belief, goal, or social intention, leading to perspective leakage and source or route confusion. We formulate this limitation as an evidence-admissibility problem: evidence should contribute to a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant agent, preserves its information source, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. To operationalize this principle, we propose PIP-ToM, an evidence-admissibility interface that constructs agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process. PIP-ToM with GPT-4o outperforms existing ToM methods across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, achieving average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%, respectively.
authors: Ziqi Liao
Jiaqi Shen
Yiming Na
Kedi Lyu
Shao-Yuan Lo
Hongxia Xie
bullets: Frames perspective leakage and source/route confusion as an evidence-admissibility problem.
Builds agent-specific evidence stores and aligns them with structured mental-state claims.
Calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process.
With GPT-4o, reports strong performance across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, with accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%.

papers.abstract: The goal of Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) is to find a population of high-performing policies that solve a decision-making problem in diverse ways. Despite recent progress, QD-RL methods predominantly rely on evolutionary operators--including black-box optimizers, mutations, and crossovers--to facilitate exploration and induce diversity. Scaling these methods becomes increasingly costly as policies and behavior spaces grow larger. Building on the Soft QD view of quality-diversity optimization, we introduce \textbf{Re}pulsive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (\textbf{RePPO}), which adapts PPO to jointly optimize a compact population of diverse, high-quality policies using a population-dependent, dynamically shaped reward. On standard continuous-control tasks, RePPO achieves a strong quality-diversity tradeoff compared with state-of-the-art QD-RL methods. Ablations further characterize this tradeoff by examining how each component affects individual quality and collective diversity. To assess RePPO's scalability, we extend our evaluation to learning from pixels and fine-tuning large language models. In pixel-based tasks, where large policies make most traditional QD-RL methods infeasible, RePPO maintains quality on par with standard PPO while achieving substantially higher diversity. Its successful application to language model fine-tuning further demonstrates, for the first time, that QD-RL methods can scale to this domain. Together, these results show that directly optimizing compact populations with RePPO provides a scalable approach to QD-RL across increasingly complex domains.
authors: Saeed Hedayatian
Harsh Shah
Celine Mneimneh
Stefanos Nikolaidis
bullets: Targets the scalability and exploration costs of evolutionary Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning.
Adapts PPO with a dynamically shaped, population-dependent reward inspired by the Soft QD framework.
Jointly optimizes a compact policy population for both individual performance and collective behavioral diversity.
Matches standard PPO quality while achieving substantially higher diversity in pixel-based tasks.
Also scales QD-RL to large-language-model fine-tuning, extending evaluation beyond conventional control settings.

papers.abstract: Repeating Transformer layers can improve language-model performance without adding parameters. A pretrained model can be adapted to support both single-pass and looped inference by reusing middle-layer weights for additional computation. Because both paths share weights, training to improve looped predictions can degrade single-pass quality. We study joint training strategies using weighted losses on both outputs, with guidance from the frozen original model. Joint supervision substantially reduces single-pass degradation compared to looped-only training, while preserving looped gains over ordinary continued training. Most of this benefit comes from adjusting the single-pass loss weight, with guidance from the frozen original model further improving the looped output. With validation-selected weights, our method preserves single-pass quality within a predefined tolerance of ordinary continued training while improving looped predictions.
authors: Jiarun Shen
Lei Zhao
Xiao Li
bullets: Layer reuse enables extra looped computation without adding parameters.
Optimizing only looped predictions can harm single-pass performance because both paths share weights.
Weighted losses for both outputs substantially reduce this degradation.
Guidance from the frozen original model further improves looped predictions.
Validation-selected weights keep single-pass quality within a preset tolerance while improving looped predictions.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is a fundamental and safety-critical task in computer vision. Recent generative approaches detect anomalies from a distributional perspective, but remain limited by local anomaly modes. Meanwhile, video anomaly anticipation (VAA), as a proactive extension beyond post-hoc detection, introduces additional challenges. In particular, the contrastive inference paradigm in VAD, which relies on ground-truth frames, is not applicable to VAA, hindering its development. To address these challenges, we propose a unified score-driven framework, termed Uni-DSM, based on denoising score matching (DSM), which models anomaly patterns through likelihood estimation and score functions over the learned data distribution. Within this unified framework, we adopt a shared noise-conditioned score transformer backbone with scene-dependent embeddings and motion-aware weighting for distribution-level modeling. Instead of introducing separate architectures, Uni-DSM unifies VAD and VAA through different inference and supervision paradigms built upon the same score-based formulation. For VAD, we instantiate an autoregressive denoising score matching (ADSM) mechanism, which progressively accumulates anomalous evidence via autoregressive denoising, enabling enhanced perception of local modes beyond visual cues. For VAA, we extend the same architecture by incorporating a lightweight auxiliary decoder and a novel self-distilled denoising score matching (SDSM) mechanism. By constructing supervision from output discrepancies instead of relying on unavailable future ground truth, our method achieves efficient training suitable or early anomaly anticipation. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both VAD and VAA while maintaining high efficiency, establishing a unified and scalable pipeline from anomaly detection to anticipation.

papers.abstract: Inverse rendering decomposes an image into intrinsic properties such as appearance, illumination, geometry, and material, yet these properties are inherently interdependent. A reliable decomposition should produce intrinsic maps that are not only individually plausible, but also mutually compatible in explaining the image. However, existing methods either model intrinsic channels in isolation or treat inverse and forward rendering as separate processes, leaving the interdependence underexploited. In this paper, we introduce IntrinSync, a unified framework that captures this interdependence through joint-channel modeling and reciprocal inverse-forward rendering. At the channel level, we jointly decompose an input RGB into albedo, shading, surface normal, roughness, and metallic maps through a 1-to-N mapping, enabling information exchange across channels throughout generation. At the process level, we establish inverse-forward reciprocity through a dual cycle-consistent objective that aligns corresponding predictions across a closed loop. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that our method achieves competitive intrinsic estimation and forward rendering performance, improving coherence and physical consistency. Beyond decomposition, IntrinSync provides a physically grounded interface for image editing, allowing intrinsic properties to be explicitly manipulated and rendered back into RGB images.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models excel across varied perception tasks, but adapting them to novel downstream settings without sacrificing generalization remains non-trivial. Existing parameter-efficient prompt learning method often yields inconsistent representations and fails to account for semantic distribution shifts. In this work, we present DiscoVL, a disentangled cross-modal representation learning framework that couples orthogonal adversarial regularization with structured cross-modal alignment for vision-language models. To address the insufficient cross-modal interaction, our DiscoVL designs a multi-branch low-rank residual aligner that decomposes representations into subspaces and enables bidirectional cross-modal feedback between visual and textual streams at each layer. Furthermore, while conventional triplet constraints overfit features to class centroids, we design an orthogonal regularization for adversarial triplet loss, which prevents centroid collapse and substantially boosts generalization. Evaluations on 15 benchmarks demonstrate that DiscoVL delivers consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods for base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset evaluation, and few-shot learning

papers.abstract: Generating high-quality and controllable camera motion is essential for AI-assisted cinematography, video synthesis, and 3D scene understanding. We introduce TKCAM, a Text- and Keyframe-conditioned CAMera-motion synthesis framework based on generative masked modeling. We represent camera dynamics using a 12-dimensional kinematic feature comprising position, velocity, and a continuous rotation representation and discretize them into hierarchical motion tokens via a Residual Vector Quantizer (RVQ). A two-stage masked transformer architecture then learns to reconstruct and refine these tokens, utilizing explicit self- and cross-attention modules for multimodal conditioning. A central feature of our framework is sparse visual keyframe conditioning: users can provide free-form text prompts together with RGB observations at selected timestamps, which provide temporally localized visual guidance for generating coherent in-between trajectories. Furthermore, to advance evaluation standards, we curate RealEstate10K-Cap, a large-scale text-camera dataset, and establish a cross-domain benchmark with a Universal CLaTr Evaluator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TKCAM surpasses recent state-of-the-art baselines on Fréchet distance (FID), text-motion matching scores, and retrieval metrics (R@K), while additional analyses evaluate temporal smoothness and cross-domain generalization. Code and RealEstate10K-Cap dataset are available at https://github.com/linearalgebrayhz/TKCAM.

During training, a masked base transformer predicts masked base-layer tokens conditioned on the text embedding from a frozen T5 encoder and visual tokens extracted by a frozen CLIP encoder, while a masked residual transformer refines higher-level residual tokens conditioned on the previously predicted tokens and the same multimodal context. papers.abstract: Accurate segmentation of thin curvilinear structures is vital for various real-world applications, from vessel analysis to road extraction. Yet their intricate geometry makes even minor pixel-wise errors enough to break the global topology, and this structural fragility turns severe domain shifts into catastrophic failures. The difficulty is most acute under cross-modality gaps, where the imaging process itself differs fundamentally between source and target. While test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a practical source-free remedy, existing methods adapt feature statistics and confidence, neither of which constrains connectivity, and thus degrade under such extreme gaps. To address this, we propose Skeleton-Guided Progressive Test-Time Adaptation (SGP-TTA). Progressive Batch Normalization (ProgBN) shifts normalization from frozen source statistics toward current target estimates under a sample-count schedule, so that the source-target balance follows the stage of adaptation rather than a fixed coefficient. Consensus Skeleton Recall (CSR) then derives a structural target from geometrically aligned multi-view predictions and updates only the BN affine parameters to preserve connected structures. Extensive experiments show that SGP-TTA consistently outperforms existing TTA methods in topological connectivity, with the largest margins under cross-modality shift. The project page is available at https://boa-jang.github.io/SGP-TTA.

papers.abstract: Audio-driven facial animation underpins real-time avatars, telepresence, and embodied virtual agents. And it must run online: each frame emitted from audio observed up to the current time, at interactive rates. Recent progress is dominated by diffusion models, which need many network evaluations per sample and are therefore a poor fit for streaming. We argue the cost is unnecessary in this domain. Audio-conditioned facial motion occupies a comparatively low-dimensional manifold, a regime where a single-pass GAN suffices. The obstacle is not capacity but stochastic structure. We show that a causal, time-invariant generator driven by i.i.d. noise cannot suppress its output spectrum over a band without collapsing its per-step innovation. We proposed FaceGAN, which dissolved the limitation by shaping the noise pathway acausally. Because the driving noise is synthetic, its future can be sampled now, so the audio-to-expression path stays causal, and the model supports fully causal operation. FaceGAN emits expression and head pose in a single forward pass per frame and matches or outperforms state-of-art approaches in generation quality. Being feed-forward with bounded attention windows, it generates indefinitely without drift.

papers.abstract: Procrustes-Wasserstein alignment jointly estimates a matching and rotation without supplied correspondences, but alternating minimization can stop at suboptimal solutions. Rubix solves the equally weighted planar problem globally under squared Euclidean loss. Each matching $σ$ of two centered $n$-point sets defines a complex correlation $z_σ=\sum_i\bar x_i y_{σ(i)}$. Their convex hull is the permutation polygon: supporting vertices give optimal matchings at fixed rotations, and the farthest vertex gives the global alignment. We prove the sharp bound of $n(n-1)$ vertices for $n\ge2$, answering Rote's rotation-assignment open problem. In exact arithmetic, assignment queries recover the polygon in $\mathcal O(n^5)$ operations. Assignment-based bounds extend the approach to three-dimensional rotations and partial matching at a supplied translation through branch-and-bound. On timed MPEG-7 shape pairs, Rubix attains every numerical reference value in 12 ms on average, 50 times faster than a rotation grid at the same accuracy. Its distances improve gravity-aligned matching of real 3D scans, shape retrieval and noisy crystal classification over alternating minimization.

On timed MPEG-7 pairs, reaches all numerical reference values in 12 ms on average—50× faster than an equally accurate rotation grid—and improves several downstream matching tasks over alternating minimization.

(c) Four defective lattice neighborhoods aligned by penalized partial Rubix to their nearest defect-free references, all correctly classified. Observations are rings, central sites cross-hairs, and reference atoms bonded. Matched reference atoms are solid, vacancies hollow and interstitials crossed (Section 8.3).

Figure A.7: Gravity-aligned registration of ETH scans. Office scans 1–2 (a,b; ceiling removed) and Courtyard scans 3–4 (c,d), before and after registration with the nominal vertical of the scanner as the gravity direction. All four solvers return the same pose. Relative to the independent-edge bound, Rubix reduces the time of the complete pipeline from 267 to 177ms and from 393 to 182ms; the rotation and translation errors are 0.546◦ and 0.124m for Office and 0.047◦ and 0.029m for Courtyard. Each row uses one viewpoint, one scale and one set of displayed points, and the projected scale bars are in meters. The two pairs are selected among the successful ones; Table A.18 reports all six.

Figure 2: Rubix on an exact six-point example. (a) The permutation polygon is the convex hull of matching correlations zσ = ∑ i x̄iyσ(i). An assignment query in direction u finds an extreme correlation beyond an unexplored chord (dashed); 36 queries recover all 18 vertices. The farthest vertex z⋆ gives the optimal matching and rotation θ⋆ = −Arg z⋆; AM stops at zAM. (b) The objective J(θ) = minσ{S − 2Re(eiθzσ)}/n over one turn, where S = ∑ i |xi|2 + ∑ j |yj | 2. Each smooth piece belongs to one polygon vertex. AM (orange) reaches a local minimum; dashed arrows join its reassigned iterates. The global minimum is blue. Rubix never samples this illustrative landscape. (c) Fixed X and rotated Y at the initial pose, AM fixed point and global optimum, each with its minimizing matching, in a common frame and scale.

Figure 4: Gravity reduces 3D alignment to a bounded yaw search. A nine-point complete-matching example. (a) Gravity directions gx, gy give leveling rotations Ax, Ay, leaving yaw θ about e3; heights (stems) remain in every edge cost. (b) Rubix bounds the blue arc from u− to u+ on u(θ) = (cos θ, sin θ) by querying its endpoints and tangent intersection uA. (c) The affine interpolant stays below the residual, nearly reaching its minimum (2.734 versus 2.765); the minimum vertex value (1.458) and independent-edge bound (1.547) are looser. (d) Algorithm 2 prunes arcs whose bound reaches incumbent U and refines the rest. Nine evaluations close the gap at 48.2◦. Residuals are summed squared errors. Partial matching fixes translation or uses Section 7.2.

Figure A.4: Unbalanced alignment across all conditions. (a) Rotations recovered within 5◦ against the shared fraction, over 200 synthetic tests per fraction. (b) Lattice 1-NN accuracy against the defect rate at thermal noise 0.08. (c) Pose success on the 212 laser-scan configurations with a reference. The settings are validation-selected in (a,b); the GW pipelines use their best test setting in (c).

Figure 3: A fixed phase budget bounds the number of matching changes (n = 7). (a) While one matching stays optimal, the phase Ψ decreases with slope − ( n 2 ) ; when the optimal matching changes, it jumps by ∆Ψ = π(L− 1 + 2I). The number above each jump is ∆Ψ/π. Over one turn, the continuous decrease and the jumps both total 42π. Each jump is at least π, so the 16 polygon vertices of this example satisfy the bound n(n− 1) = 42. (b) The highlighted jump of 6π: its reassignment cycle visits L = 5 points counterclockwise and encloses I = 1 further point (star).

Figure A.3: Fewer classification errors across three polycrystals. The rows show the three scenes, and the columns show the true lattice labels and the predictions with AM (PCA) and with Rubix. Black rings mark errors. Gray atoms are not scored: their neighborhoods cross a grain boundary, or they lie within 3.5 units of the boundary of the domain. Both methods score the same 1,190, 1,071 and 1,006 atoms, drawn at a common physical scale. The errors fall from 285 to 139, from 257 to 149 and from 255 to 179, which is 330 fewer overall; in the first scene, Rubix corrects 186 errors of AM and introduces 40.

Figure 9: Faster yaw search under three matching models. Median times and interquartile ranges over 72 scenes, including unresolved runs: (a) complete matching after centering; (b) prescribed-cardinality and (c) penalized matching at fixed translation. Rubix and the vertex bound close every gap. From coarse to fine targets, the independent-edge bound closes 72, 72, 50 gaps in (a), 72, 72, 67 in (b), and all 72 in (c). At 10−6, paired median vertex/Rubix time ratios are 1.38, 1.35, 1.21.

Figure A.2: MPEG-7 alignment and retrieval. The silhouettes are aligned from 64 boundary points, and the full outlines are shown. (a) Three pairs of the same class aligned to the gray target by AM (PCA, orange) and by Rubix (blue), with the mean squared PW costs J and one scale per class. (b) A selected apple query and its four nearest neighbors in their computed orientations; × marks shapes of other classes. AM and Rubix retrieve 0 of 4 and 4 of 4 same-class neighbors here; Table 4 evaluates all queries.

Figure A.5: Gravity-aligned matching on ETH scans. AM and Rubix start from the same initial yaw on 32-point subsets, with the nominal vertical of the scanner as the gravity direction. From AM to Rubix, the mean squared 3D residual falls from 8.461 to 0.695m2 in the Office example and from 286.3 to 11.805m2 in the Courtyard example. Each row shows every point and every matched edge from one viewpoint and at one scale, with the heights retained. The examples are selected for large errors of AM; Table 8 reports all 96 initializations.

Figure 8: Partial alignments found by Rubix and missed by unbalanced GW. (a) 40-point sets with 30% overlap: targets are rings (shared targets dark); rotated sources are solid when shared. Titles give rotation errors. (b) A noisy square neighborhood (σnoise = 0.08): observed atoms are rings and the site a cross-hair. Each nearest reference is aligned and bonded, solid when matched, hollow otherwise; unmatched observations are crossed. Predicted classes appear below. Balanced Rubix uses 24 atoms. (c) Planar scans, with gray targets and reported pose errors. (d) ETH Office from above, floor/ceiling removed, with gray targets, supplied reference translation and reported yaw errors. Each panel uses the first dataset-ordered case where Rubix succeeds and displayed baselines fail (Appendix F.9).

Figure 5: Bounding rotations through quaternion lifts. (a) An illustrative chart cell q̃ = (1, ξ1, ξ2, ξ3) with ξ1, ξ2, ξ3 ∈ [− 1 2 , 1 2 ]. Its eight raw corners (teal) define the cell, and its central segment ξ1 = ξ2 = 0 (blue) contains the pure yaw rotations. (b) On this yaw section, in the coordinates (Q00 −Q33, 2Q03) of Q = qq⊤ and not of the raw quaternion, the endpoint lifts Q± and the exterior cross lift B−+ enclose the arc of physical rotations (blue). Assignment values at these query matrices bound the correlation score throughout the region. The full three-dimensional construction uses at most 36 queries per box before reuse; the illustrated section uses three.

Figure A.8: Less search inside native GLORES [20]. Scans from the Slippage and Navigation sequences before registration and after fitting with the native bound and with the Rubix bound. J is the sum of squared residuals over the retained points, in m2; hollow points are trimmed (216 of 239 and 220 of 244 points are retained). Both solvers reach the 1% tolerance with equivalent poses. Rubix reduces the nodes from 1,800 to 917 and from 2,650 to 1,170, and the times from 2.85 to 1.96 s and from 3.97 to 2.29 s. Each row uses one display rotation and scale. For each sequence we show the case with the largest objective before registration among those with 256 beams and ρkeep = 0.9 on which both poses succeed; Table 7 covers all 240 configurations.

Figure A.1: Accuracy and computation in planar applications. (a) Fraction of 200 MPEG-7 pairs that attain the numerical reference against mean time, including initialization: AM with 1–100 random starts, grids with 36–1,440 angles, AM (PCA), and Rubix. (b) 1-NN accuracy on noisy lattice neighborhoods; the solver curves and their bands of ±1.96 standard errors use five draws, while GW and the bond-order descriptor use three separate draws (Appendices F.5 and F.6).

The horizontal positions are equally spaced and labeled by the tilt angle; faint points show every error, blue lines the medians and bands the interquartile ranges. (a) Full rotation error, and the median of the floor ∠(R∗ĝy, ĝx) imposed by the constraint (dashed). (b) Translation error after centering, in centimeters. Every fit reaches a gap of 10−6 in the summed squared error.

Figure 11: Rubix closes every spatial-alignment gap. Complete SE(3) alignment with a 15 s limit and mean-squared gap target 10−5. (a) Solved scenes against time. (b) Paired times; points below the diagonal favor Rubix, and triangles mark nine host timeouts whose completion times are unknown. Both variants return identical poses and matchings throughout; total CPU time includes initialization, assignments, bounds and feasible updates.

Figure 10: Witness bounds close more joint yaw–translation gaps. Each curve counts solved scenes out of 24 under (a) prescribed-cardinality and (b) penalized matching, at a summed-squared gap of 10−4. Triangles mark unresolved runs’ last observed times; the dotted line marks 10 s. Full-face closes 20 and 15 gaps, one-assignment 18 and 15, the independent-edge bound 11 and 9, and gated bounds 17 and 15. All 192 runs are included.

(a) Median vertex count (dots) and range across the three families, with the sharp bound n(n− 1) (dashed). (b) Median time per pair for full polygon reconstruction, the pruned Rubix search, a 360-angle grid and AM (PCA). Full reconstruction stops at n = 200.

At a target of 10−5 for the numerical gap in the mean squared error, Rubix closes all three cases, whereas the host with its rotation-cap bounds alone stops above the target in (b,c). Both variants return identical poses and matchings throughout the study.

Bold marks the highest score in each column.

Edge and vertex denote the independent-edge and vertex bounds. Times are medians; ratios are paired baseline/Rubix medians. Totals add identical front-end times. All use 1-NN with ten labeled neighborhoods per class (n = 24, three draws of 200 test neighborhoods). Bold marks the highest accuracy in each column.

GLORES [20] and PLICP [16] use the native C++ implementations of Section 8.4.1; UGW [68] and partial GW [17] run in Python at their best setting on these configurations, with optional refinement by trimmed ICP. papers.selection_reason: Global correspondence-free point set alignment; relevant to 3D geometry perception and registration.
papers.title: Rubix: Global Correspondence-Free Point Set Alignment through Assignment Geometry
papers.tldr: Rubix globally solves correspondence-free planar point-set alignment by converting matching-and-rotation search into geometry of a permutation polygon.
